## Introduction

Fernway HR proposes a short employee pulse survey to be run every six months in an external survey tool. The survey takes about ten minutes and covers four themes: Workload, Manager support, Growth, and Tools and processes. Each theme contains three questions, making twelve questions in total. Statements marked Likert use a five-point scale: Strongly disagree, Disagree, Neutral, Agree, Strongly agree. Multiple-choice questions provide fixed response options within brackets. The design responds to last year’s recurring comments about out-of-hours on-call, unclear promotion criteria, and slow laptop replacements by asking neutral, single-topic questions. The questions are written to avoid double-barrelled items and to ask about one issue at a time. Leadership will receive group-level summaries and recommended next steps, not individual responses. Approval is requested for the wording, response handling, and reporting approach below, so the survey can be administered consistently for two years. The design is deliberately conservative to support safe reporting and useful learning.

## Workload

1. In the last six months, I could complete my core responsibilities during my scheduled working hours. [Likert]
Why: This answer helps HR and the COO decide whether workload is stable enough to maintain current team sizes, or whether capacity planning, recruitment, project sequencing, or workload-balancing actions are needed during the next half-year planning cycle.

2. How often were you contacted for work outside your scheduled working hours? [Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Always] [Multiple choice]
Why: This response guides decisions about on-call expectations, rota design, escalation policies, and whether managers need reminders to respect agreed working boundaries while still supporting customers. It can also show whether the issue is occasional or persistent.

3. Please describe one factor that affects how predictable your workload is. [Open]
Why: HR will group these comments by theme to decide whether to test a pilot such as clearer intake rules, protected focus time, revised sprint planning, or another workload-stability intervention. Responses will be reviewed with operations leads to decide whether a small-scale change is warranted.

## Manager support

4. My manager is available to discuss work priorities when needed. [Likert]
Why: This helps HR and department heads decide whether manager coaching, manager capacity planning, 1:1 cadence guidance, or team-based support tools should be included in the next management development cycle or operational review for people managers.

5. Which best describes how often your manager provides feedback on completed work? [Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Always] [Multiple choice]
Why: The answer informs whether Fernway needs a common feedback framework, manager training on giving and receiving feedback, or guidance about feedback frequency during busy project phases. It also helps distinguish support gaps from workload peaks.

6. Please describe one manager behaviour you would like to see more often or less often. [Open]
Why: HR will summarise these behaviours to decide whether to update manager expectations, add coaching, adjust team practices, or provide resources that improve day-to-day support without singling out individuals. Themes will be reported only when the group threshold is met.

## Growth

7. I understand the criteria used for promotions at Fernway. [Likert]
Why: This informs whether HR should rewrite the career framework, run manager briefings, publish clearer examples, or create a simpler promotion criteria guide that is easier for employees and panels to use. The answer also indicates whether communication rather than policy is the priority.

8. Which area best describes your development need for the next six months? [Technical skills, Project management, Leadership, Commercial skills, Customer-facing skills, Other] [Multiple choice]
Why: The pattern of responses helps HR and learning partners prioritise programs, choose topics, and allocate budget to skills development that supports current business priorities while leaving room for role-specific needs. It also helps decide whether development content is needed at company, department, or role-family level.

9. Please describe one factor that affects your ability to develop at Fernway. [Open]
Why: HR will group these factors to decide whether changes are needed in onboarding, role design, feedback, internal mobility, manager conversations, or promotion transparency. Responses will support the next development review without identifying individuals or small groups.

## Tools and processes

10. The laptop or device issued to me is adequate for my role. [Likert]
Why: This helps IT and Finance decide whether hardware standards are appropriate across roles, whether specific teams need different specs, or whether the refresh policy should be changed to improve reliability and productivity. It also helps identify whether the issue is role-specific or broadly consistent.

11. How long did it take to receive a replacement laptop after you submitted a replacement request? [Less than one week, 1-2 weeks, 3-4 weeks, More than four weeks, I have not requested one] [Multiple choice]
Why: This response will support decisions about IT service levels, procurement steps, stock buffers, and whether slow replacements are a common issue or limited to particular roles, locations, or equipment types. It helps determine whether a policy change, process change, or communication improvement is most appropriate.

12. Please describe one tool or process step that could be changed. [Open]
Why: HR and operations leads will summarise these comments to decide which tool changes, workflow adjustments, or process owners should be addressed in the next six-month improvement plan. Only recurring themes will inform decisions, and they will be reported without individual attribution.

## Anonymity and how results are used

All responses are collected through an external survey tool. Fernway stores no names or email addresses. Results are reported only when a group contains seven or more respondents, reducing the chance that an individual can be identified. Free-text answers are read only by the HR team. HR will summarise recurring themes for leadership and department heads and will not quote comments. Summary findings will be used to shape workload planning, manager support, development programs, and IT or process changes. If a theme is unique to a small group, HR will report it as a broader concern without details that could identify the source. Trends will be compared only across survey periods and only at the group threshold. This approach protects participants while still giving Fernway useful directional evidence. If response volume for a group is too low, HR will combine it with another group where analytically appropriate, or report it at company level.

## How the algorithm works

Dijkstra’s shortest-path algorithm solves the single-source shortest-path problem: given a source node, it finds the shortest distance from that source to every other reachable node. The main idea is greedy: at each step, the algorithm chooses the unsettled node that currently has the smallest tentative distance from the source, declares that distance final, and then uses that node to try to improve the distances to its neighbors.

The algorithm keeps a value usually called `dist[v]`, which is the shortest distance to `v` discovered so far. This value is only tentative until `v` is settled. Initially, `dist[A] = 0` for the source, and every other node has distance `∞`. All nodes start unsettled. A priority queue is used to quickly find the unsettled node with the smallest tentative distance. In many implementations, you can either update a node’s priority using `decrease-key`, or insert a newer better entry and ignore outdated entries later.

The repeated step is:

1. Remove from the priority queue the unsettled node `u` with smallest `dist[u]`.
2. Mark `u` as settled. Its distance is now final.
3. Relax every edge incident to `u`. If there is an edge `u-v` with weight `w`, check whether going through `u` improves `v`:

   \[
   dist[u] + w(u,v) < dist[v]
   \]

   If this is true, update `dist[v]` and record `u` as the predecessor of `v`.

Because the graph is undirected, relaxing “from `u`” means considering all edges touching `u`, not just edges that point out of `u`.

Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights. The reason is that the algorithm finalizes a node as soon as it has the smallest tentative distance among unsettled nodes. If all edge weights are non-negative, then any path from the source to an unsettled node cannot become shorter by traveling through some node with a larger tentative distance. Negative weights break this assumption: a node that was already settled could later be reached through another node plus a negative edge, producing a shorter path. For example, if `C` were settled at distance 2 and later `B` could be reached at distance 4 with a negative edge from `B` back to `C`, the true shortest distance to `C` might become smaller than 2, but Dijkstra would have already stopped improving `C`.

If two nodes ever have the same smallest tentative distance, the rule here is to settle the alphabetically first one.

## The example graph

We use the undirected graph with source `A` and edge weights:

`A-B 4`, `A-C 2`, `B-C 1`, `B-D 5`, `C-D 8`, `C-E 10`, `D-E 2`, `D-F 6`, `E-F 3`

All edge weights are positive distances, so Dijkstra is applicable.

## Step-by-step trace

In the table below, the first row is the initial state. After that, one row records the state after each node is settled and all its incident edges have been relaxed. The entries are tentative distances from `A`.

| Node settled | A | B | C | D | E | F |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Initial state | 0 | ∞ | ∞ | ∞ | ∞ | ∞ |
| A | 0 | 4 | 2 | ∞ | ∞ | ∞ |
| C | 0 | 3 | 2 | 10 | 12 | ∞ |
| B | 0 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 12 | ∞ |
| D | 0 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 10 | 14 |
| E | 0 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 10 | 13 |
| F | 0 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 10 | 13 |

After settling `A`, the algorithm discovers `B = 4` and `C = 2`. Since `C` is smaller, `C` is settled next. When `C` is settled, relaxing `C-B` improves `B`’s already-known distance from `4` to `3`. Then `B` is settled, and relaxing `B-D` improves `D`’s already-known distance from `10` to `8`. Next, `D` is settled, and relaxing `D-E` improves `E`’s already-known distance from `12` to `10`. Finally, `E` is settled, and relaxing `E-F` improves `F`’s already-known distance from `14` to `13`. No tie for the smallest tentative distance occurs during this trace.

## Final distances and paths

| Node | Distance from A | Shortest path |
|---|---:|---|
| A | 0 | A |
| B | 3 | A → C → B |
| C | 2 | A → C |
| D | 8 | A → C → B → D |
| E | 10 | A → C → B → D → E |
| F | 13 | A → C → B → D → E → F |

The shortest path to `D` is not the direct edge `C-D`, because `A → C → B → D` has length `2 + 1 + 5 = 8`, which is better than `A → C → D` with length `2 + 8 = 10`. Similarly, the shortest path to `F` goes through `E`, because reaching `F` through `E` costs `10 + 3 = 13`, while reaching it directly from `D` costs `8 + 6 = 14`.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a node as settled too soon, or popping an outdated priority-queue entry without checking whether it matches the node’s current best distance; Dijkstra is only safe when the node being settled is the current minimum among all unsettled nodes.
- Running Dijkstra on a graph with negative edge weights and expecting it to correct already settled distances; negative edges can make a later path shorter after a node has already been finalized.
- Updating a neighbor’s distance but forgetting to update or store the predecessor pointer, which can produce correct distances while still making it impossible to reconstruct the actual shortest path.

## Situation

Quarry’s proposal is a **12% increase on $240,000**, or **$268,800 per year**, for three years, with the same **50 seats** and next-business-day support. That does not meet our needs: we want **no price increase**, **70 seats**, **4-hour priority response**, and the right to leave after year 2.

We have some leverage. Quarry is pushing multi-year contracts before its **31 May quarter close**, and we can offer a three-year commitment, annual prepayment, a public case study, and reference customer support. However, our BATNA is not powerful: Basalt’s quote is attractive on annual price, but migration cost and operational risk keep us close to renewal. The renewal deadline, 30 June, and our reliance on continuous reporting also limit pressure tactics.

## Our BATNA

Basalt three-year cost including migration:

- Basalt annual fee: **$255,000 × 3 = $765,000**
- Migration cost: **$60,000**
- **Total: $825,000**

Accepting Quarry’s proposal as it stands:

- Renewal price: **$240,000 × 1.12 = $268,800 per year**
- Three-year cost: **$268,800 × 3 = $806,400**

Comparison:

- Basalt is **$18,600 more expensive over three years** than Quarry’s proposal.
- Basalt is a real alternative because its annual fee is lower and migration is not enormous, but it is not dramatically better. The migration delay and reporting-cycle risk make it imperfect. If Basalt’s quote does not include 70 seats or 4-hour support, the gap becomes larger.

## Interests

**Our interests**

- Hold cost as close to $240,000 per year as possible.
- Secure 70 seats now to support hiring.
- Improve incident response to 4 hours for priority issues.
- Keep flexibility to exit or reprice after year 2.
- Avoid migration disruption and protect quarterly reporting.

**Quarry’s interests**

- Sign a multi-year renewal before 31 May to meet fiscal-year targets.
- Lock in three years of committed revenue.
- Improve cash flow, especially if we pay annually in advance.
- Gain a named customer case study and reference calls.
- Avoid churn to Basalt and defend its installed-base account.

Candidly, our strongest pressure point is timing. Our weakest point is that staying put is not obviously expensive enough to justify disruption. We must make Quarry believe the renewal is already “expensive enough” for them to buy upgrades.

## Concessions

| Concession | Given by | Estimated value per year in dollars | When to trade it |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 70 seats included at the negotiated price | Quarry | $96,000 | Open with this demand; do not reduce seats unless they fix price and give exit rights. |
| 4-hour response for priority incidents | Quarry | $40,000 | Early; trade against our three-year commitment and annual prepayment. |
| Right to terminate after year 2 with 60 days’ notice and no penalty | Quarry | $60,000 | Late; trade only for case study, reference work, and prepayment. |
| Three-year committed term with annual renewal mechanics | us | $18,000 | Early, to appeal to their 31 May close pressure. |
| Pay annually in advance | us | $12,000 | Mid-negotiation, if they resist seats or support terms. |
| Public case study and reference calls | us | $8,000 | Final stage, only after price, support, seats, and exit rights are agreed. |

## Opening position

Open with:

- **Price:** $240,000 per year, fixed for the term, no price increase.
- **Seats:** 70 user seats.
- **Support:** 4-hour response for priority incidents, with clear definition of “priority” and an escalation path.
- **Exit terms:** right to terminate after year 2 on 60 days’ written notice, with no termination fee and pro-rata refund of prepaid fees if we exit.
- **Other terms:** no automatic renewal, and seat additions priced on a per-seat basis beyond 70.

Our walk-away point should be disciplined:

- **Do not accept the $268,800 proposal unchanged.** It is worse than our goals and barely better than the Basalt BATNA once migration is considered.
- For the full target package — 70 seats, 4-hour priority response, and year-2 exit — treat **$255,000 per year** as the practical ceiling. Above that, Basalt’s lower annual price plus migration friction becomes too hard to justify.
- If Quarry refuses the 4-hour SLA or the year-2 exit, lower the ceiling to **$245,000 per year**.
- We are willing to use the three-year term, annual prepayment, case study, and references to buy seats, support, and optionality — not to fund a price increase for unchanged service.

## Summary

The external accessibility audit of the Brookmere online shop found 14 issues. Each issue was given an estimate in engineering hours, so this summary groups them by release priority rather than by page or WCAG level. The main concern is that several failures sit in the two most commercially important journeys: checkout and sign-in. If customers with disabilities cannot sign in or complete a purchase, the failure is not just an accessibility problem; it directly affects conversion, support workload and product trust.

For the next release, I recommend fixing Tier 1 first: five checkout and sign-in issues worth 20 hours. These include a payment button that cannot be reached by keyboard, a card number field without a visible label, red-only error messages, address errors without text descriptions, and a five-minute session timeout with no warning. If these are not fixed, some users may be unable to use the shop at all. Tier 2 adds seven other important issues worth 22 hours, and Tier 3 contains two further issues worth 14 hours. Total effort: 56 hours.

## How we prioritised

We prioritised the findings by risk to customers and to the shop, using the audit levels as a starting point. A Level A issue means a basic barrier: someone may be unable to perceive, understand, navigate or operate the site. A Level AA issue is a common accessibility expectation: the site may still be usable for some people, but it is harder than it needs to be.

We then weighted these issues by page. Checkout and sign-in are high-stakes journeys because the user is already trying to complete a purchase or access their account. A barrier there is more damaging than the same barrier on a secondary page. The rule used here is: Tier 1 is any Level A failure on checkout or sign-in; Tier 2 is any other Level A failure, or a Level AA failure on checkout or sign-in; Tier 3 is everything else.

## Tier 1: fix before the next release

- F1 — Labels or Instructions: Shoppers who rely on screen readers, magnification or keyboard-only navigation may not know the card number field is for card details, so they may enter the wrong information or abandon the purchase.
- F2 — Use of Color: People with colour blindness or low vision may not realise a sign-in error occurred because the message is only red, and they may repeatedly submit the same wrong password.
- F3 — Keyboard: Keyboard-only users, including people with motor disabilities or users avoiding a mouse, cannot reach the Place order button, so they cannot complete a purchase.
- F8 — Timing Adjustable: People who type slowly, use speech input, have cognitive disabilities or use mobile devices can be logged out before finishing checkout, losing their entered card and delivery details.
- F11 — Error Identification: Screen reader users, low-vision users and people with cognitive disabilities cannot identify which address field is wrong without text error descriptions, leaving them unable to fix the order.

Tier effort: 20 hours

## Tier 2: fix this quarter

- F4 — Non-text Content: Screen reader users and people using text-only browsing miss the message in the hero image, so they do not get the same home page experience.
- F6 — Focus Visible: Keyboard users cannot see which sign-in field or link is selected after the focus indicator is removed, so they may enter passwords into the wrong box.
- F7 — Bypass Blocks: Keyboard and screen reader users must listen through repeated navigation before reaching search results, which makes repeated searches slow and tiring.
- F9 — Captions: Deaf and hard-of-hearing users cannot understand the product video information without captions, which can affect buying decisions.
- F12 — Link Purpose: Screen reader users and keyboard users cannot tell where “click here” links go because the link text does not describe the destination.
- F13 — Info and Relationships: Screen reader and keyboard users cannot understand the help centre structure or find answers quickly because headings are missing and levels skip.
- F14 — Status Messages: Screen reader users are not told that an item has been added to the basket, so they may think nothing happened and add duplicates.

Tier effort: 22 hours

## Tier 3: schedule in the backlog

- F5 — Contrast: Low-vision users and people in bright light may struggle to read product details because the body text contrast is too low.
- F10 — Reflow: People with low vision, small screens or zoom users cannot read account settings at 320 px without sideways scrolling, which makes personal details hard to review.

Tier effort: 14 hours

## Total effort

Total effort: 56 hours. I suggest starting Tier 1 in this order: first F3, because the Place order button should be reachable by keyboard before the checkout can be called complete; then F1, because the card number field must be clearly identifiable for payment; then F11, because users who make an address mistake need a clear text explanation of what to fix; then F8, because preventing lost checkout data is valuable but can follow the smaller checkout fixes; then F2, as a short sign-in fix that can be bundled nearby. If capacity is tight, start Tier 2 immediately with F14 and F9, because these affect screen-reader users and deaf users in important product journeys.

## The trade-off

CAP theorem talks about distributed systems like your EU and US services. They hold the same data or work, and they stay in sync over the network between regions. If that network breaks, it is a “partition”: the two regions can no longer hear from each other reliably. Each side is alive, but they cannot agree in real time.

A helpful analogy is two ticketing booths at opposite ends of a stadium. If the phone line between them cuts, either one booth stops selling until they can verify with the other, or both keep selling and risk issuing duplicate tickets. CAP formalizes that tension for software.

When that happens, CAP says you have to choose how the system behaves. You can either stop or slow down some requests until the regions can stay consistent. That is choosing consistency. Or you can keep answering requests, knowing the EU and US might temporarily make different decisions and show different values. That is choosing availability. A common misreading is “pick any two” of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. The phrase came from a simplified way of naming three properties, but the useful mental model is not a permanent pick. It is a choice you make operationally when the network behaves badly. A company can choose differently for carts, seats, and likes. In practice, partitions are not optional when you run across regions, so the real choice appears during bad network conditions: be consistent or stay available. On normal days, your systems can be both; CAP is mainly about what happens when a partition hits.

## Scenario 1: Flash-sale shopping cart

During a flash sale, customers add items quickly. The EU and US each accept cart updates locally if the link between them fails. Under the consistency choice, when the regions cannot talk, the cart might refuse to add a new item, freeze the cart, or say “try later.” Users would see frustrating blocks during peak demand, even though they are simply trying to save something they want.

Under the availability choice, each region keeps adding items to the cart. A user might see a cart that is briefly out of sync: one region may show a newer item than the other, or a price/promo might look stale for a few seconds. But customers do not lose the act of adding an item, and checkout rechecks stock anyway.

Business says losing an added item is far worse than a briefly stale cart. During a flash sale, a blocked cart can also create support load and missed revenue, because the customer may not return after a network glitch. That points away from refusing customers during a network split.
Our choice: availability

## Scenario 2: Concert seat booking

Seats are exclusive inventory. The business says two fans must never be sold the same seat. If EU and US split, the seat database cannot safely tell both regions “this seat is still free” without risk.

Under availability choice, both regions keep selling. A seat might be sold in EU and US at the same time because neither region can see the other's new order during the partition. The business outcome is a double sell. Later you would need refunds, apologies, or a seat reassignment process. Users would see success at checkout, then discover a conflict.

Under consistency choice, the system makes a single source of truth for the seat or refuses writes when it cannot check with the authoritative region. A user in one region might see “seats are temporarily unavailable,” “please try again,” or a delayed response while the system verifies ownership. Some fans get a worse experience during the split, but no one is sold the same seat twice.

Business values preventing double-sold seats over uninterrupted buying. A delayed seat response is annoying, but a false success is expensive: it can break trust and create operational work that scales with the incident.
Our choice: consistency

## Scenario 3: Likes counter

Likes are social feedback, not money or inventory. During a split between EU and US, people should be able to tap “like” and immediately see the button respond. Most users understand a small social metric moving around; they do not expect likes to be legally binding.

If you choose consistency, the system may refuse or delay a like until the regions can agree. Users might see a spinning button, an error, or a like that disappears because it did not propagate. The app can feel broken over a network issue that users cannot perceive.

If you choose availability, each region accepts the like locally and updates its own count. A post viewed from US might show one extra like while EU shows one fewer for a few seconds. When the partition heals, the counts can merge, and the button usually still shows the user's own action because that is stored locally. The small difference is acceptable because likes are approximate in the moment.

Business says the like button must always respond, and temporary lag is fine.
Our choice: availability

## Glossary

- Partition: A network break that prevents systems in different regions from reliably communicating. The regions may still work, but they cannot coordinate in real time.
- Consistency: All working systems agree on the same important facts at the same time. For seats, it means the system will not show or sell two conflicting truths.
- Availability: The system keeps responding to requests even when parts of it cannot communicate. It does not guarantee every response contains the latest global truth.
- Eventual consistency: Different regions may disagree for a short time, but they will catch up and agree once the partition heals or updates propagate.
- Latency: The delay between doing something and seeing the effect in another region. It is normal, and network partitions make it feel more visible to users.

output.text:
# 1. Welcome and Our Values

Welcome to Harbourlight Analytics. This handbook is written for you, not for lawyers, and it is meant to be read in your first week, kept handy, and used again whenever a practical question comes up. We are a 30-person data consultancy with one office in a mid-sized city and a handful of colleagues who work mostly from home. We have grown from 8 people to 30 in 18 months, and we have tried to keep the things that made the early days work: direct conversations, shared responsibility, simple systems, and trust in people to do good work without being micro-managed.

This handbook is not a rulebook written to catch people out. It is a shared source of truth so that you do not have to rely on folklore, Slack history, or someone’s memory of a decision made at a coffee shop. If a manager points you to this handbook, it is so you can find an answer quickly, not because we enjoy bureaucracy.

We believe that good operations should make people’s work easier, not harder. That means we try to be clear about expectations, fair in how we treat people, and honest when something needs to be improved. Where this handbook gives a number, use that number. Where it gives a process, follow it step by step. Where it gives a value, use your judgement, and when in doubt, ask.

Harbourlight Analytics is a workplace where people are expected to behave like adults: to be straight with one another, to finish what they start, to reduce complexity instead of creating more of it, and to make space for colleagues who are different from them, quieter than them, newer than them, or working from a different location.

Our four values are the foundation of how we work. They are not decoration. They are used in everyday decisions: how we give feedback, how we handle client work, how we treat time off, how we communicate, and how we make room for each other in a small company where everyone has a real impact.

## Be candid

Be candid means telling people what you need to tell them, early and clearly, without being unkind. It does not mean blurting things out without thought. It means not hiding a delay, not pretending a plan is good when it is not, and not letting a small misunderstanding grow into a big problem.

In practice, candour sounds like:
- Saying “I need more time” before the deadline has passed.
- Telling a colleague that a report has a flaw before the client sees it.
- Giving a manager a straight answer about workload instead of nodding and then falling behind.
- Asking a question when something is unclear, instead of spending half a day guessing.

Everyday example: You are preparing a client dashboard and notice that a metric is based on incomplete data. You tell your project lead on the same day, explain the issue, and propose two simple ways to present it. That is candour.

## Own the outcome

Own the outcome means taking responsibility for the result, not just the task assigned to you. We trust people to see things through, including the messy parts. Owning the outcome does not mean suffering in silence. It means you care enough to chase what is needed, flag what is at risk, and keep the work moving.

In practice, ownership sounds like:
- Following up on a missing file instead of waiting for someone else to remind you.
- Asking for clarification when instructions are unclear.
- Telling the team early if a deliverable will change because new information has appeared.
- Looking beyond your own task to the final outcome for the client.

Everyday example: You are responsible for pulling data for a weekly report. The usual source is down. Instead of saying “that is not my problem,” you find the backup source, let the team know what changed, and deliver the report with a clear note about the data source. That is owning the outcome.

## Make it simple

Make it simple means doing the useful thing in a way that people can follow without effort. Data consultancy can become complicated quickly, and there is sometimes a temptation to make things look more sophisticated than they need to be. We prefer clarity. Simple does not mean careless. It means thoughtful.

In practice, making it simple sounds like:
- Explaining a finding in one sentence before showing the details.
- Using a clear file name instead of “final_v3_FINAL_actual.”
- Turning a confusing meeting into a short decision and a short note.
- Choosing a repeatable process over a clever one-off trick.

Everyday example: Your team needs a weekly update for a client. Instead of building a dashboard with 12 charts, you create a simple summary with the 3 metrics that matter, a short note on what changed, and a link to the backup detail. The client understands it immediately. That is making it simple.

## Leave room for others

Leave room for others means creating space in the room, on the call, in the document, and in the workflow. We are a small company, and everyone contributes to the culture. Some of us are loud, quick, and comfortable speaking first. Others think carefully and want to contribute if the environment allows it. Leaving room for others means being aware of the space you take and deliberately making space for others.

In practice, leaving room sounds like:
- Waiting a beat before answering so a quieter colleague can speak.
- Asking for input from someone who has not had a chance to contribute.
- Writing things down so that people in different time zones or working patterns can follow.
- Not assuming that office-based people know something remote colleagues do not.

Everyday example: You lead a meeting and notice that a remote colleague has not said much. You pause and say, “I want to make sure we hear your view before we decide.” You then write the decision in a note so everyone can follow up. That is leaving room for others.

Who to ask: People Operations

# 2. How We Work

How we work is based on a simple idea: we give people enough structure to cooperate, and enough freedom to do good work. We are not a company that tries to watch every minute. We are a consultancy that depends on reliable colleagues, clear communication, and mutual respect.

## Core hours and your working day

Core hours are 10:00–16:00, Monday to Friday. During core hours, we expect you to be available for work meetings, colleague collaboration, and normal work communication. Outside core hours, you arrange your own day around your responsibilities, your team’s needs, and your contract.

The standard working week is 37.5 hours. Your contract may state a specific start and finish time, but the expectation is that you make your time work in a way that supports both your output and your colleagues.

Some people work from the office. Some work mostly from home. The way we work is designed so that both patterns are treated the same. If something works well for a colleague at home, it should not be a second-class way of working. If a colleague is in the office, they should not expect extra credit for being there. We judge work by quality, reliability, and collaboration, not by location.

A good working day might look like this: you use the early part of the day for focused work, attend stand-up at 10:15, move into meetings during core hours, and then finish up with a clear note about what is done, what is blocked, and what is next. Another person might shift the same hours around school pick-up, a quiet morning block, and an evening wrap-up. That is fine as long as expectations are clear.

## Team stand-ups

Team stand-ups are at 10:15. They are short. They are not meant to be status theatre. The point is to help the team start the day with a shared view of what matters, what is blocked, and what needs attention.

A good stand-up contribution is brief:
- What you are working on.
- Where you need help.
- Anything the team needs to know.

If your team is not using the stand-up well, say so. Stand-ups are meant to serve the team, not to consume the team.

## Communication tools

We use one chat tool and one shared calendar. That is intentional. Too many channels make it hard to find information, and it is unfair to expect new starters to learn a secret map of where things live.

Use chat for normal work communication: quick questions, updates, coordination, and small decisions.

Use the shared calendar for meetings, leave, team events, and anything that needs visibility.

If a request is urgent, call. Do not use chat for urgent requests, then wait for someone to reply while the issue burns. Urgent work should go by phone, not chat.

A simple rule:
- Quick question: chat.
- Scheduled meeting: shared calendar.
- Urgent issue: phone.

## Treating office and home equally

People in the office or at home are treated the same. That sounds obvious, but it requires habits.

If you are in the office:
- Include remote colleagues properly in meetings.
- Do not have side conversations that exclude people on the call.
- Put decisions in writing if they affect the wider team.
- Assume that “we all know this” may not be true for someone who was not in the room.

If you work mostly from home:
- Make your availability visible when it matters.
- Use the shared calendar so others can see your working patterns.
- Raise problems early if you are blocked.
- Ask for what you need, because silence can look like ease when it is not.

If you manage a team, you are responsible for making sure office presence does not become the invisible default. If a decision happens because someone was physically nearby, that is how unfair cultures form.

## Making the day work

Your first week should include:
- Confirming your working hours with your manager.
- Checking calendar access and chat access.
- Understanding your team’s stand-up format.
- Knowing who to contact if something is broken.
- Knowing what “urgent” means on your team.

You do not need to ask permission for every variation in your day. You do need to be considerate and reliable.

If you are changing your usual pattern in a way that affects others, tell your manager and your team. If you are temporarily unavailable, update your calendar and let people know in the normal channel. If something is urgent, phone.

## Meetings and time

Meetings should have a reason. If a meeting has no agenda, it is fair to ask what the decision or outcome is. If you are in charge of a meeting, keep it simple.

Good meetings usually include:
- A clear topic.
- A clear owner.
- A clear decision or next step.
- A note if the meeting affects people who were not there.

Please respect people’s calendars. If you cancel late, send a short message. If you book outside core hours when it is not needed, explain why. If you need deep work, protect time for it and say so.

## Availability

During core hours, your goal is reasonable availability. That does not mean every chat must be answered instantly. It means you should not be invisible when your team needs you, and you should make your status clear when you cannot be reached.

If you are in a meeting, that can be visible on your calendar. If you are doing focused work, a status update can help. If you are unavailable because of leave, your calendar should reflect it.

We trust people to manage their time. We ask people to be considerate of the fact that others are working around them.

Who to ask: your manager

# 3. Employment Basics

This chapter covers the basic terms that affect your role, your status, and the practical details of your employment. If you ever find a conflict between your contract and this handbook, your contract and any applicable local law take precedence.

## Your contract and offer letter

Your contract is the formal record of your employment with Harbourlight Analytics. It should be clear, simple, and available to you when you need it.

Contracts are permanent unless a fixed term is stated in the offer letter. A fixed-term role will say what the end date is and, where applicable, how the fixed term may end or be renewed. If you are unsure whether your role is permanent or fixed-term, check your offer letter and contract, then ask People Operations.

## Before you start

Before your start date, People Operations may send you practical information and requests for paperwork. Try to complete what you can in good time so your first week is about learning and working, not chasing forms.

If something is missing or unclear, ask. A good first week is not a test of secret knowledge. It is an introduction.

## Probation

Every new starter has a 3-month probation period with a check-in at the end of each month.

Probation is a two-way period. It gives the company a chance to confirm that your skills, approach, and behaviour fit the role. It also gives you a chance to decide whether the role is what you expected.

The probation check-ins are not just paperwork. They are meant to be useful conversations.

A typical probation check-in covers:
- What has gone well.
- What feels confusing or difficult.
- What skills you need more practice with.
- What feedback you have for the company or the manager.
- Whether expectations are clear.
- Whether there are any blockers.

During probation, notice is 1 week on either side. That means you give 1 week’s notice if you resign, and the company gives 1 week’s notice if it ends your employment during probation, subject to any applicable legal requirements.

After probation, notice is 4 weeks on either side. That means you give 4 weeks’ notice if you resign, and the company gives 4 weeks’ notice if it ends your employment, subject to any applicable legal requirements.

## Resigning during or after probation

If you decide to resign, tell your manager first. Then confirm your resignation in writing to People Operations, including your requested last working day. Your notice must follow the rules above.

If you are resigning because you are unhappy, consider saying so. We may not be able to fix everything, but we cannot learn if you do not tell us.

## Changes to your personal details

Personal details changes go to People Operations within 2 weeks.

Examples of personal details include:
- Your home address.
- Your legal name.
- Your bank details.
- Your emergency contact.
- Other information the company needs for payroll or employment records.

Keeping details up to date protects you. It ensures your pay goes to the right place, your records are correct, and we can contact the right person if needed.

## Changing your job, manager, or department

Internal changes are part of a small company. If you want to discuss a change in your role, your manager is usually the right place to start. If you are not sure who to speak to, ask People Operations.

We will try to be fair and clear. A small company sometimes needs people to wear more than one hat. That is fine, as long as expectations are honest.

## Where to find your records

If you need a copy of your contract, offer letter, or another employment record, ask People Operations.

Who to ask: People Operations

# 4. Pay and Benefits

This chapter explains how you are paid and what benefits you have. Pay and benefits are practical things, but they matter. A pay mistake or a benefit question can cause unnecessary worry, so we try to be clear.

## Salary

Your salary is the amount stated in your contract or offer letter.

Salaries are paid monthly on the 25th, or on the last working day before it if the 25th is not a working day.

Your pay is normally paid into the bank account you have provided. If your bank details change, tell People Operations within 2 weeks.

If your pay is wrong, tell your manager or People Operations as soon as you notice. Pay errors can usually be fixed quickly if they are reported quickly.

## Salary bands and review

Salary bands are reviewed every April.

A salary band is a range of pay levels used for roles with similar scope and responsibility. It helps us make pay decisions more consistently and gives you a clearer sense of what the role is worth within Harbourlight Analytics.

If you have questions about your role’s band, your manager or People Operations can explain where you sit and how the band works.

## Private health insurance

You have private health insurance from day 1.

There is no waiting period. If you need to set it up, activate a card, add eligible details, or ask what is covered, contact People Operations.

Health insurance is not a reward for staying long. It is there because you matter from the beginning.

## Pension

We make an employer pension contribution of 6% of salary.

To receive the full employer contribution, your employee contribution must be at least 3%. The employer contribution is made against your employee contribution of at least 3%. If your employee contribution is lower, the employer match may be lower according to the scheme terms.

Pension is one of the things people tend to postpone, and that is understandable. It can be complicated, and the future feels far away. But it is usually easier to make a small, steady choice than a stressful large one later. If you have questions, ask People Operations before you decide.

## Personal learning budget

Everyone has a personal learning budget of €1,200 per year.

The learning budget is meant to help you grow in your role. It can support courses, books, conferences, coaching, tools that help your work, or other learning that has a reasonable connection to your role and our work.

How to use your learning budget:
- Think about what would help your work now or in the near future.
- Talk to your manager if you need help shaping the request.
- Send a simple request to your manager, including what you want, why it helps, and the cost.
- If approved, follow the purchase or expense process your team uses.
- If relevant, share what you learned with your manager or team.

We trust you to use it well. You do not need to spend the whole amount just because it exists. If there is a specific course you have been wanting to take, do not assume it is out of reach. Ask.

## Home-office allowance

New starters receive a one-off home-office allowance of €500.

This allowance is intended to help set up a reasonable home working environment. It is not a salary increase, and it is not a recurring payment.

How to claim:
- Buy suitable equipment for home working.
- Keep your receipt or invoice.
- Submit the claim through the normal expense process.
- If you are unsure whether something qualifies, ask before buying.

Examples of reasonable items might include a comfortable chair, desk support, monitor stand, keyboard, mouse, lighting, or equipment to improve your home workspace.

## Cycle-to-work scheme

We offer a cycle-to-work scheme.

If you want to use the scheme, ask People Operations for the steps and any provider requirements.

## Other pay questions

If you have a question about:
- Your salary.
- Your bank details.
- Your payslip.
- Tax-related pay questions.
- Payroll processing.

Contact Finance.

If you have a question about:
- Benefits.
- Health insurance.
- Pension setup.
- Learning budget eligibility.
- Home-office allowance.
- Cycle-to-work.

Contact People Operations.

Who to ask: Finance for pay, People Operations for benefits

# 5. Leave and Time Off

Time off matters. Taking leave well is part of working well here. A good time-off culture is not just about entitlements; it is about planning ahead, communicating clearly, and not leaving colleagues in the dark.

We have 7 types of leave:

| Leave type | Entitlement | How to request |
|---|---|---|
| Annual leave | 25 days per year, plus 8 public holidays | Request in the shared calendar and get approval from your manager; for leave longer than 3 consecutive days, give at least 2 weeks’ notice where possible |
| Sick leave | 10 days per year on full pay; a doctor’s note is needed after 5 consecutive days of absence | Tell your manager as early as possible and record the absence; provide a doctor’s note if absence reaches 5 consecutive days |
| Parental leave (primary carer) | 16 weeks on full pay | Talk to your manager and People Operations, confirm expected dates, and agree a return plan |
| Partner leave | 4 weeks on full pay, to be taken within the first 6 months | Ask your manager and People Operations as early as possible and agree dates within the first 6 months |
| Bereavement leave | 3 days, or 5 days for a partner, child or parent | Tell your manager as soon as possible and record the leave with People Operations |
| Jury and public duty leave | Paid at full salary for as long as the duty lasts | Tell People Operations as soon as you know the dates and provide the official request if asked |
| Unpaid leave | Up to 20 days per year, by agreement with your manager | Discuss the request with your manager and People Operations, agree the dates in writing |

The table above is the summary. The details below explain how each type works.

## Annual leave

Annual leave is 25 days per year, plus 8 public holidays.

Annual leave is meant to be restorative. It is not just an allowance to accumulate. We would rather you take sensible time off during the year than build up a large balance and then feel pressured to use it all in one stressful period.

How to request annual leave:
- Check the shared calendar for your team’s existing leave.
- Discuss your dates with your manager if there is a real chance of conflict.
- Enter the dates in the shared calendar as annual leave.
- Get approval from your manager.
- Make sure handover is clear before you go.

Requests for annual leave longer than 3 consecutive days need at least 2 weeks’ notice. This allows the team to plan without guessing.

If you need leave at short notice for something unexpected, tell your manager as soon as possible and explain the situation. We understand that life happens.

## Carrying over annual leave

Up to 5 unused days can be carried over. Carried-over days must be used by 31 March.

If you think you may not be able to use your annual leave during the year, speak to your manager early. Do not let leave build up quietly. A small conversation in the second half of the year is much better than a large problem in March.

## Sick leave

Sick leave is 10 days per year on full pay.

If you are sick:
- Tell your manager as early as possible.
- Make it clear what you can or cannot do that day.
- Record the absence if asked.
- If your absence reaches 5 consecutive days, provide a doctor’s note.

If you have a long-term health issue or a condition that affects your work, talk to your manager or People Operations. We want to support sensible adjustments where we can.

If you are unwell, rest. Do not work through illness just to appear strong. If you are better enough to do a little light work, say so clearly. If you are not, say that too.

## Parental leave

Parental leave for the primary carer is 16 weeks on full pay.

Parental leave is a significant life event. We want to handle it with clarity and care.

How to request parental leave:
- Tell your manager and People Operations as early as you are comfortable.
- Agree your expected start date.
- Discuss a return date.
- Agree a simple plan for how your work will be covered.
- Keep key details in writing so there is no confusion.

If your situation changes, tell People Operations as soon as you can.

## Partner leave

Partner leave is 4 weeks on full pay. It must be taken within the first 6 months.

Partner leave is available to support you when your partner has a child. If you are planning for this, talk to your manager and People Operations in advance so the timing works well for you and the team.

## Bereavement leave

Bereavement leave is 3 days. For the death of a partner, child or parent, bereavement leave is 5 days.

If you need bereavement leave:
- Tell your manager as soon as possible.
- You do not need to give a long explanation.
- People Operations can record the leave and help with any paperwork needed.

We understand grief can be messy and non-linear. If you need a short extension or a gradual return, tell your manager or People Operations.

## Jury and public duty leave

Jury and public duty leave is paid at full salary for as long as the duty lasts.

If you are called for jury service or another form of public duty:
- Tell People Operations as soon as you know the dates.
- Provide the official request if we ask for it.
- Let your manager know so work can be planned.

## Unpaid leave

Unpaid leave is up to 20 days per year, by agreement with your manager.

Unpaid leave can be used for personal matters that do not fit into other leave categories. Because it is unpaid, it is important to understand the effect before you take it.

How to request unpaid leave:
- Speak to your manager about what you need and when.
- Ask People Operations to confirm how pay and benefits are affected.
- Get approval before the leave starts.
- Record the dates clearly.

## Good handover before leave

Before taking leave, make things simple for the people around you:
- Tell your team what is finished, in progress, and waiting.
- Share relevant files or access if appropriate.
- Give a realistic view of what should wait until you return.
- Do not leave urgent decisions for someone else to guess.

This is not about perfection. It is about respect.

## When returning from leave

When you return:
- Ask for a short catch-up if you have been away for a while.
- Check your calendar and messages gently.
- Confirm what is needed from you first.
- Let your manager know if you need a gradual return.

Who to ask: People Operations

# 6. Health, Safety and Wellbeing

Health, safety, and wellbeing are not separate from work. They are the conditions that allow good work to happen. We are a small company, so we do not have a large corporate safety machine, but we do have clear expectations and some practical supports.

## General safety

A safe workplace is one where you can focus on your work without being worried about basic hazards.

Some simple habits help:
- Keep walkways clear.
- Report damaged furniture or equipment.
- Use cables properly and do not create trip hazards.
- Take breaks when you need them.
- If something looks unsafe, say so.

If you see a hazard in the office, tell your manager or People Operations. Do not wait for someone else to discover it.

## First aid

A trained first-aider is named on the office noticeboard.

If you are in the office and need first aid:
- Tell the nearest first-aider.
- If it is urgent, call for emergency help first.
- Tell your manager or People Operations afterwards so the incident is recorded.

If you work mostly from home, you should still know who to contact at work if you are injured while working.

## Home working and your setup

If you work from home, you are responsible for keeping your working environment reasonably safe and suitable.

Home workers do a short workstation self-assessment in their first month.

The self-assessment is not a trap. It is a chance to identify issues early: back discomfort, poor lighting, awkward screen height, noise problems, or anything else that is making work harder than it needs to be.

A basic home workstation check includes:
- A chair that supports your back and arms.
- A screen at a comfortable eye level.
- A keyboard and mouse position that avoids strain.
- Adequate lighting.
- Enough space to work without awkward twisting or reaching.
- A quiet place where you can concentrate when needed.

If you need help improving your setup, talk to your manager or People Operations. If you use your home-office allowance, use it wisely.

## Wellbeing support

Everyone can use the confidential employee assistance line, free, at any time.

You do not need to be in crisis to use it. You do not need to ask permission. You do not need to explain your reasons to your manager. The line is confidential.

If you prefer, you can also tell your manager that you are using a support resource without sharing the details.

## If something feels wrong

You do not have to suffer quietly because work feels intense. Some pressure is normal. Ignoring warning signs is not healthy.

If you are struggling:
- Speak to your manager if you can.
- Speak to People Operations if you prefer a different route.
- Use the confidential employee assistance line.
- Take a break.
- Ask for help before the problem becomes large.

Wellbeing is not just about wellness campaigns. It is about whether people can speak up honestly without being punished.

## Workload and realistic expectations

If your workload is not realistic, say so. A small consultancy can drift into overcommitment when everyone is helpful and nobody wants to disappoint.

A practical approach is:
- List what is on your plate.
- Identify what is urgent and what is merely loud.
- Ask your manager what should be paused.
- Adjust the plan.

Do not hide overload. Overload causes mistakes, bad client experiences, and avoidable stress.

## Office practicalities

The office should be treated as a shared working environment.

Please:
- Clean up after yourself.
- Respect shared spaces.
- Keep confidential materials stored properly.
- Use equipment carefully.
- Do not block exits or safety equipment.
- Tell People Operations if something needs fixing.

Who to ask: People Operations

# 7. Equipment, Security and Data

Equipment and data handling are not technical details reserved for IT. They are part of your professional responsibility. We handle client information, internal data, and intellectual property. Treating these things with care protects clients, colleagues, and the company.

## Company laptop

Everyone gets a company laptop.

Your laptop is a work tool, and it may also be the tool through which you access confidential client information. Because of that, it comes with basic security requirements.

Your company laptop must have:
- Full-disk encryption.
- Automatic screen lock after 5 minutes.

These requirements are mandatory. Do not disable them for convenience. If you think a requirement is causing a real work problem, contact IT instead of changing the setting.

## Password manager

Password manager use is mandatory.

This is not about control. It is about avoiding predictable passwords, reducing the chance of account compromise, and making sure you can manage access in a sustainable way.

Please:
- Use the company-approved password manager.
- Store work credentials in it, not in personal notes.
- Do not reuse passwords across important work accounts.
- Use a strong master password.

If you are unsure which password manager is approved, ask IT.

## Client data

Client data stays on company systems and is never copied to personal devices.

This rule is simple because it is important. Personal phones, personal laptops, and personal cloud accounts are outside our control. They are not safe places for client work.

You must not:
- Email client data to a personal account.
- Save client files on a personal drive.
- Copy client data to a personal phone or personal laptop.
- Store client information in unapproved apps.
- Leave client data in public places or on unmanaged devices.

If you need to work on client data, use the approved company systems.

If you are unsure whether something counts as client data, assume it does until you know better.

## Working carefully with data

Some practical habits protect everyone:
- Use the right folder or system for the client.
- Keep access as limited as needed.
- Do not share files outside the approved system.
- Label documents clearly so others know what they are.
- When in doubt, ask before sending.

Confidentiality is not just about secrecy. It is about doing the boring things consistently: correct access, correct storage, correct sharing.

## If equipment is lost or stolen

Lost or stolen equipment is reported to IT within 1 hour.

If this happens, do not wait until the next working day. Do not assume it will turn up.

What to do:
- Tell IT immediately through the normal urgent route.
- If urgent, use the phone route as described in How We Work.
- Tell your manager.
- Give IT the last known location and details if you know them.
- If you suspect data access is at risk, say so clearly.

The 1-hour reporting rule exists because speed matters.

## Device loss is not automatically a data breach

If you report quickly, we can act quickly. If you delay, a small mistake can become a serious incident. Do not hide it because you are embarrassed.

## Software and accounts

Use approved software and accounts. Do not install unknown tools that may collect data or compromise your device.

If you need a new tool:
- Tell your manager or People Operations.
- If it involves client data, involve IT before you use it.

## Access when you change roles

If your role changes, your access should change too. If you no longer need access to a system, it should be reviewed. If you need more access for a new project, ask first.

Access is not a status symbol. It is a tool.

## Backups and saving work

Work should be saved in approved company systems. Do not rely solely on desktop folders or local storage if the company system provides the correct place.

If you have questions about where to save something, ask.

## Returning equipment

If you leave the company, return equipment on your last day. This is covered in Leaving Harbourlight.

Who to ask: IT

# 8. Code of Conduct

1. Be truthful in your work, including about findings, limitations, risks, and mistakes.
2. Protect confidential and client information by using approved systems and not storing data where it should not be.
3. Treat colleagues, clients, and partners with respect, including when you disagree with them.
4. Do your work diligently, ask for help when needed, and tell people early when a deadline or outcome may be at risk.
5. Use company time, money, equipment, and resources honestly and only for legitimate work purposes.
6. Avoid conflicts of interest, and declare anything that might look like a conflict before it becomes a problem.
7. Follow company policies on safety, security, data, and professional behaviour, and ask when you are unsure.
8. Raise concerns when something seems wrong, unsafe, unfair, or misleading, and do not knowingly ignore a serious issue.

The commitments above are the basic expectations of working at Harbourlight Analytics. They apply whether you are in the office, at home, on a client call, in a chat, or writing a report.

## What this looks like in practice

For colleagues:
- Be straightforward.
- Do not spread rumours.
- Do not belittle someone’s contribution.
- Respect different working styles.
- Give credit where it is due.
- Ask questions instead of assuming the worst.

For clients:
- Be honest about what you know and what you do not know.
- Do not overstate certainty.
- Do not present data in a misleading way.
- Protect client information.
- Do not make promises that have not been approved.

For company resources:
- Use budgets for their stated purpose.
- Claim expenses accurately.
- Do not use company equipment for risky or inappropriate activity.
- Report lost, damaged, or potentially compromised equipment promptly.
- Do not bypass security controls.

## Conflicts of interest

A conflict of interest happens when your personal interests could influence, or appear to influence, your work judgement. It does not need to be intentional to be a problem.

If something feels like a conflict, raise it early. Examples may include:
- A side project that competes with client work.
- A family relationship that affects a hiring or procurement decision.
- A gift that could look like an attempt to influence work.
- Outside work that affects your ability to do your job.
- Access to information that could give someone an unfair advantage.

You do not need to be certain that a conflict exists. You just need to declare it. It is much easier to manage a potential issue early than to explain it later.

## Gifts and hospitality

Use good judgement. Gifts or hospitality that are excessive or meant to influence decisions are not appropriate. If something is uncertain, ask People Operations before accepting.

## Respect and inclusion

We expect a workplace where people can be themselves, do their best work, and be treated fairly.

Please:
- Do not use discriminatory or harassing language.
- Do not tolerate behaviour that makes others uncomfortable.
- Include colleagues who may not be physically present.
- Be mindful of how you use your voice in meetings.
- Do not make assumptions about people based on age, gender, nationality, background, disability, or working pattern.

Small companies can create culture quickly. Culture is mostly made up of small repeated actions, not annual statements.

## Raising a concern

If something worries you at work, you should be able to raise it.

You may have a concern about:
- Unfair treatment.
- Safety.
- Data handling.
- Client work that seems misleading.
- Inappropriate behaviour.
- Financial or ethical problems.
- A pattern that seems wrong.

If you are able, start by talking to your manager. If that is not appropriate, or if you are not comfortable doing so, go to People Operations. If People Operations is part of the concern, speak to a senior leader you trust or use the confidential route below.

## Raising a concern anonymously

You can raise a concern without putting your name to it.

To do this:
- Write down what you are concerned about.
- Describe what happened, where, when, and who was involved if you know.
- Describe the impact or risk.
- Send it to People Operations through an anonymous route you are comfortable using.
- If you have evidence, describe where it is rather than sending unnecessary confidential files.

Anonymity can make investigations harder, but it is better than silence if you are worried about retaliation.

## Good faith protection

Nobody will be penalised for raising a concern in good faith.

A concern does not need to turn out to be exactly right. If you raise it honestly, we will not treat that against you. Retaliation against someone for raising a concern in good faith is not acceptable.

## What happens next

When a concern is raised, we will:
- Listen.
- Ask for enough detail to understand the issue.
- Consider who needs to be involved.
- Protect confidentiality as far as reasonably possible.
- Follow up fairly.
- Record the concern.

If you raise something serious, do not be surprised if people need to ask careful questions. That is not distrust; it is how a small company tries to get things right.

## If you are unsure

If you are not sure whether something is a conduct issue, it is usually better to ask than to guess.

You can ask:
- Your manager.
- People Operations.
- IT, if the issue involves equipment or data.

Who to ask: People Operations

# 9. Growth, Feedback and Reviews

Growth at Harbourlight Analytics is not something that happens only when someone gets promoted. Growth happens when you get better at your work, learn from feedback, improve your judgement, and contribute more clearly to the team.

## Monthly one-to-one

Everyone has a monthly one-to-one with their manager.

The one-to-one is your time. It is not just a status meeting. It is a place to discuss:
- What you are working on.
- What is going well.
- What is stuck.
- What support you need.
- What feedback you want to give.
- What you want to learn.
- How you are feeling about the work.

A good one-to-one is usually short but honest. If it becomes only a list of tasks, ask to spend some time on the bigger picture. If you have something important to discuss, send a short agenda beforehand.

## Feedback

Feedback is part of ordinary work. It should not be rare, dramatic, or hidden until a review.

Good feedback is:
- Specific.
- Timely.
- Kind.
- Useful.
- Focused on behaviour and outcomes, not character attacks.

If you receive feedback:
- Listen.
- Ask questions if something is unclear.
- Think about what you can use.
- Thank the person if appropriate.
- Decide what you will try next.

If you give feedback:
- Say it early.
- Explain the impact.
- Offer a practical next step.
- Do not pile on.
- Consider whether the person can hear it well now.

Feedback is not a performance report. It is information.

## Formal reviews

Reviews happen 2 times per year, in April and October.

A review is not a surprise if feedback has been happening throughout the year. It is a more structured moment to step back, look at progress, and plan ahead.

A review usually includes:
- Your work since the last review.
- Strengths and what is going well.
- Areas to develop.
- Learning and support needs.
- Career direction.
- Goals for the next period.

You may be asked to prepare notes. Useful preparation includes:
- Achievements you are proud of.
- Challenges you faced.
- Feedback you received and what you did with it.
- Skills you want to improve.
- Support you need.
- Work you want more or less of.

Promotions are discussed at the April review.

If you are interested in promotion, ask early in the year what would need to change. Do not assume the right to promotion is automatic. In a small company, promotions are usually tied to role scope, responsibility, impact, and readiness, not simply time served.

If a promotion is not possible at a given time, ask for clear reasons and what evidence would change the conversation later.

## Career growth in a small company

At 30 people, roles may not have large corporate ladders. Growth can happen through:
- Owning bigger pieces of work.
- Leading client conversations.
- Mentoring newer colleagues.
- Improving technical depth.
- Taking on specialist skills.
- Managing projects.
- Helping simplify processes.
- Becoming more trusted with complex or sensitive work.

You do not need to wait for a formal title to grow. But you do need clarity about what growth means in your role.

## Learning support

Use your personal learning budget of €1,200 per year if it can help your growth. If you want to learn something, say so. If you need time to learn, say so. If you need a different kind of challenge, say so.

Growth is easier when expectations are clear and when people are not afraid to say what they want.

## When growth feels stuck

If you feel stuck:
- Ask for a review of your role.
- Ask your manager what “next level” would look like.
- Ask for feedback that is honest, not soft.
- Ask for opportunities, not just advice.
- Ask for clarity about the difference between development and promotion.

Sometimes a small change in work can create a big change in engagement. Sometimes it cannot. Either way, talking openly helps.

Who to ask: People Operations

# 10. Leaving Harbourlight

Leaving a job is not the end of being a professional person. We want departures to be clear, respectful, and practical for everyone involved. If you leave Harbourlight Analytics, do it well. If you stay, remember that how people leave says something about the culture as much as how they arrive.

## Resigning

If you decide to resign:
- Tell your manager first.
- Then confirm your resignation in writing to People Operations.
- Include your requested last working day.

Your notice period depends on whether you are in probation.

During probation, notice is 1 week on either side. After probation, notice is 4 weeks on either side.

If you have a fixed-term contract, check your contract for what it says about the end date.

## Planning your notice period

Use your notice period practically.

During notice, you should:
- Tell your team what is happening if appropriate.
- Hand over work clearly.
- List current tasks and their status.
- Share relevant files and contacts where appropriate.
- Finish or hand over client deliverables where reasonable.
- Return company equipment on your last day.

A handover does not need to be a novel. It should be clear enough that someone else is not guessing.

A good handover note includes:
- What is finished.
- What is in progress.
- What is waiting.
- What needs attention first.
- Key client contacts or context.
- Where files and documents are stored.
- Any risks or caveats.

## Exit conversation

You will have an exit conversation with People Operations.

This is not just a formality. It is a chance to say what worked, what did not, and what you hope the company learns.

In the exit conversation, you can talk about:
- Why you are leaving.
- Your experience with your manager and team.
- What you would improve.
- Whether you would recommend working here.
- Any concerns you still have.

If you do not want to answer a question, you do not have to. But honest feedback helps the company become better for the people who remain.

## Unused annual leave

Unused annual leave is paid out.

If you have questions about how your unused annual leave is calculated, ask People Operations. Check your leave balance before your last day so there are no surprises.

## Returning equipment

Return equipment on your last day.

Company equipment may include:
- Laptop.
- Charger.
- Adapter.
- Mouse or keyboard if issued.
- Headphones if issued.
- Security pass or office access card.
- Any other company-owned item.

If you bought home-office equipment using the home-office allowance, ask People Operations whether the item is company property or yours, because arrangements can vary.

If an item is damaged or lost, say so honestly.

## Accounts and access

If you are leaving, your access to company systems will be handled as part of your departure. Do not try to keep copies of client data, files, or internal information after you leave.

Client data stays on company systems and is never copied to personal devices. That rule continues to apply beyond your last day.

Do not delete files in a way that harms the team. If you have something personal in a work account, remove it appropriately, but do not remove work materials the team needs.

## References

References confirm dates and role.

If a future employer asks for a reference, they can usually confirm basic employment information such as your dates of employment and role. People Operations can explain the reference process.

If you need a reference, ask People Operations. If a reference would require more detail from your former manager, they may be contacted. We will try to be accurate and fair.

## After you leave

You leave with your reputation. You leave with the work you did. You also leave with the way you handled the exit.

If you leave well, you may find yourself working with colleagues again later. The data consultancy world can be small.

## If you are managing someone who is leaving

If someone on your team resigns:
- Thank them honestly.
- Plan a practical handover.
- Inform the team appropriately.
- Avoid making them feel guilty for leaving.
- Ask for feedback.
- Follow People Operations’ process for equipment and records.

Leaving is not a betrayal. It is part of working life in a small company.

Who to ask: People Operations
