1. Executive Summary

Ember & Oak Coffee Roasters is a small-batch speciality coffee roastery that will operate in Halbrook, a city of about 400,000 people. The business is founded by Priya Anand and Tom Keller, who bring complementary experience: Priya has eight years of experience as a head roaster at a regional roastery, and Tom has ten years of experience in hospitality sales and café management. The company will lease a 180 m² light-industrial unit, install roasting and ventilation equipment, and operate using one 15 kg drum roaster. It will buy green coffee from two importers and sell traceable single-origin coffee through three channels: wholesale to independent cafés and restaurants, an online subscription offering one 1 kg delivery per month, and retail sales at the city's two weekly farmers' markets.

This plan requests a loan of 60,000 to complete a total start-up investment of 105,000. The founders will contribute 45,000 of their own money. The requested funding will support the core assets and opening costs required to begin trading: a roaster costing 60,000, unit fit-out and ventilation costing 25,000, and working capital of 20,000. The plan is written to support the bank’s credit assessment and to serve as the company’s operating plan for its first three years.

The market opportunity is clear enough for a local speciality roaster but not overstated. Halbrook has 180 independent cafés and 65 chain outlets. The nearest speciality roastery is 70 km away, while two national roasters supply most cafés in the city. A survey conducted by the founders among 40 independent café owners found that 22 owners were open to switching roaster if offered fresher coffee and barista training. That is 55.0% of the surveyed group. The plan does not assume that every independent café will become a customer. It sets a realistic target of 30 wholesale accounts by the end of Year 3, which represents 16.7% of the city's 180 independent cafés. This target is ambitious but grounded in the survey finding, the gap in local speciality supply, and the founders’ direct access to café operators through wholesale sales and training.

The revenue model is built around three channels with different roles. Wholesale provides the largest and most stable base: 6,000 kg in Year 1, 9,000 kg in Year 2 and 12,000 kg in Year 3, all at 22 per kg. Online subscriptions build recurring revenue and brand loyalty: average subscribers of 300 in Year 1, 550 in Year 2 and 800 in Year 3, each paying 18 per month for 12 months. Farmers' market sales add local visibility, direct customer learning and immediate cash sales: 30,000 in Year 1, 36,000 in Year 2 and 40,000 in Year 3. Total revenue is projected at 226,800 in Year 1, 352,800 in Year 2 and 476,800 in Year 3, for a three-year total of 1,056,400.

The cost structure is simple and suitable for bank review. Cost of goods sold is assumed at 38% of total revenue in every year, giving a consistent gross margin of 62.0%. Rent is 24,000 per year, utilities and insurance are 9,000 per year, and depreciation on the roaster is 12,000 per year, based on a 60,000 cost depreciated straight-line over five years. Salaries including the founders rise from 72,000 in Year 1 to 98,000 in Year 2 and 124,000 in Year 3, reflecting growth in customer service, production support and sales activity. Marketing rises from 15,000 to 18,000 to 20,000 across the three years. Tax, interest and inflation are ignored in the financial tables.

The plan shows operating profit of 8,616 in Year 1, 57,736 in Year 2 and 106,616 in Year 3. Operating margins are 3.8% in Year 1, 16.4% in Year 2 and 22.4% in Year 3. Year 1 is intentionally realistic: the company will still be building accounts, brand awareness and production routines, while fixed costs such as rent, salaries, marketing, utilities and depreciation are already being carried. The operating profit is positive, and the 20,000 working capital budget is included in the funding request to help manage the slower cash conversion that is normal in a first year of roastery trading. From Year 2, revenue growth and operating leverage improve profitability materially.

The funding request is sized conservatively. The loan amount of 60,000 equals 57.1% of total start-up costs, with the founders contributing 42.9%. If the loan is repaid over five years with an equal annual principal component, the annual principal repayment would be 12,000. Operating profit plus depreciation, which removes the non-cash depreciation charge, is 20,616 in Year 1, 69,736 in Year 2 and 118,616 in Year 3. Before interest and tax, which are excluded from the plan tables, these figures cover the annual principal repayment 1.7 times in Year 1, 5.8 times in Year 2 and 9.9 times in Year 3. The Year 1 cover is the tightest, which is why the working capital element and the conservative wholesale target are important. By Year 3, the business is substantially more profitable and has a clearer service record with wholesale and subscription customers.

Ember & Oak is therefore not a speculative expansion. It is a focused roastery with a clear local market, a small number of revenue channels, a defined funding requirement and financial projections based on stated volumes and prices. The plan is confident because the product, experience and local gap are strong. It is realistic because Year 1 profitability is deliberately shown as modest, and the three-year path depends on disciplined execution across wholesale, subscription retention, market selling and cost control.

2. Company and Products

Ember & Oak Coffee Roasters will operate as a small-batch speciality roastery in Halbrook. The company will be located in a leased 180 m² light-industrial unit. This type of space is suitable for roasting, packaging, storage and small-scale dispatch operations. The physical assets will be deliberately modest: one 15 kg drum roaster will be the centre of production, with unit fit-out and ventilation required to operate the roasting equipment safely and effectively. The initial capital plan reflects this simple but essential asset base: 60,000 for the roaster, 25,000 for unit fit-out and ventilation, and 20,000 for working capital.

The business will sell roasted coffee in three ways. The first is wholesale to independent cafés and restaurants. Wholesale is expected to be the foundation of the company because independent venues need reliable deliveries, consistent quality, fresh roast dates and practical support for staff. The plan assumes 6,000 kg of wholesale volume in Year 1, 9,000 kg in Year 2 and 12,000 kg in Year 3, all sold at 22 per kg. This creates a wholesale revenue line that grows from 132,000 to 198,000 to 264,000 across the three-year period.

The second channel is an online subscription. Each subscription customer receives one 1 kg delivery per month and pays 18 per month for 12 months. The company plans average subscriber numbers of 300 in Year 1, 550 in Year 2 and 800 in Year 3. At 18 per month for 12 months, one subscriber generates 216 in annual revenue if fully paid for the year. Subscription revenue is therefore projected at 64,800 in Year 1, 118,800 in Year 2 and 172,800 in Year 3. This channel is important because it creates recurring demand, supports cash planning and gives the founders direct feedback from end consumers.

The third channel is retail sales at the city's two weekly farmers' markets. This is not expected to become the largest channel, but it plays a practical role. It provides direct customer contact, allows new roast profiles to be tested, supports local brand visibility and generates retail revenue of 30,000 in Year 1, 36,000 in Year 2 and 40,000 in Year 3. The farmers' market operation also helps convert visitors into wholesale leads or subscription customers, although the plan does not depend on this happening.

The product range will be based on traceable single-origin lots purchased from two importers. For a lending officer unfamiliar with coffee, this means that each batch of green coffee can be linked to a specific origin or supplier lot, rather than being bought solely as a generic commodity. In a speciality roastery, traceability matters because flavour, seasonality and quality control are part of the customer promise. Using two importers also reduces the risk of relying on a single supply relationship.

The 15 kg drum roaster supports the company's small-batch positioning. A drum roaster is the most common machine used for developing roasted coffee in small and medium roasteries. A 15 kg capacity allows the company to roast smaller lots, manage different origins separately and adapt more quickly to wholesale or subscription demand than a large industrial production line would allow. This flexibility is useful in a new roastery because it can reduce waste, respond to customer feedback and test new lots without committing to excessive inventory.

The company's products are not intended to compete directly with mass-produced national coffee brands on price or scale. Ember & Oak will compete by offering closer proximity, fresher coffee, better communication, traceable lots and hands-on support for café customers. This positioning matches the market survey result: 22 of 40 surveyed independent café owners said they were open to switching roaster if offered fresher coffee and barista training. The product and service offer is therefore directly shaped by that feedback.

The business model is also deliberately narrow. Ember & Oak will not begin by building a large café network, opening multiple sites, or selling unrelated merchandise. The company will focus on roasting and distributing coffee in Halbrook through three defined channels. This narrow focus supports the funding request because the loan can be linked clearly to production equipment, premises readiness and working capital needed to run a small roastery.

In the first three years, the company will use this plan to manage cash, production and customer acquisition. Because the founders come from roasting and hospitality backgrounds, they understand that quality consistency is not only about the roaster but also about packaging, storage, delivery timing, customer service and staff training. The company and product strategy is therefore built around reliable execution of a limited number of high-quality coffee offerings rather than trying to serve every possible customer in the city.

3. Market Analysis

Halbrook is a city of about 400,000 people. For a small-batch roastery, the city size is important because it suggests enough population density to support multiple independent coffee venues, regular farmers' markets and direct consumer subscription sales. The market structure is also known: there are 180 independent cafés and 65 chain outlets. The independent segment is the most relevant for Ember & Oak because chain outlets are more likely to operate under central supply arrangements, while independent cafés are often more open to local suppliers and specialised products.

The plan does not assume that all 180 independent cafés are available customers. The two national roasters supply most cafés in the city, so the market already has established incumbent suppliers. The opportunity lies where incumbents are less able to compete: freshness, proximity, small-lot flexibility, direct communication, traceable single-origin products and barista training. The nearest speciality roastery is 70 km away. That distance creates a real local gap, even though it does not eliminate competition. A roaster 70 km away may still supply some cafés, but it is less able to offer immediate delivery, frequent sampling, quick troubleshooting and in-person training compared with a local operator.

The survey evidence is the most direct support for the wholesale model. The founders surveyed 40 independent café owners. Of these, 22 were open to switching roaster if offered fresher coffee and barista training. This is 55.0% of the surveyed owners. The result is promising but not over-interpreted. A survey of 40 owners shows a strong signal among the group surveyed, but it does not guarantee conversion across all 180 independent cafés. The plan therefore sets a target of 30 wholesale accounts by the end of Year 3. This represents 16.7% of the independent café population. If the 30 accounts were active and contributed evenly, the average annual volume across the 30 accounts would be 400 kg in Year 3, which is approximately 33 kg per month per account. This is presented as a volume sensitivity, not a commitment from any customer.

The survey response also clarifies the practical customer proposition. Independent café owners are not simply looking for another coffee supplier. They are open to change if the supplier improves coffee freshness and supports their staff through training. Ember & Oak's wholesale sales plan is built on these two points. Fresher coffee is supported by a local roaster, smaller batches and direct delivery. Barista training is supported by Tom Keller's hospitality sales and café management background, and by Priya Anand's technical roasting and coffee knowledge.

The subscription channel is different from the wholesale channel because it reaches consumers directly. The plan assumes average subscribers of 300 in Year 1, 550 in Year 2 and 800 in Year 3. The plan does not rely on unverified national subscription statistics. It simply uses the stated subscriber assumptions and the fixed monthly price of 18. This gives a clear revenue line: 64,800 in Year 1, 118,800 in Year 2 and 172,800 in Year 3. The subscription model is attractive because it builds predictable recurring revenue, but it also depends on retention. Customers may leave if coffee quality falls, deliveries are inconsistent or communication becomes impersonal. The plan therefore treats subscription growth as a service operation, not merely a marketing campaign.

The farmers' market channel provides a local test bed. The company will sell at the city's two weekly farmers' markets. Revenue is projected at 30,000 in Year 1, 36,000 in Year 2 and 40,000 in Year 3. These figures are modest compared with wholesale and subscription revenue, but their strategic value is meaningful. Farmers' markets give the founders direct conversations with coffee drinkers, visibility in the community, and a practical place to understand retail preferences. The markets also create opportunities to introduce visitors to the subscription service or to refer them to local cafés that serve Ember & Oak coffee.

The target of 30 wholesale accounts by the end of Year 3 is central to market credibility. It is not an unrealistic share of the independent café market, but it will require sustained sales effort. The plan assumes the company will focus on cafés and restaurants that value freshness and training, rather than competing on the lowest price. This focus should improve customer quality and reduce the risk of winning accounts that are primarily price-sensitive and unstable.

The market analysis also recognises limitations. The city's coffee consumption habits are not quantified beyond the stated café counts and survey. The plan therefore does not make claims about total market spending or the share of revenue captured by national roasters. It relies on the known number of independent cafés, the known distance to the nearest speciality roastery, the known survey response and the founders' practical ability to sell and train customers. This makes the plan more defensible than a projection based on unverified city-wide spending data.

In summary, the market provides a credible base for a small local speciality roaster: enough independent cafés, a gap in local speciality supply, survey evidence of willingness to switch, two established retail market events, and a subscription model that can be managed with direct customer relationships. The plan is confident because the market gap is real. It is realistic because it targets 30 wholesale accounts rather than claiming the entire city market.

4. Competition

The competitive environment is clear from the stated market facts. Ember & Oak will compete mainly with two national roasters that already supply most cafés in the city, with the nearest speciality roastery located 70 km away, and with the general status quo of independent café buyers who already have supply arrangements. The company will also compete indirectly for the attention of subscription and farmers' market customers in a broader coffee retail market.

The two national roasters are the most significant structural competitors. They likely have scale, established distribution and familiarity with cafés across Halbrook. Their strengths include consistent supply, established account relationships and possibly lower cost per unit because of volume. These are real advantages. Ember & Oak should not pretend that national suppliers are weak. However, national roasters are less well positioned to offer very local responsiveness, small-batch roasting flexibility, quick delivery and direct barista training. A large supplier cannot easily provide the same level of face-to-face service to many independent venues as a small local roaster.

The nearest speciality roastery, 70 km away, competes more directly on quality positioning. It may supply cafés that value speciality coffee but accept a longer supply distance. Its location is an advantage because it is already established, but it is a disadvantage when cafés need frequent deliveries, immediate problem solving, local brand presence and hands-on training. A 70 km distance also reduces the practicality of quick customer service and short supply cycles. Ember & Oak's local presence is therefore a competitive strength.

Barista training and customer education are likely to be important differentiators. The founders' survey found that 22 of 40 independent café owners were open to switching roaster if offered fresher coffee and barista training. This suggests that quality alone may not be enough to win accounts. Many café owners value practical support that helps their baristas use the coffee effectively. A local roastery can combine product supply with education more naturally than a remote supplier. Priya Anand and Tom Keller can provide the technical coffee side and the hospitality service side, which supports this position.

Traceable single-origin lots are another differentiator. For the lending officer, this means the company can communicate where each coffee lot comes from and how it has been roasted. National roasters may offer this in some product lines, but Ember & Oak can build its whole brand around small-batch traceable sourcing. The use of two importers also means the company can offer variety while managing supply risk.

Farmers' markets create a competitive advantage in visibility. Ember & Oak will sell at the city's two weekly farmers' markets, while the two national roasters and the remote speciality roaster may have little regular physical presence in those local settings. This gives Ember & Oak a chance to become recognised through direct interaction. It also allows the business to test retail bags, receive immediate feedback and build a base of subscription customers who know the brand personally.

The competitive strategy is not to take a broad share of the city's coffee supply. Instead, Ember & Oak will focus on independent venues that value freshness, service and training, and on direct consumers who prefer a small-batch local roaster. This focus makes the plan realistic. It does not assume that national roasters will be displaced. It assumes that a portion of the market will value a local speciality provider enough to switch or add a second supplier.

There are competitive risks. Independent cafés may be reluctant to change because switching suppliers requires retraining, staff confidence and trust in consistency. Cafés may also be financially pressured and may prefer cheaper options. Subscription customers may be attracted by many coffee sellers online. Ember & Oak will need to compete through reliability and relationships, not merely through the fact that it is a new local business.

Overall, the competitive position is credible because the company has specific advantages: local proximity, small-batch roasting, two founders with directly relevant experience, traceable sourcing, direct market presence and a practical wholesale service proposition. The main risk is execution: the company must prove that its coffee and service are consistently good enough to win and retain independent accounts. The plan addresses this through the financial assumptions, marketing and sales plan, and risk management section.

5. Operations

Operations will be centred on the 180 m² light-industrial unit and the 15 kg drum roaster. The unit will need fit-out and ventilation before production can begin. The start-up cost for fit-out and ventilation is 25,000, which reflects the need to operate roasting equipment safely and comfortably. The operating plan assumes that these costs are completed before revenue-generating activity begins. The roaster itself costs 60,000 and will be depreciated straight-line over five years at 12,000 per year.

The core operational process is straightforward: purchase green coffee from two importers, receive and store green coffee, roast selected lots in batches, allow roasted coffee to rest as required by the production method, package the coffee, store packaged inventory, fulfil wholesale orders, fulfil subscription orders, prepare retail inventory for farmers' markets, deliver orders and record lot quality information. Although this sounds simple, each step requires discipline because quality and traceability are the basis of the business.

Green coffee will be bought from two importers. Using two importers is important because it reduces reliance on one supplier and gives the company flexibility in sourcing. Green coffee is unroasted coffee and is the main raw material for roasted coffee. The cost inputs assume that green coffee, packaging and subscription shipping together account for 38% of total revenue each year. This is a key operational and financial assumption. If production efficiency, packaging waste or shipping cost deviates from plan, gross profit will be affected because cost of goods sold is a large variable cost.

The 15 kg drum roaster is suitable for small-batch flexibility. It allows different lots to be roasted separately, which supports traceability and quality control. It also allows the founders to adjust production to demand. However, a single roaster is a concentrated operational asset. If the roaster is unavailable, production is directly affected. The operating plan therefore assumes routine maintenance, careful scheduling and a production mindset that avoids unnecessary rework or over-roasting. The ventilation and fit-out investment also supports safe and efficient operation.

Wholesale operations require reliable scheduling and customer communication. Independent cafés need regular deliveries, predictable quality and the ability to contact the roaster quickly if there is an issue. The company will support accounts with direct contact, sample introductions, delivery coordination and barista training. The volume assumptions of 6,000 kg in Year 1, 9,000 kg in Year 2 and 12,000 kg in Year 3 are based on stated sales plans, not on assumed capacity claims. The operations plan is to manage these volumes through batch scheduling and inventory discipline.

Subscription operations are different from wholesale operations because they involve many smaller customer relationships. Each subscriber receives one 1 kg delivery per month. This means the company must manage monthly production, packaging, order consolidation and shipping. Shipping costs are included within the 38% cost of goods sold assumption. Subscription operations will require consistent packaging, clear customer service and reliable fulfilment because late or damaged deliveries directly affect retention.

Farmers' market operations are labour-intensive and seasonal in nature, but they are a planned part of the retail model. Selling at two weekly farmers' markets requires product preparation, display, transport, sales effort and cash handling. Revenue is projected at 30,000, 36,000 and 40,000 across the three years. This channel must be managed so that it supports the brand without consuming disproportionate founder time relative to its financial contribution. In Year 1, when wholesale accounts are still being developed, market selling also has a direct lead-generation role.

Inventory management will be important because both wholesale and subscription customers expect freshness. Too much roasted inventory risks quality decline and waste; too little risks service failures. The working capital of 20,000 is included in the funding request to support inventory, order timing and early cash flow differences. The company will need to balance green coffee purchases, roasted inventory and retail packaging without overextending cash.

Quality control is part of operations, not a separate overhead. Because the business sells traceable single-origin coffee, it must maintain records linking green lots to roasted batches and customer orders. This supports both quality assurance and customer confidence. Priya Anand's roasting background is central to this control system. Tom Keller's café management experience supports customer-facing quality consistency, because a café's experience of coffee is also affected by extraction, grinder calibration and barista technique.

Operational staffing will be funded through the salary line. Salaries including the founders are 72,000 in Year 1, 98,000 in Year 2 and 124,000 in Year 3. The increase reflects the growing workload across production, fulfilment, delivery, training and market activity. The plan does not assume an oversized team in Year 1. Instead, the founders will personally cover many functions, and the salary budget will support additional practical help as the company becomes busier.

The operational risk is concentrated in three areas: roaster availability, production quality and cash timing around inventory. The roaster is a single asset; quality errors can damage early customer relationships; and inventory purchases can consume working capital before sales convert to cash. The plan addresses these risks through maintenance discipline, founder technical expertise, small-batch flexibility, two green coffee importers, conservative Year 1 revenue assumptions and the inclusion of working capital in the funding request.

The operating model is deliberately simple: one production location, one roaster, two green coffee suppliers, three sales channels and a small team. This simplicity is an advantage because the company can manage its costs and focus on quality. It also makes the financial plan easier for the bank to assess. The key operational success factor is not complexity but consistency: the company must produce, package, deliver and support coffee reliably across all channels for three years.

6. Marketing and Sales

Marketing and sales will be executed in a practical, channel-specific way. The business will not spend its marketing budget on broad brand advertising. The 15,000 marketing budget in Year 1, rising to 18,000 in Year 2 and 20,000 in Year 3, will be directed toward customer acquisition and retention across wholesale, subscription and farmers' market sales. The plan focuses on activities that can be measured through accounts won, subscribers acquired and market sales achieved.

Wholesale sales will be the core commercial activity. The target is 30 wholesale accounts by the end of Year 3. This will be pursued among independent cafés and restaurants in Halbrook, using the survey insight that 22 of 40 surveyed café owners were open to switching if offered fresher coffee and barista training. The sales approach will therefore be built around demonstration and service: offering samples, arranging tastings, showing roast flexibility, explaining traceable single-origin lots and providing practical barista training. A wholesale account is not won once; it must be retained through consistent quality, reliable delivery and responsive communication.

The wholesale proposition should be clearly differentiated from the two national roasters that supply most cafés. Ember & Oak will compete by being local, by roasting smaller batches, by providing faster communication and by helping customers get the best from the coffee. Tom Keller's ten years of hospitality sales and café management experience is directly relevant here. He understands café operations and can speak credibly to independent owners about staff support, workflow, drink quality and customer expectations. Priya Anand's eight years of head-roaster experience adds technical credibility and supports quality assurance.

Subscription sales will use a direct digital and community-based approach. The model is simple: one 1 kg delivery per month for 18 per month. The plan assumes average subscribers of 300 in Year 1, 550 in Year 2 and 800 in Year 3. Subscriber growth will depend on consistent coffee quality, reliable shipping, clear communication and retention. The subscription channel is not just a revenue source; it also gives the company a direct relationship with end consumers. This is valuable because café customers may become subscribers, and market visitors may become regular online buyers.

Farmers' market selling will support both revenue and marketing. The two weekly farmers' markets are expected to generate 30,000 in Year 1, 36,000 in Year 2 and 40,000 in Year 3. Market selling will be used to introduce the brand, explain single-origin lots, collect feedback and convert engaged visitors into repeat customers. The sales experience at the market should be educational but simple: customers should understand what they are buying, why it is roasted locally and how to use it at home.

Brand building will focus on the company's three main credibility points: Halbrook local presence, small-batch roasting and traceable sourcing. The brand should not rely on exaggerated claims. The facts are already strong enough: a local roaster, two importers, traceable single-origin lots, two founders with relevant experience, and a direct market presence. For the bank, this is more persuasive than a generic brand narrative because it is tied to operational actions.

The marketing plan must also manage acquisition cost discipline. In Year 1, the company will need to build awareness while sales are still developing. The marketing budget of 15,000 is therefore expected to support early sampling, market presence, customer acquisition and subscription conversion. In Year 2 and Year 3, marketing rises to 18,000 and 20,000 to support a larger customer base and broader account conversion. The increase is modest relative to expected revenue growth, which supports the plan's operating profit improvement.

A key sales principle will be conversion through experience. Coffee decisions can be difficult for customers to make from a written description alone. Tasting is therefore central. Wholesale prospects will be offered samples and tastings. Subscription marketing will aim to reduce hesitation by presenting a clear monthly product and straightforward delivery terms. Farmers' market customers can taste and buy on the spot. This approach aligns marketing spend with a direct proof point: the product must perform in real customer use.

Sales execution will require founder discipline. In Year 1, Priya and Tom will need to balance production, delivery, customer service and selling. The plan assumes that sales effort will continue consistently even when production becomes busy. Independent café sales can be slow because owners are cautious about changing suppliers. The 30-account target by Year 3 reflects this reality: it is a staged target rather than an assumption that accounts will convert immediately.

Retention is as important as acquisition. In wholesale, retention depends on reliable coffee, reliable delivery, quick problem resolution and useful training. In subscription, retention depends on monthly consistency, packaging quality and customer service. In farmers' markets, retention depends on familiarity, quality and approachable communication. If retention is poor, marketing spend will be wasted on replacing lost customers. The plan's financial structure assumes stable gross margins and controlled operating costs, so retention is essential to reaching the projected operating profits.

The sales and marketing plan is therefore realistic and targeted. It uses direct channels, leverages founder skills, relies on product demonstration and keeps marketing spend within planned amounts. The most important commercial assumption is not a single sales event but the company's ability to create a small but reliable customer base over three years.

7. Management and Staffing

The management strength of Ember & Oak is its founder experience. Priya Anand brings eight years of experience as head roaster at a regional roastery. This experience is central to product quality, roaster management, green lot handling, production scheduling and consistency. For a small speciality roaster, the roaster is not merely an operator; it is a key determinant of whether customers accept the product. Priya's experience supports quality control and helps the company make credible product claims without needing a large technical team.

Tom Keller brings ten years of experience in hospitality sales and café management. This is equally important because Ember & Oak's wholesale model depends on independent cafés. Tom understands the pressures faced by café owners and baristas: staffing, workflow, drink quality, customer complaints, service consistency and supplier relationships. His background supports the sales plan, especially the emphasis on barista training and practical customer support. He can also help shape operations so that production and delivery meet café expectations.

The founders' skills are complementary. A roaster who can deliver excellent coffee but cannot sell may struggle to build wholesale accounts. A hospitality operator who can sell but cannot control roast quality may damage customer trust. Together, Priya and Tom cover the two most important business functions: making the product reliably good, and converting customers into repeat accounts and subscribers.

The staffing plan is reflected through the salary line. Salaries including the founders are budgeted at 72,000 in Year 1, 98,000 in Year 2 and 124,000 in Year 3. In Year 1, the founders will personally cover many tasks, including production oversight, sales calls, delivery, market presence, subscription fulfilment, customer service and administrative control. The salary budget is therefore not only a labour cost; it is the company's capacity to meet growing service demand without overburdening the founders.

As revenue grows, the need for support becomes clearer. By Year 2 and Year 3, the plan anticipates additional help for packing, dispatch, market selling, delivery coordination and customer support. The salary line increases from 72,000 to 98,000 between Year 1 and Year 2, and then to 124,000 in Year 3. This increase is significant, but it is tied to a much larger revenue base. Total revenue increases from 226,800 to 476,800, while salaries increase by 52,000 from Year 1 to Year 3. Gross profit increases by 155,000 over the same period, which gives room for the salary increase while still improving operating profit.

The management structure is deliberately small. This is realistic for a company funded by a 60,000 loan and a 45,000 founder contribution. The business does not have the resources to support a large management layer. Instead, it should maintain clear responsibilities: Priya as the technical lead on roasting and quality; Tom as the commercial lead on sales, customer relationships and market operations; and both founders sharing responsibility for cash control, compliance and company direction.

Founder commitment will be visible through the funding request. The founders are investing 45,000 of their own money, which is 42.9% of total start-up costs. This personal investment aligns their interests with the bank's interest in disciplined execution. It also means the founders have direct accountability for the company's early cash position. If Year 1 revenue runs slower than planned, the personal contribution and the 20,000 working capital element become important buffers.

A realistic staffing risk is key-person dependency. Priya's roasting knowledge and Tom's hospitality relationships are central. If one founder is absent for an extended period, the other can cover some functions, but not all of them at the same depth. The company should reduce this risk by cross-training support staff, documenting production routines, keeping green lot and roast records clear, and maintaining a customer base that is not dependent on one individual for every sale.

The company should also avoid overhiring too early. Year 1 salaries of 72,000 must be supported by operating profit of only 8,616. The plan therefore depends on disciplined cost management and not adding payroll before revenue can support it. By Year 2 and Year 3, higher salaries are justified by larger volumes and a more established customer base. The staffing plan is therefore conservative at the start and gradually builds capacity.

For the bank, the management plan should be seen as simple but relevant. The company has two founders with directly useful experience, a modest staffing cost line and a clear need to grow payroll only as revenue grows. The main management challenge is not organisational complexity but consistency: the founders must maintain quality, service and cash discipline while growing from 300 to 800 average subscribers and from 6,000 kg to 12,000 kg of wholesale volume.

| Depreciation | 12,000 | 12,000 | 12,000 | 36,000 |
| Total operating expenses | 132,000 | 161,000 | 189,000 | 482,000 |
| Operating profit | 8,616 | 57,736 | 106,616 | 172,968 |

Cost of goods sold is calculated as 38% of total revenue in each year. Year 1 cost of goods sold is 226,800 multiplied by 38%, which equals 86,184. Year 2 cost of goods sold is 352,800 multiplied by 38%, which equals 134,064. Year 3 cost of goods sold is 476,800 multiplied by 38%, which equals 181,184. Because cost of goods sold is 38% of revenue, gross profit is always 62.0% of revenue. Year 1 gross profit is 140,616, which is 62.0% of 226,800. Year 2 gross profit is 218,736, which is 62.0% of 352,800. Year 3 gross profit is 295,616, which is 62.0% of 476,800. The three-year total gross profit is 654,968, which is 62.0% of the three-year total revenue of 1,056,400.

Operating profit is calculated as Gross profit minus Total operating expenses. Year 1 operating profit is 140,616 minus 132,000, which equals 8,616. Year 2 operating profit is 218,736 minus 161,000, which equals 57,736. Year 3 operating profit is 295,616 minus 189,000, which equals 106,616. The three-year total operating profit is 172,968.

The gross margin for each year is 62.0%. The operating margin for Year 1 is 3.8%. The operating margin for Year 2 is 16.4%. The operating margin for Year 3 is 22.4%. The three-year operating margin is 16.4%, based on total operating profit of 172,968 divided by total revenue of 1,056,400.

The change in operating profit from Year 1 to Year 3 is driven primarily by revenue growth and operating leverage. Total revenue increases from 226,800 to 476,800, an increase of 250,000. Because gross margin remains at 62.0%, gross profit increases from 140,616 to 295,616, an increase of 155,000. At the same time, Total operating expenses rise from 132,000 to 189,000, an increase of only 57,000. The main reason operating expenses rise more slowly than gross profit is that several costs are fixed or grow more slowly than revenue. Rent remains 24,000 per year, utilities and insurance remain 9,000 per year, and depreciation remains 12,000 per year. Marketing rises only from 15,000 to 20,000, and salaries rise from 72,000 to 124,000. Although salaries are a significant increase, the increase of 52,000 is much smaller than the 155,000 increase in gross profit. This creates the operating profit improvement from 8,616 in Year 1 to 106,616 in Year 3.

Year 1 is the weakest year because the company is still building revenue while carrying most of its fixed operating costs. Rent, salaries, marketing, utilities and insurance are already in place before the company has achieved the higher revenue levels of Year 2 and Year 3. In Year 1, gross profit of 140,616 covers Total operating expenses of 132,000, leaving a positive but thin operating profit of 8,616. This is realistic for a roastery in its first year. The plan does not hide this fact. Instead, it shows why the working capital request is prudent.

Year 2 improves because revenue grows by 55.6% from Year 1 to Year 2, while cost of goods sold rises proportionally at 38% of revenue. Gross profit increases by 78,120 from Year 1 to Year 2. Total operating expenses increase by 29,000 from Year 1 to Year 2, mainly because salaries increase by 26,000 and marketing increases by 3,000. Rent, utilities and depreciation remain unchanged. This produces operating profit growth from 8,616 to 57,736.

Year 3 improves further because revenue grows by 35.1% from Year 2 to Year 3. Gross profit increases by 76,880 from Year 2 to Year 3. Total operating expenses increase by 28,000 from Year 2 to Year 3, mainly because salaries increase by 26,000 and marketing increases by 2,000. Rent, utilities and depreciation remain unchanged. Operating profit rises from 57,736 to 106,616. The plan therefore shows that profitability depends not on a change in gross margin, because the margin is fixed, but on converting revenue growth into gross profit while controlling operating expenses.

The financial plan also supports the loan servicing discussion. Because depreciation is a non-cash expense, operating profit plus depreciation provides a useful proxy for cash available from operations before working capital changes and before interest and tax. Operating profit plus depreciation is 8,616 plus 12,000, which equals 20,616 in Year 1. It is 57,736 plus 12,000, which equals 69,736 in Year 2. It is 106,616 plus 12,000, which equals 118,616 in Year 3. These figures exclude interest and tax because the financial tables ignore those items. They also exclude changes in working capital, which is why the 20,000 working capital element remains important.

9. Risks and Mitigations

A business plan should not present the future as certain. Ember & Oak has several risks that a lending officer should expect to see addressed. The first is customer acquisition. The plan targets 30 wholesale accounts by the end of Year 3. This is achievable but not guaranteed. The second is subscription retention, because revenue depends on average subscribers of 300, 550 and 800 rather than one-off purchases. The third is input cost risk, because cost of goods sold is assumed at 38% of total revenue and includes green coffee, packaging and subscription shipping. The fourth is working capital risk, because inventory purchases may occur before customer payments arrive. The fifth is key-person and production risk, because a small company depends heavily on founder expertise and one roaster. The sixth is debt service risk, especially in Year 1 before interest, if not managed carefully.

The following table summarises the six main risks and how the company intends to manage them.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wholesale account acquisition is slower than the plan assumes, so Year 1 and Year 2 volumes fall short. | Medium | High | Focus sales on independent cafés indicated by the survey, use samples, tastings and barista training, target 30 accounts by Year 3, and maintain realistic Year 1 volumes. |
| Subscription churn is higher than planned, reducing average subscribers below 300, 550 and 800. | Medium | High | Maintain consistent quality, reliable monthly shipping, clear customer communication, controlled marketing spend and a simple 1 kg monthly product. |
| Green coffee, packaging or shipping costs exceed the 38% of revenue assumption, reducing gross profit. | Medium | High | Use two importers, monitor lot costs, control packaging waste, manage shipping volumes and keep production efficient without over-roasting. |
| Working capital pressure occurs because inventory, rent, salaries and market costs are paid before enough revenue is collected. | Medium | Medium | Include 20,000 working capital in the funding request, use founder contribution of 45,000, monitor cash weekly, and avoid over-ordering green coffee or retail stock. |
| Founder availability or single-roaster capacity creates a production bottleneck or service disruption. | Medium | High | Use the founders' complementary experience, maintain the roaster and ventilation system, schedule production carefully, and build support capacity as salaries grow. |
| Debt service is not affordable if Year 1 performance is weaker than projected or interest and working capital needs are higher than expected. | Medium | High | Keep Year 1 loan-funded costs controlled, show positive Year 1 operating profit of 8,616, use working capital prudently, and rely on Year 2 and Year 3 operating profit improvement. |

The most serious risk is not a single event but the accumulation of small problems. If wholesale accounts delay, subscription churn rises, and green costs increase at the same time, Year 1 cash flow could become tight. The plan mitigates this by avoiding excessive debt, requiring a founder contribution, including working capital, using two importers, keeping marketing spend within budget and building a target that is 30 accounts out of 180 independent cafés rather than assuming widespread market adoption.

Another risk is quality failure. In speciality coffee, a few inconsistent roast batches can damage reputation quickly. Priya Anand's eight years of head-roaster experience is a mitigation, but it is not enough on its own. The company must maintain clear lot records, roast samples before releasing new lots, train baristas properly and monitor wholesale customer feedback. The farmers' markets provide early direct feedback, which can help identify issues before they affect larger wholesale accounts.

Debt service risk requires the most careful framing. The financial tables exclude interest and tax, so the plan cannot quantify exact debt service. However, it can show the underlying operating profitability. Year 1 operating profit of 8,616 is positive, and operating profit plus depreciation of 20,616 provides a buffer before working capital changes. The founders' 45,000 contribution and the 20,000 working capital element are specifically intended to reduce the chance that a slow start leads to an inability to meet early obligations. If Year 1 revenue is strong and Year 2 growth follows, the loan servicing position improves rapidly.

The risk management approach is therefore practical. The company will monitor revenue by channel, track wholesale accounts, watch subscription activity, monitor cost of goods sold against the 38% assumption, control cash by reviewing payments and receipts weekly, and maintain the production facility proactively. These controls are not sophisticated, but they are appropriate for a small company and directly tied to the numbers in the plan.

10. Funding Request

Ember & Oak Coffee Roasters requests a five-year loan of 60,000. The total start-up requirement is 105,000, made up of a roaster costing 60,000, unit fit-out and ventilation costing 25,000, and working capital of 20,000. The founders will contribute 45,000 of their own money. The loan therefore funds 57.1% of the total start-up requirement, while the founders contribute 42.9%. This structure is important for the bank because the founders are taking meaningful financial risk, and the requested loan is sized to the core assets and opening working capital needed to operate a small roastery.

The funding request is directly linked to the business model. The roaster is the essential production asset, costing 60,000. The 180 m² light-industrial unit cannot operate as a coffee roastery without fit-out and ventilation, costing 25,000. The working capital of 20,000 is required because the company will need to buy green coffee, packaging and retail inventory, pay rent, salaries, utilities and marketing costs, and wait for revenue to convert into cash. This is particularly relevant in Year 1, when the company has not yet built a long operating history.

The plan shows that the business can support the funding request through operating profit. Operating profit is 8,616 in Year 1, 57,736 in Year 2 and 106,616 in Year 3. Over three years, operating profit totals 172,968. Year 1 is positive but modest, which is realistic. The company should not be judged only on Year 1 profit because the first year includes establishment costs, market education, account acquisition and production testing. The 20,000 working capital budget and 45,000 founder contribution are specifically included to help the business navigate Year 1.

The loan servicing position can be assessed using operating profit plus depreciation. Depreciation of 12,000 per year is a non-cash accounting charge. Adding depreciation back to operating profit gives a useful proxy for operating cash available before working capital changes and before interest and tax, because the financial tables ignore interest and tax. Operating profit plus depreciation is 20,616 in Year 1, 69,736 in Year 2 and 118,616 in Year 3. If the loan were repaid over five years with an equal annual principal component, the annual principal repayment would be 12,000. Year 1 cash operating profit covers that principal repayment 1.7 times before interest and tax; Year 2 covers it 5.8 times; and Year 3 covers it 9.9 times.

The strongest support for the loan is not the Year 1 figure alone but the combination of three-year cash generation and controlled cost structure. The company has a gross margin of 62.0% in every year because cost of goods sold is fixed at 38% of revenue. Total revenue grows from 226,800 to 476,800 across the three years, increasing gross profit by 155,000 while Total operating expenses increase by only 57,000. This operating leverage is what produces the profit growth and supports the loan.

The founders are not asking the bank to fund an oversized start-up. The funding request is limited to the main equipment, the necessary premises work and a working capital reserve. The loan amount is fully supported by tangible production assets and the projected operating plan. The founders are contributing a significant personal investment, the Year 1 profit is positive, the three-year profit total is substantial relative to the loan amount, and the financial plan is based on stated volumes, prices and costs rather than speculative market claims.

Ember & Oak Coffee Roasters is therefore seeking a 60,000 five-year loan on a reasonable and focused basis. The company has a local market gap, relevant founder experience, a simple product and service model, a realistic wholesale target, a subscription model that builds recurring revenue, and a three-year financial plan that moves from cautious Year 1 profitability to strong Year 3 operating profit. The requested funding should allow the business to install its equipment, prepare its premises, buy initial inventory and begin trading in Halbrook with a clear plan for growth and repayment.
