# Introduction and Goals

This guide is the migration plan for Basketly’s move from one monolithic web application to eight independently deployed services. It is written for the 60 engineers across our nine product teams and their managers. Most readers will know the monolith well, but few will have led a migration of this size. The purpose of this document is to give every team the same answer to the same practical questions: what happens first, what happens next, what must not be skipped, and how we will know whether a step is working or failing.

The migration will take roughly 18 months. It is not a rewrite and it is not a big-bang launch. We are using the strangler-fig pattern: a routing layer in front of the monolith gradually directs traffic for one extracted capability to a new service at a time, while the monolith continues to serve everything else. The goal is not to create services for their own sake. The goal is to remove the monolith as the main constraint on delivery speed, reliability, and peak trading.

The first extraction, Notifications, is now recorded in Case Study: Extracting Notifications; the next teams should read it before planning a cutover.

The business problem is visible in the constraints described in the next chapter. A full deploy takes 38 minutes, we deploy only twice a week, the test suite is long and flaky, modules reach directly into each other’s tables, and the release freeze in the four weeks before Christmas compresses our ability to make risky changes exactly when reliability matters most. We want to change that pattern by creating services that can be tested, deployed, scaled, and rolled back independently.

The target end state is eight services, extracted in the approved order: Notifications, Search, Catalog, Inventory, Cart, Orders, Payments, and Checkout. Each service owns its data. No service reads another service’s tables. Queries use synchronous APIs. State changes are communicated through events through a message broker. The routing layer, a message broker, a container platform, and relational databases are used as generic infrastructure components rather than as product-specific magic. The migration will be supported by change data capture from the monolith’s database, the transactional outbox pattern in new services, automated reconciliation, contract testing, production-like load testing, and controlled traffic shifts.

The programme has five explicit goals.

First, reduce deployment coupling. By the end of the programme, a team should be able to deploy its service without building and deploying the whole monolith. The monolith will still exist for a time, but it should shrink after each capability is extracted.

Second, protect checkout reliability. Checkout is the commercial centre of Basketly. At peak traffic, checkout latency must improve, not degrade. The cut-over gate is defined later: an error rate above 1% for 5 minutes, or checkout p95 latency above 800 ms for 10 minutes, is a rollback trigger. Those thresholds are deliberately stricter than the current peak p95 of 1.9 seconds because a service extraction that makes checkout slower is not a migration win.

Third, establish data ownership. Today, several modules read and write each other’s tables directly. That is the most dangerous hidden coupling. The migration requires an explicit table ownership map, an end to direct cross-module table writes, and a controlled path for moving writes from the monolith to a service.

Fourth, make testing a migration engine rather than a migration blocker. A 52-minute flaky suite cannot be the only safety net. Each service needs fast unit and contract tests, a deterministic integration environment, and end-to-end checkout journeys that can be run repeatedly with confidence.

Fifth, create a governance model that can survive the next eighteen months. This includes who approves readiness, how teams handle the Christmas release freeze, how incidents are triaged during cutover, and how we prevent “half-migrated” states from becoming permanent.

The programme is deliberately conservative. Every step should be small enough to reverse, observable enough to trust, and valuable enough to justify the additional infrastructure. We are not trying to create eight services at once. We are trying to create eight clear boundaries that can be verified one by one.

# The Current Monolith

Basketly’s current system is one Python web application with approximately 640,000 lines of code and one relational database containing 212 tables. The application serves shopper pages, administration workflows, background jobs, search, cart, checkout, order history, returns, stock updates, payment calls, and notifications from a single deployable unit. This is not a trivial monolith. It contains most of Basketly’s domain logic, operational knowledge, and historical exceptions.

The deployment model has 14 identical instances behind a load balancer. A full deploy takes 38 minutes, and the organisation deploys twice a week. That is not simply slow; it shapes behaviour. Teams batch changes, avoid risky refactors, and defer non-urgent fixes because the deploy cost is high. The release freeze in the four weeks before Christmas compounds this: the most commercially sensitive period is also the period with the least deployment capacity.

The database is the second major coupling point. The 212 tables are not neatly grouped by bounded contexts. In many places, a module that should communicate with another module through a service interface reads and writes that module’s tables directly. That means a schema change in one area can break code in another area, and a migration cannot be performed by moving code alone. It must also move data access, ownership, validation, and eventing.

Traffic is high and predictable. Peak load reaches 2,300 requests per second on Saturday mornings. Checkout p95 latency at peak is 1.9 seconds. That latency includes work for inventory checks, pricing, payment provider calls, order creation, and notifications triggered by the order. During peak, the system is close enough to its practical limits that any additional synchronisation or poorly designed service fan-out can make things worse rather than better.

Background work runs in a job queue inside the same codebase. Emails, stock updates, and search indexing are part of the same application and therefore share its deploy cycle, failure modes, and resource limits. If checkout traffic spikes while a large stock-indexing job is running, the same process pool and queue workers can compete for the same capacity. This makes the current system operationally coherent but also operationally fragile: a batch job can affect an interactive path.

The test suite takes 52 minutes and is flaky about 1 run in 6 for reasons unrelated to the change. This is a major migration risk because migration depends on frequent verification. If every validation is a long, noisy test suite run, teams will avoid running it, ignore failures, or treat a red run as normal. The migration therefore requires a different testing model, described in Chapter 8.

There are five specific coupling patterns the migration must address.

Schema coupling is the most severe. Direct table access hides dependencies from code review and prevents clean service boundaries. A migration phase is not complete until we have removed those direct dependencies and replaced them with an API, an event, or a read-only projection owned by the correct service.

Deployment coupling is the second pattern. Even if two modules are logically separable, if they are deployed together they cannot fail or be scaled independently. The routing layer helps expose this: when we route one capability to a new service, we can see whether the monolith can still continue serving the rest.

Queue coupling is the third. Background jobs inside the monolith can consume resources needed by web requests and can depend on table shapes that migration will change. The migration plan therefore moves queue ownership alongside the service that owns the data, not as an afterthought.

Test coupling is the fourth. A shared test suite is a shared deployment risk. A flaky test can block the release of an unrelated change, and a long suite discourages frequent verification. Each new service should carry its own fast tests, and the monolith should retain only the tests needed until it is decomposed.

Observability coupling is the fifth. In a monolith, one request may contain many logical steps. Once services are involved, we need a request identity that follows through the routing layer, synchronous calls, events, and queue retries. Without that, incident response becomes guesswork. The migration should therefore treat tracing, structured logging, and metric correlation as platform work, not optional polish.

The current monolith is not “bad code” in a general sense. It encodes years of Basketly trading rules. The migration must preserve that knowledge while making it independently deployable. The danger is not that we will rewrite too little; it is that we will move code without moving ownership, validation, tests, metrics, and rollback responsibility. The rest of this guide is organised around preventing that outcome.

# Target Architecture

The target architecture is a strangler-fig system built around a routing layer and eight capabilities. The routing layer sits in front of the monolith and the services. By default, it sends a request to the monolith. For an extracted capability, the routing layer sends the request to the owning service. This is the primary control point for gradual cutover and rollback. It is not a code-level rewrite switch inside the monolith; it is an operational boundary that can be changed without redeploying the monolith.

Each of the eight services owns its own relational database. A service may cache data, may maintain read models, and may store local event records, but it does not read another service’s tables. If a capability needs information owned by another service, it uses a synchronous API for queries or an event for state changes. Synchronous APIs are appropriate when the caller needs an immediate answer, such as fetching a product price or reserving stock. Events are appropriate when the consequence can be processed asynchronously, such as sending a notification after an order is created or updating a search index after a product price changes.

All services run on the same container platform and use the same operational conventions: health checks, readiness probes, structured logs, request IDs, metric names, alert templates, and secret handling. The shared platform is what keeps eight services from becoming eight small monoliths. The platform team provides the service template, but the owning team owns the behaviour of its service.

The message broker is the backbone for state-change communication. Events are published from the transactional outbox pattern: a service writes to its own database and records the event in the same transaction. A relay then publishes the event to the broker. This avoids the dual-write problem: application code never updates a database and a broker in two separate systems. If the database transaction commits, the event is eventually published. If it rolls back, the event is not published.

A small shared identity and contract mechanism is needed, but it is not a separate business service. Contract artefacts include synchronous API request and response shapes, event schemas, and topic or queue names. These artefacts are versioned and tested. Breaking changes require a deprecation period and explicit sign-off. This is the governance that prevents one team’s “internal refactor” from becoming another team’s production incident.

The target architecture also changes how the checkout path works. Checkout is not a single long database transaction that reaches into cart, inventory, payment, and order tables. It is an orchestration. The checkout service validates the request, calls Cart and Catalog synchronously for current state, calls Inventory for reservation, calls Payments for payment processing, and creates Orders either synchronously or through a confirmed workflow with compensating actions. The exact order is defined in the service plan, but the principle is constant: checkout may coordinate, but it does not own other services’ data.

Background jobs are replaced by event-driven consumers. Notifications consumes order and customer events. Search consumes catalog and inventory events. Inventory consumes order and return events. The monolith job queue may continue to run for capabilities that have not yet migrated, but each migrated capability moves its queue responsibility into the owning service.

The target table below defines the eight services, the data they own, the owning team, and the migration phase in which they are introduced. The table is the authoritative summary for ownership and phase assignment. Later chapters expand the operational consequences without repeating the summary.

| Service | Data it owns | Owning team | Phase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Notifications | message templates, channel preferences, delivery attempts, unsubscribe and suppression data, delivery status events | Communications Team | Phase 1 |
| Search | search indexes, autocomplete dictionaries, synonyms, ranking configuration, query analytics read models | Discovery Team | Phase 1 |
| Catalog | products, categories, product attributes, price rules, publication state | Catalog Team | Phase 2 |
| Inventory | stock levels per warehouse, reservations, adjustment ledger, warehouse allocation configuration | Supply Chain Team | Phase 2 |
| Cart | anonymous and authenticated cart state, cart lines, cart merge history, cart expiry data | Cart Team | Phase 3 |
| Orders | order history, order items, order status, return requests, return status | Order Management Team | Phase 3 |
| Payments | payment attempts, provider references, refunds, reconciliation records, idempotency keys for financial operations | Payments Team | Phase 4 |
| Checkout | checkout sessions, orchestration state, checkout idempotency records, saga compensation records | Checkout Team | Phase 4 |

The architecture has three hard rules.

Rule one: one owner per table. A table may be read by a migration projection for a limited time, but once a service is authoritative, only that service writes the data. Any direct write path left behind is a failed migration.

Rule two: synchronous queries, asynchronous state changes. A service should not depend on another service’s event to answer a customer-facing question that must be immediate. If a shopper needs to know whether an item is available now, that is a synchronous reservation or query concern. If a warehouse stock adjustment can be processed later, that can be an event.

Rule three: every migration path must have an exit. For every extracted capability, we must know when the monolith path is no longer needed. That means monitoring reads and writes to the legacy table, removing dead code, and deleting obsolete routes. A capability is not migrated just because it exists in a new service.

# The Strangler-Fig Approach

The strangler-fig approach is chosen because the monolith cannot be replaced safely all at once. The routing layer allows us to move one capability at a time while preserving the existing system as a fallback. The key operational principle is that migration is not a single deployment. It is a series of controlled traffic shifts, each with an observable exit condition.

A capability is extracted in four general states. The first state is discovery: the team maps routes, jobs, tables, metrics, and business rules related to the capability. The second state is shadowing: the new service receives replicated requests or events but does not affect production customer outcomes. The third state is gradual traffic shifting: a small percentage of users or entities are routed to the service, then increased in stages. The fourth state is ownership: the service is authoritative for its data and the monolith path is removed.

The routing layer is central. For read-oriented capabilities such as Search and historical Orders queries, traffic can be shifted by request percentage. For write-oriented capabilities, percentage means percentage of stable entities, not independent requests. For example, 1% of Cart traffic should mean 1% of cart IDs or user IDs, selected consistently. Otherwise the same cart could be handled by both paths and create divergence. Checkout, Cart, and Orders therefore require stable-key routing.

Each shift has a decision gate. Before moving from 1% to 5%, from 5% to 25%, and from 25% to 50%, the owning team and the migration board review the same set of signals: error rate, latency, business metrics, broker lag, database lag, reconciliation results, and support complaints. Expansion is not automatic. A service that performs well at 1% may fail at 50% because of cache behaviour, connection pool limits, broker partition hot spots, or event replay load.

Shadowing is the first useful step for read services. Search is a natural shadow candidate because a new search service can answer queries in parallel, and the results can be compared without showing them to shoppers. For write services, shadowing is more careful. Notifications can shadow message generation without sending messages by writing the intended delivery attempt and comparing it with the monolith decision. Checkout cannot shadow a payment without side effects, so its shadowing is limited to validation, pricing, reservation dry runs, and orchestration timing in a non-production or sandbox environment.

The strangler-fig pattern also requires that the monolith continue to behave correctly for customers still on the old path. That means during migration some data may exist in two places: authoritative in the service, projected in the monolith for compatibility. This is allowed only when it is driven by events or a projection consumer, not by application code writing the same record to two databases. The migration data plan in Chapter 7 explains how projections are kept consistent and when they can be removed.

We will know the pattern is working when three facts are true. First, routing changes are the primary way production behaviour changes, not monolith code changes. Second, an incident can be narrowed to either the monolith path or the service path quickly. Third, after each successful cutover, the monolith loses tables, code, jobs, and tests rather than merely gaining a new service.

We will know the pattern is failing when the routing layer becomes the source of hidden business logic, when teams maintain permanent duplicate code paths, or when rollback requires emergency database surgery instead of a controlled traffic shift. Those are governance failures, not merely technical issues, and they are addressed in Chapter 10.

# Migration Phases

The migration is organised into four phases. Each phase extracts a coherent group of capabilities and adds the platform, data, and testing capability needed for the next phase. The phase order is fixed because later phases depend on boundaries created earlier. Notifications and Search establish the routing and eventing pattern. Catalog and Inventory establish the core product and supply data model. Cart and Orders extend the pattern to the customer journey and its durable record. Payments and Checkout are last because they have the highest financial and operational risk.

## Phase 1: Foundation and Low-Risk Capabilities

Phase 1 builds the strangler-fig foundation and extracts Notifications and Search. This phase is deliberately chosen because Notifications has a relatively small blast radius and Search is read-heavy and can be shadowed. The work is not only to launch two services but to prove that the routing layer, service template, message broker, outbox pattern, contract tests, and rollback process are reliable enough for more complex capabilities.

The first concrete task is to create the routing layer with an operational change process. Every routing change must have an owner, a scope, a rollback path, and a monitoring dashboard. The routing layer should expose metrics by backend, route, and capability. If the routing layer cannot show which backend is receiving traffic, it cannot be trusted.

The second task is to create the shared service template. It should include request tracing, structured logging, health and readiness endpoints, database migration scripts, a local development environment, and CI/CD templates. The goal is that a team can start a new service in days, not weeks.

The third task is to implement the transactional outbox pattern in Notifications as the first service. Notifications is a good candidate because its state changes are mostly delivery attempts and preference changes, and it can consume events without directly creating irreversible financial effects. The outbox implementation should be reusable, tested with duplicate delivery, and verified under broker restart.

Search follows Notifications because it tests the same pattern at higher read volume. Search is not a trivial service: at 2,300 requests per second, an inefficient index or cache design will be visible immediately. The service should begin with read-only shadow traffic and then gradually serve live traffic. Its first milestone is not “index is built”; it is “results match accepted business expectations and latency is acceptable under production-like load.”

Phase 1 completion requires the following evidence. The routing layer is in production and has been used for at least one rollback drill. Notifications is serving all notification traffic from its own database with no direct monolith table writes for its owned data. Search is serving all search traffic with acceptable p95 latency and no material regression in conversion or no-result rates. Contract tests cover the event schemas published by the first services. The platform team has run a full load test using production-like data.

Case Study: Extracting Notifications records how the first of these services, Notifications, overran its plan and rolled back once.

## Phase 2: Product and Supply Foundations

Phase 2 extracts Catalog and Inventory. These services form the product and supply foundation for commerce. Catalog is the source of truth for products, categories, and prices. Inventory is the source of truth for stock levels and reservations. Together they reduce direct table access across the 212-table schema and create stable identifiers and events that later services can trust.

The first task is a comprehensive table ownership audit. The team should classify every relevant table as monolith-only, Catalog-owned, Inventory-owned, or obsolete. Direct cross-module table access must be listed, even if it is “only read” or “only admin,” because read access can become a hidden coupling during later phases.

Catalog migration follows the ownership audit. Catalog should take over product, category, attribute, and price data. The service should expose synchronous query APIs for cart and checkout, and publish events for product updates, price changes, and publication status changes. Search consumes those events. Any monolith admin workflow that currently writes catalog tables must move to Catalog APIs before Catalog can be considered authoritative.

Inventory follows Catalog because inventory rows depend on stable product identities. Inventory owns stock levels per warehouse and reservation records. This is one of the most dangerous data domains because reservation races can cause overselling. The service must implement conditional reservation updates, reservation expiry, and an adjustment ledger. It should publish events for stock changes, reservation expiry, and cancellation.

Phase 2 completion requires evidence that product and supply data are no longer shared through tables. Catalog must have zero direct table writers outside its service boundary. Inventory must demonstrate that reservations never exceed available stock under load, including duplicate reservation requests and network retries. Reconciliation must prove that total inventory, reservations, and order decrements agree with the authoritative data model. The monolith job queue should no longer be responsible for migrated catalog or inventory background work.

## Phase 3: Customer Journey Services

Phase 3 extracts Cart and Orders. These services extend the migration from product and supply data into the customer journey. Cart owns active shopping state. Orders owns the durable history of what happened and what the customer can see. This phase is less financially dangerous than Checkout or Payments, but it is operationally visible because shoppers notice lost carts, missing order history, and confusing returns.

Cart is extracted first because checkout orchestration needs a clean cart contract. Cart owns cart lines, expiry, and merge state. It should query Catalog synchronously for product and price information and use Inventory availability information according to the business rules decided during design. Cart should not reserve inventory; reservation belongs in Checkout. That separation prevents carts from holding stock indefinitely and makes checkout failures easier to reason about.

Orders is extracted after Cart because Orders is largely event-driven and read-heavy, except for admin and customer-initiated return workflows. Orders owns order history, order items, status, and returns. It consumes order-created events from Checkout and payment or refund events where relevant. It should provide query APIs for customer account pages and support tools. Historical data migration is a major concern because customers must be able to see past orders without gaps.

Phase 3 completion requires that Cart and Orders can operate without direct table access to Checkout, Payments, Catalog, or Inventory. Cart must show no lost carts during a staged user traffic shift. Orders must show complete historical coverage and correct status transitions. Return eligibility rules must be tested against production-like history, including edge cases such as partial refunds, cancelled items, and warehouse adjustments.

## Phase 4: Financial and Transactional Core

Phase 4 extracts Payments and Checkout. These capabilities are deliberately last because they carry the highest commercial and compliance risk. Payments integrates with external payment providers and must not introduce double captures, lost captures, or inconsistent refunds. Checkout orchestrates cart, inventory, payment, and order creation, and must meet stricter latency and reliability expectations than any other service.

Payments is extracted before Checkout so that Checkout can orchestrate a stable payment boundary instead of a changing monolith payment path. Payments owns payment attempts, provider references, refunds, reconciliation records, and idempotency keys. It should not be a general “orders” service or a copy of the order model. It should own only payment and refund facts.

Checkout is extracted last. It uses Cart, Inventory, Payments, and Orders, but it must not own their data. Its role is orchestration: validate the cart, ensure inventory reservation, obtain payment authorisation or capture according to policy, create the order, and handle compensating actions when a step fails. Checkout must be designed for partial failure, because provider calls and database commits do not happen atomically across multiple services.

Phase 4 completion requires evidence that the new checkout path can handle peak Saturday traffic with checkout p95 latency below the rollback threshold defined in Chapter 9. It also requires financial reconciliation: no unexplained provider charge mismatches, no duplicate order creations, and a tested rollback procedure for in-flight checkouts. The programme is not complete until the monolith checkout route can be disabled without emergency intervention.

# Service-by-Service Plan

## Notifications

Notifications is the first service because its failure mode is usually recoverable and visible. It moves email, SMS, and push message generation, message templates, channel selection, delivery attempts, retry logic, and preference enforcement. It does not own customer identity, order history, product data, or payment status. It owns only the facts needed to decide whether and how to message a customer.

The data it takes over is message templates, channel preferences, delivery attempts, suppression and unsubscribe records, and delivery status. It may store a short-lived snapshot of message context for audit and debugging, but it should not become a second source of truth for orders, carts, or catalog items.

Its dependencies on the monolith are user contact information, marketing consent, order context, and account state. These should be consumed through events or queried through the appropriate owning service once those services exist. During the migration, the monolith may provide these inputs through an internal compatibility API or through projected events. Dependencies on other services are mostly event consumers: Orders emits order lifecycle events, Inventory may emit stock-replenishment events, and Catalog may emit back-in-stock or price-change events where permitted.

The specific risks are duplication, stale preferences, and provider rate limits. Duplicate messages can occur if events are replayed and delivery attempts are not idempotent. Preference drift can occur if consent is checked in the monolith and again in Notifications with inconsistent logic. Provider throttling can create backlog during order peaks, especially if templates are changed or batch campaigns compete with transactional messages. We will know these risks are present if duplicate-send rate rises, suppression checks are bypassed, or delivery lag increases beyond the accepted service-level objective.

See Case Study: Extracting Notifications for the first extraction's actual template overrun, rollback, and measured result.

## Search

Search moves product search, autocomplete, synonym handling, ranking configuration, and search analytics. It owns the searchable projection of product data, not the product master itself. It may also own autocomplete dictionaries and search-term analytics, because those are derived from query behaviour.

The data it takes over is the search index, autocomplete state, synonyms, ranking configuration, and query analytics read models. It consumes Catalog events for product and price changes and Inventory events for stock status, where the ranking or filtering logic requires availability.

Its dependencies on the monolith are primarily the web routes that currently invoke search logic. Its dependencies on other services are Catalog for product facts, Inventory for stock status, and Orders or Cart for popularity signals only if those signals are explicitly part of ranking. Search should not synchronously query Orders during a search request, because that would couple high-volume read traffic to order history latency.

The specific risks are stale results, index rebuild load, latency regression, and conversion damage. A search result showing an out-of-stock item is tolerable if the cart or checkout path correctly prevents purchase, but it damages trust. A search index rebuild that locks resources can degrade peak service. We will know these risks are present if search latency increases, no-result rates rise, click-through to catalog conversion falls, or index lag exceeds the threshold set by the team.

## Catalog

Catalog moves product records, category trees, product attributes, publication state, and price rules. It becomes the authoritative source for the data that shoppers see and that Cart and Checkout use to validate a purchase. Catalog does not own inventory quantities or reservations; it may own price and product facts only.

The data it takes over is products, categories, attributes, price records, and publication metadata. During migration, Catalog may project a compatibility representation into monolith tables if monolith features still depend on those tables, but that projection must be event-driven and time-boxed.

Its dependencies on the monolith are administrative workflows, legacy cache keys, and any code that reads or writes product and price tables directly. Its dependencies on other services are primarily consumers: Search consumes catalog updates, Cart queries Catalog, Checkout queries Catalog, and Notifications may consume price-change events. Catalog may also depend on Inventory for publication rules such as “do not display when out of stock,” but that should be expressed through an availability query or event rather than by Catalog writing to Inventory.

The specific risks are price inconsistency, hidden table readers, and cache invalidation failures. The most serious operational failure is a shopper seeing one price on a product page and another price in checkout. We will know this risk is present if shadow comparisons detect price differences, checkout cart totals disagree with catalog prices, or legacy tables still receive writes after the cutover.

## Inventory

Inventory moves stock levels per warehouse, reservations, cancellation releases, and adjustment history. It is one of the most sensitive services because incorrect behaviour directly causes overselling or phantom stock. Inventory should own a reservation model that can be understood by Checkout and audited by Operations.

The data it takes over is stock levels per warehouse, reservations, reservation expiry, adjustment ledgers, and warehouse allocation configuration. It should not own product definitions or order lifecycle history, although it will reference product IDs and order or checkout identifiers.

Its dependencies on the monolith are direct table writes from stock update jobs, order cancellation paths, warehouse admin screens, and stock adjustment workflows. Its dependencies on other services are Catalog for product identifiers, Checkout for reservation requests, and Orders for cancellation and returns. Inventory should publish events for stock changes and reservation outcomes so that Search, Notifications, and admin projections can react without querying the Inventory database.

The specific risks are overselling, reservation expiry races, and adjustment double application. Overselling can occur if reservations are not made atomically or if retries are not idempotent. Adjustment errors can occur if warehouse corrections and order decrements are both applied twice during cutover. We will know these risks are present if reservations exceed available stock in reconciliation reports, duplicate reservation attempts create multiple active holds, or support tickets report items visible in cart but unavailable at checkout.

## Cart

Cart moves active cart state, cart lines, anonymous cart identity, authenticated cart merge behaviour, and cart expiry. Cart owns what the shopper has tentatively chosen. It does not own inventory reservation, payment, or order creation.

The data it takes over is cart identifiers, user or session associations, cart lines, metadata, and merge history. Cart should store enough information to reconstruct the cart across sessions, but it should not store a full frozen order snapshot. Prices and product availability must be validated during checkout, because cart state can be stale.

Its dependencies on the monolith are session management, cart persistence, and code paths that currently modify cart tables directly. Its dependencies on other services are Catalog for product and price queries, Inventory for availability rules, and Orders for post-order cart clearing. During migration, the routing layer must ensure that a given cart is handled consistently by either Cart or the monolith, never both.

The specific risks are cart loss, inconsistent merge behaviour, and stale price or availability assumptions. Cart loss is a commercial incident because it directly reduces conversion. Merge errors can leave duplicate items or delete items unexpectedly. We will know these risks are present if carts disappear after login, cart totals change unexpectedly, or the same cart is modified on two paths and the merge audit log shows conflict.

## Orders

Orders moves order history, order items, status, returns, and customer-visible order records. Orders becomes the customer-facing history of purchases. It does not own payment facts or inventory movements, although it will reference them and react to their events.

The data it takes over is orders, order lines, status transitions, return requests, and return status. It may project order history into a search or support read model, but it should not maintain a duplicate order database for convenience.

Its dependencies on the monolith are admin order screens, support tools, customer account pages, legacy email triggers, and any code reading order tables directly. Its dependencies on other services are Checkout for order creation, Payments for payment and refund status, Inventory for returns and cancellations, and Search or Notifications for downstream use of order events.

The specific risks are historical gaps, incorrect status transitions, and duplicate order records. Historical gaps can occur during backfill if partitioning, time zones, or legacy status codes are misunderstood. Status transition races can make an order appear paid while a later event marks it cancelled. We will know these risks are present if reconciliation against legacy data finds missing orders, if support sees contradictory order states, or if order-created events are processed more than once.

## Payments

Payments moves external payment provider integration, payment attempts, provider references, refunds, reconciliation, and payment idempotency. It does not own checkout orchestration, order history, cart state, or customer profile data. It owns payment facts.

The data it takes over is payment attempt records, provider transaction identifiers, refund records, reconciliation status, and idempotency keys. It may store a minimal amount of metadata needed to reconcile with the provider, but it should avoid storing sensitive payment details that can be kept by the provider or tokenised securely.

Its dependencies on the monolith are current payment calls, provider callbacks, refund admin flows, and any legacy table records that represent payment state. Its dependencies on other services are Checkout for payment requests and Orders for downstream order status. It should expose synchronous APIs for payment operations where immediate confirmation is required, and events for confirmed payment, failed payment, captured payment, and refund completion.

The specific risks are double capture, lost capture, refund inconsistency, and provider callback races. Double capture is a direct financial and reputational incident. Lost capture can mean a customer’s payment is approved or settled without an order. We will know these risks are present if provider reconciliation reports unmatched captures, if duplicate attempts have the same outcome but different internal states, or if a refund succeeds externally but fails internally.

## Checkout

Checkout moves orchestration only: it validates the request, consults Cart and Catalog, requests an inventory reservation, initiates payment, creates or requests an order record, and triggers compensating actions on failure. Checkout owns checkout session and saga state, not cart lines, product prices, inventory quantities, payment records, or order history.

The data it takes over is checkout sessions, orchestration status, idempotency records, and saga compensation data. It should store enough state to resume or roll back a failed checkout without creating duplicate orders or duplicate payments.

Its dependencies on the monolith are the current checkout controller, transaction boundaries, provider calls, inventory checks, and order creation code. Its dependencies on other services are Cart for current basket state, Catalog for product and price validation, Inventory for reservation, Payments for payment processing, and Orders for order creation or status confirmation. It may publish checkout lifecycle events for monitoring, fraud, or operational analytics, but downstream consumers must not depend on checkout internals.

The specific risks are partial failures, timeout amplification, duplicate orders, and peak latency. Checkout is the most likely place for synchronous fan-out to create latency problems. A payment provider timeout can leave an order unresolved. A reservation can succeed while payment fails, requiring cancellation. A duplicate browser submission can create two orders if idempotency is incomplete. We will know these risks are present if checkout p95 crosses the threshold in Chapter 9, if reservations exist without orders, if payment captures exist without orders, or if duplicate order IDs appear for the same cart.

# Case Study: Extracting Notifications

After the target architecture was approved, the Messaging team, five engineers, was given Notifications as the first extraction. The team planned six weeks and took nine. The overrun is part of the story, not an embarrassment to hide. The next teams will face similar surprises, so the Messaging team recorded what happened and what they would do differently.

Weeks one to three were used to build the service and its own database, and to place an outbox in the monolith to publish "message requested" events. The first milestone was not customer traffic. It was proving that the monolith could publish a message request without the application writing to both the monolith database and the new service database. That constraint is described in the target architecture and data-migration plan. The team used the shared outbox pattern so that a committed monolith transaction also produced a record that a relay could publish later. The outbox was used because the monolith and the new service could not be allowed to drift by writing to two databases. The relay separated the database transaction from broker publication, which made retries, broker lag, and crash recovery easier to test.

Week four was shadow mode. The new service rendered every message but did not send it, and its output was compared with the monolith's output. Shadow mode was useful precisely because it exposed differences before customers saw them. The team found rendering differences in 3% of messages. All differences came from old templates with hard-coded locale formatting. That finding matched the warning that migrated code can look complete while still depending on legacy data shapes and legacy rendering assumptions. The comparison did not prove the service could deliver messages; it proved the rendering and formatting logic agreed with the monolith. That is why it was valuable even though no messages were sent.

Weeks five and six were spent fixing templates. This was the main overrun. It also changed the team's estimate for future legacy clean-up work. The Messaging team later wrote that budgeting time for legacy clean-up is not padding; it is part of the migration. The next teams should expect similar work in other services, where old records, statuses, and formats carry business meaning.

Traffic was shifted 5%, 25%, 50%, and then 100% over weeks seven to nine. The shift at 25% was treated as a canary release: it was large enough to surface production behaviour, but small enough that the team could stop and inspect it. This mirrors the gradual traffic method in the cut-over plan.

One rollback happened at 25%. Duplicate SMS messages were sent to 1,140 customers because a retry was not idempotent. The rollback trigger fired after 6 minutes. The team routed traffic back to the monolith path, stopped further expansion, and then fixed the defect by adding an idempotency key per message. The rollback did not require restoring the whole database. It used the normal rollback path: stop sending new requests to the service and use the monolith compatibility path while the defect was fixed. Because the rollback path was already defined, the team did not need to invent an emergency procedure while customers were receiving duplicates.

The end state is measurable. The service now sends 1.2 million messages a day. Notification-related deploys of the monolith dropped from about one a week to zero. The monolith's job queue lost 40% of its load. Those results show the first extraction reduced deployment coupling, freed queue capacity, and made one capability independently deployable. These measurements also validated the phase choice.

The Messaging team recorded three lessons: budget time for legacy data clean-up; make every consumer idempotent before shifting traffic; and shadow mode was worth every day it took. Those lessons are not optional advice. They are requirements for the next extractions.

1. Budget time for legacy data clean-up, because the main overrun was old templates with hard-coded locale formatting, and later services will also need to reconcile old records, statuses, and formatting rules before they become authoritative (see the chapter Data Migration).
2. Make every consumer and retry path idempotent before shifting live traffic, because the 25% rollback happened when a retry created duplicate SMS messages; idempotency is part of cutover readiness, not a post-cutover enhancement (see the chapters Testing Strategy and Cut-Over and Rollback).
3. Use shadow mode before write cutover, even when it consumes weeks, because shadow mode exposed the 3% template differences before they reached customers and prevented a larger trust problem (see the chapter The Strangler-Fig Approach).
4. Treat traffic increases as canary releases with explicit review gates, because the shift to 25% surfaced the defect while the team could still use the rollback trigger and return to the monolith path in minutes (see the chapter Cut-Over and Rollback).
5. Record rollback outcomes and fix the underlying defect before the next expansion step, because the team's recovery depended on routing back to the monolith, stopping further traffic growth, and adding an idempotency key per message (see the chapter Organisation and Governance).

# Data Migration

Data migration is the hardest part of this programme. The eight services will fail operationally if they are deployed with clean code but share a poorly mapped database. The migration data plan therefore starts before the first service is cut over and continues until the last legacy table is retired.

The first step is a data ownership inventory. The 212 tables must be grouped by business domain and labelled. Each table should have one authoritative owner: monolith, Catalog, Inventory, Cart, Orders, Payments, Checkout, Search, or Notifications. Some tables may be operational or technical and remain monolith-only temporarily, but no table should remain “shared by several modules.” Shared table ownership is the condition the migration is intended to remove.

The second step is to find direct table access in code. A static search for table names, query builders, ORM models, and migration files is not enough. The team must inspect background jobs, admin reports, ad hoc scripts, and support tools. Direct access can survive for months after the main application path is migrated. The correct detection method is database-level monitoring of client application names, roles, and query sources combined with code review.

The third step is change data capture from the monolith database into service databases during shadowing and migration. Change data capture is used to keep a new service database in sync with the monolith before the service takes writes. This is not the final steady-state integration mechanism. It is a migration tool that lets us move read paths first and build confidence before moving write paths. Change data capture pipelines need lag monitoring, schema-change alerts, and replay capability. If change data capture lag grows during peak Saturday traffic, the service may appear correct at low traffic and fail at peak.

The fourth step is the transactional outbox pattern in new services. When a service owns a capability, its normal write path is: begin transaction, write domain records, write an outbox event record, commit. A separate relay publishes the outbox event to the message broker. Consumers process events with at-least-once semantics, so consumers must be idempotent. The outbox pattern prevents the application from making two separate writes to two systems and is the primary guard against dual writes.

The fifth step is backfill and reconciliation. When a service takes ownership, it may need historical rows that were previously in monolith tables. Backfill must be idempotent and restartable. It should use stable primary keys and avoid assuming that a batch job will finish. Reconciliation is not a single check after backfill. It is a set of repeatable invariants: total row counts by state, checksums for critical fields, counts of orders by date, reservations against stock, payment captures against orders, and notifications suppressed against preferences. Differences must be classified as expected migration artefacts, data-quality issues, or defects.

The sixth step is read migration. For read-heavy capabilities, the service should first serve shadow reads, then serve a percentage of live reads. Search, Orders history, and Catalog queries can often move reads before writes. During read shadowing, request and response differences should be sampled rather than fully duplicated because full duplication at 2,300 requests per second may be too expensive.

The seventh step is write migration. Write migration is the point where ownership changes. It should be done by stable entity bucket, not by random request. For a cart migration, 1% means 1% of carts. For checkout, 1% means 1% of new checkout sessions. For payments, 1% means 1% of new payment attempts, with special care for provider callbacks that may arrive late. During write migration, the service writes its own database and records outbox events. If the monolith still needs the data, an event-driven projection consumer updates monolith compatibility tables. That consumer is not an application dual write; it is a controlled migration projection with its own lag and reconciliation metrics.

The eighth step is decommissioning. A legacy table or route is ready for removal only after monitoring shows no reads and no writes for an agreed period. Decommissioning is not just deleting code. It includes removing migration flags, removing compatibility tables, removing obsolete job handlers, and updating runbooks.

Several data-specific pitfalls are expected. Primary key collisions can occur when new service identifiers are generated independently from monolith sequences. A safe approach is to use a distributed identifier strategy with a pre-agreed namespace and avoid relying on local auto-increment assumptions across systems. Time zone and daylight-saving changes can affect partitioning, reservation expiry, and report reconciliation. Legacy free-text statuses need a mapping table and a validation script before they are used in service status models. Large tables need backfill batches sized by peak load, not by average load.

We will know data migration is failing if event lag is high, reconciliation deltas grow, duplicate events create duplicate state, or legacy tables continue to receive writes after the owning service is supposed to be authoritative. We will know it is succeeding if every table has an owner, every service write has a corresponding event or API contract, every projection has a known consumer and removal date, and every critical invariant passes under production-like load.

# Testing Strategy

The current 52-minute flaky suite cannot be the primary safety net for a service migration. It should remain useful as a smoke and regression suite for the monolith while that monolith still exists, but it must be supplemented with deterministic tests that can be run frequently and interpreted quickly. The testing strategy has seven layers.

Unit tests should live with each service and cover domain rules in isolation. A unit test should not depend on the full application, the monolith database, or a real external provider. For Checkout, this means testing orchestration decisions without making real payment calls. For Payments, it means testing provider request construction and response handling with deterministic stubs. For Inventory, it means testing reservation logic, expiry, and adjustment rules with in-memory or transactional database fixtures.

Component tests should run each service with its own relational database, its own outbox relay, and a local broker emulator. They should prove that a write and its event are atomic in the service transaction, that duplicate events do not create duplicate side effects, and that retries are handled correctly. These tests are the main defence against the outbox and message broker becoming sources of duplicate state.

Contract tests are essential. Because services communicate through synchronous APIs and events, a provider change can break a consumer even if the provider’s own tests pass. Contract testing should be split into two directions. Consumer tests express what a consumer expects, such as a Cart service requiring a product price field. Provider tests prove that the provider satisfies the agreed contract. Event contracts should be versioned and compatibility-checked in both directions: new producers must not remove required fields, and consumers must tolerate additive fields unless they explicitly require strict validation.

Integration tests should run across service boundaries in a production-like environment. They should use containers or isolated virtual machines, real message broker topics or queues, and real database migrations. They should cover at least one happy path and one failure path for each migrated capability. For example, Inventory integration tests should prove that a reservation can be cancelled after a payment failure without leaving the item unavailable. Checkout integration tests should prove that a payment timeout does not create a second charge.

End-to-end tests should cover shopper journeys and operational workflows, not just individual services. The core journey is search, view product, add to cart, checkout, confirm order, receive confirmation, view order history, initiate return, refund, and notify. The operational journey is stock adjustment, reservation, cancellation, restock, reconciliation, and search refresh. End-to-end tests should use anonymised production-like data and should be deterministic enough to run on every release candidate.

Performance tests should be run before every significant traffic shift, and before the final Checkout cutover. The baseline is the current system’s peak of 2,300 requests per second and checkout p95 of 1.9 seconds. The target is not merely “similar,” but the operational threshold defined in Chapter 9. Performance tests should include production-like request mixes: browsing, search, cart updates, checkout, order history, and background events. They should also test broker lag and database connection saturation. A service that passes functional tests at low traffic may fail at peak because of cache misses, index rebuilds, lock contention, or event backlog.

Data migration tests should be treated as first-class automated tests. Before every backfill, the team should run reconciliation in a production-like environment. The tests should assert row counts, key relationships, and business invariants. They should also assert that replaying the migration does not corrupt state and that an interrupted job can resume. For financial data, tests should include deliberately delayed provider callbacks, duplicate captures, duplicate refunds, and late cancellations.

Flaky testing should be managed deliberately. The current failure rate of about 1 run in 6 unrelated to the change is a delivery tax that cannot be tolerated during migration. Tests that fail intermittently should be quarantined with an owner, a reason, and a target date. A quarantined test cannot block every deployment, but it also cannot remain in the default gate forever. The migration gate should use deterministic tests; flaky tests may run for information but must not determine cutover readiness unless they have been made reliable.

The testing order for each service is fixed. Before code is written, contracts are drafted. During development, unit and component tests are added with every change. Before shadow traffic, integration and performance tests pass in a production-like environment. Before write cutover, data reconciliation and rollback drills pass. After cutover, contract tests remain in the pipeline to prevent regressions.

# Cut-Over and Rollback

Cut-over is a controlled traffic shift through the routing layer. It is not a flag that silently swaps code inside the monolith. Every extracted capability gets a route or route group in the routing layer, with metrics by backend, percentage of traffic, and error behaviour. The routing layer must make the current backend visible to operators. If operators cannot answer “what percentage is going to the service?” and “which backend is handling this request?” within seconds, the cutover is not operationally safe.

For read-only or idempotent read paths, traffic is shifted by request percentage. A typical sequence is 1%, then 5%, then 25%, then 50%, then 100%. The exact steps can vary by capability, but the principle is the same: small steps, explicit monitoring, and a pause between increases. Search is a good fit for this pattern because a query can be retried safely and shadow comparisons can catch result regressions.

For stateful write paths, traffic is shifted by stable entity percentage. 1% means 1% of carts, 1% of orders, 1% of checkout sessions, or 1% of payment attempts, depending on the capability. The routing layer uses a consistent hash or sticky key so that a given entity is not handled by both paths. This is essential for Cart, Orders, Payments, and Checkout. For example, if a cart is created in Cart, subsequent requests for that cart should continue to route to Cart until the migration owner explicitly moves it back.

Before live traffic moves, each service runs in shadow mode where possible. Shadow traffic can compare latency, response shape, business result, and resource usage without affecting customers. For write services that cannot be shadowed directly, the team should use sandbox provider integrations and dry-run orchestration paths.

Once live traffic begins, each expansion step must be reviewed by the owning team and the on-call rotation. The expansion should happen during a low-risk window, preferably not immediately before Saturday peak traffic and not during the freeze period described in Chapter 10. Each window should have a clear owner, an abort command, and a rehearsed rollback path.

The rollback criteria for migrated traffic are measurable and non-negotiable. Rollback is triggered if there is an error rate above 1% for 5 minutes, or checkout p95 latency above 800 ms for 10 minutes. The error rate is measured on the routed path and includes timeouts, server errors, rejected requests that should have succeeded, and failed orchestration responses. Checkout p95 latency is measured at the routing layer from the start of the request to the accepted response or final failure.

When a rollback is triggered, the first action is to stop further traffic expansion. The second action is to route back to the monolith path for new work. The third action is to drain in-flight work carefully. For stateless reads, drain is simple. For stateful writes, the team must decide whether in-flight entities continue on the service or move back to the monolith. A checkout already in payment should continue and be reconciled, not abandoned mid-call. A reservation already placed should be cancelled or attached to an order according to the saga rules, not left to expire accidentally.

Rollback does not normally mean restoring a database. Restoring a database is a last resort and should be reserved for catastrophic corruption. The normal rollback is a traffic and ownership rollback: stop sending new requests to the service, ensure the monolith path can serve those requests, and use event projections or reconciliation jobs to bring the monolith into agreement with the service state if necessary. This is why compatibility projections and event lag monitoring are part of migration, not optional convenience.

A successful rollback rehearsal is a cutover gate. Each service must perform a rehearsed rollback in a production-like environment. The rehearsal should answer these questions: how long does it take to shift traffic back, can the monolith accept the redirected load, are there in-flight records that need manual handling, and can the team prove no duplicate side effects were created?

Case Study: Extracting Notifications shows why a rollback trigger must be observed and acted on within minutes.

We will know a cutover is successful when the service can serve 100% of the capability with no unresolved rollback trigger, no reconciliation drift beyond tolerance, no unexpected queue backlog, and no support or business metric regression. We will know it is risky when manual database fixes are required to keep the system consistent after normal traffic shifts.

# Organisation and Governance

Governance exists to prevent a migration of this size from becoming eighteen months of ad hoc decisions. The programme needs clear ownership, a standard readiness process, and a predictable response to the Christmas freeze.

There are nine product teams. Eight teams own one of the eight target services, as listed in Chapter 3. The ninth team becomes the Platform and Migration Team. Its job is not to own Checkout, Payments, or Catalog business logic. Its job is to provide the shared strangler-fig machinery: routing layer, service template, message broker configuration, outbox relay, change data capture pipelines, contract testing infrastructure, observability defaults, and migration runbooks. This distinction matters. Product teams own behaviour; the platform team owns the migration engine.

Each service has one owning team and one accountable on-call rotation. The owning team writes the service, operates the service, responds to alerts, and proposes traffic increases. The Platform and Migration Team supports the infrastructure but does not take responsibility for business correctness. If Notifications sends the wrong message, the owning team investigates. If the message broker relay is down, the platform team investigates and the owning team validates impact.

A service is ready to take traffic only after a Service Readiness Decision is recorded. The decision is made by the Service Readiness Board. The board is chaired by the principal engineer, who wrote this guide. Its standing members are the platform lead, the QA lead, the data architecture lead, the SRE or reliability lead, and the owning team lead. For Checkout and Payments, the CTO must also approve the readiness decision because those services affect money movement and peak trading reliability. The board records the decision as approved, approved with conditions, or rejected, and each record must include the evidence reviewed.

Readiness evidence includes published contracts, passing contract tests, passing integration tests, passing performance tests at expected peak load, data reconciliation results, rollback rehearsal results, operational dashboards, alert rules, runbooks, and an on-call rotation. A team may not begin write cutover on the basis of code review alone. A dashboard that exists but has no thresholds is not sufficient. A rollback path that has not been rehearsed is not sufficient.

The freeze in the four weeks before Christmas is handled as a hard scheduling constraint, not as a suspension of engineering discipline. During the freeze, the programme does not increase traffic to newly migrated services for Checkout, Payments, Cart, Orders, Inventory, or Catalog. It does not cut over new capabilities. It does not perform schema changes that affect cross-service contracts. It does not perform data backfills that could affect peak trading. It may run non-production migration work, contract tests, reconciliation reports, and rollback rehearsals in non-production environments. It may deploy urgent bug fixes and capacity changes to already stable services if they are needed for reliability, but those changes require the normal incident-level review.

If a service is not ready before the freeze begins, its cutover is postponed. If a service is live before the freeze and has a failure during the freeze, the first response is rollback to the monolith or the last known stable route. The freeze is not a time to debug architectural decisions under peak load. It is a time to protect the trading window and to complete migration work safely after the holiday period.

The programme runs a weekly migration forum. Each phase has a written exit report. The report lists completed services, remaining risks, reconciliation status, open rollback conditions, and traffic percentages. If a team is blocked by platform work, the block is logged with an owner and a date. If a migration gate is repeatedly missed, the board decides whether to pause extraction and reduce scope in the monolith. The goal is not to be heroic; it is to be predictable.

# Risks and Mitigations

The following table records the eight principal risks for the migration. It is not exhaustive, but it captures the failures most likely to derail the programme. Each mitigation is tied to a control already described in earlier chapters.

| Risk | What can go wrong | How we will know | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data ownership drift | Services and monolith continue to write the same entity through compatibility code, producing divergent records. | Reconciliation deltas grow, legacy tables receive unexpected writes, shadow comparisons disagree. | Enforce one writer per table, use event projections only during migration, monitor table access, require readiness sign-off before cutover. |
| Inventory overselling | Reservations, cancellations, or restock jobs race and allow stock to be oversold. | Reservation counts exceed available stock, checkout failures spike, operations reports negative stock or phantom availability. | Inventory owns atomic reservation updates with idempotency keys, reservation expiry, adjustment ledgers, load testing, and invariant reconciliation. |
| Payment inconsistency | Captures, refunds, or callbacks are processed twice or lost, causing money mismatches. | Provider reconciliation shows unmatched captures or refunds, duplicate attempts appear, customers report charged without orders. | Payments owns idempotent provider calls, transactional outbox, sandbox rehearsal, daily reconciliation, and CTO approval before cutover. |
| Checkout latency regression | Synchronous service fan-out makes checkout slower than the monolith, especially at Saturday peak. | Checkout p95 exceeds 800 ms for 10 minutes, timeouts increase, conversion falls during load tests. | Pre-peak load tests, staged traffic shifts, caching and query budgets, circuit breakers, strict p95 rollback trigger, and no cutover just before peak or freeze. |
| Eventual consistency confusion | Customers or operations see stale search, cart, inventory, or order information. | Search shows stale prices, carts contain unavailable items, order status contradicts payment or inventory facts, support complaints increase. | Use synchronous APIs for critical immediate queries, versioned events for state changes, read-after-write consistency where required, and event lag SLOs. |
| Contract breakage between teams | A provider changes an API or event shape and breaks a consumer service in production. | Consumer contract tests fail in CI but are ignored, 4xx/5xx errors spike after deploy, duplicate events or missing fields appear in dashboards. | Versioned contracts, consumer-driven tests in provider pipelines, compatibility rules, deprecation windows, and readiness gate checks before traffic changes. |
| Operational blind spots | Incidents span monolith, routing, services, broker, and databases, and no team can explain the cause quickly. | Error rate exceeds 1% for 5 minutes without a clear backend, broker lag is discovered after user impact, alerts are noisy or absent. | Standard service template with tracing, request IDs, routing dashboards, broker lag alerts, per-service runbooks, rollback rehearsals, and on-call ownership. |
| Programme fatigue and freeze compression | Teams accumulate migration work and normal feature work, then defer risky decisions until the freeze. | Missed phase gates, unfinished rollback drills, last-minute changes before the freeze, increased stress and errors. | Weekly forum, phase exit reports, pause when gates fail, no cutover during freeze, explicit platform support, and a fixed readiness decision model. |

# Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| backfill | The controlled copy of historical rows from the monolith into a service database before or during ownership change. It must be idempotent, restartable, and verified by reconciliation. |
| bounded context | A business boundary around a capability such as Payments or Inventory, where one team owns the data and meaning. In this guide, each target service maps to a bounded context and owns its tables. |
| canary release | A controlled rollout in which a small percentage of traffic is sent to the new backend before a larger shift. In this migration, the 5% and 25% steps used during the Notifications cutover were canary releases. |
| change data capture | A migration technique that streams changes from the monolith's database into service databases while a capability is being moved. It is used for shadowing and read migration, not as the final service-to-service integration method. |
| contract tests | Tests that verify an API or event shape between teams is honoured. They should run in continuous integration and must pass before a service is allowed to take live traffic. |
| data ownership | The rule that one service is the authoritative writer for a set of records. During migration, compatibility projections may exist, but they must be monitored and removed once ownership moves. |
| decommissioning | The final removal of obsolete monolith code, tables, routes, and jobs after a service has taken full traffic. It is complete only when monitoring shows no residual reads, writes, or business need. |
| dual write | Writing the same data to two databases from application code. The migration prohibits dual writes because they can leave the monolith and service in inconsistent states. |
| end-to-end tests | Tests of a full shopper or operational journey across multiple services, such as checkout to order history to return. They validate integration and business outcomes rather than a single component. |
| event | An asynchronous message published through the message broker to communicate that something happened, such as a payment completed or stock changed. Events are used for state changes rather than immediate queries. |
| idempotency | The property that lets the same request or event be processed more than once without creating duplicate effects. The Notifications rollback showed that retry paths must be idempotent before cutover. |
| load balancer | The component that distributes incoming requests across application instances. It remains relevant for the monolith and services, while the routing layer decides which application backend should receive a request. |
| message broker | Infrastructure that receives events from services and delivers them to consumers. It supports state-change communication but requires lag monitoring and idempotent consumers. |
| monolith | The current one Python web application and PostgreSQL database from which capabilities are being extracted. It remains authoritative for unmigrated capabilities and can serve as a fallback path. |
| outbox relay | The component that reads event records written by the transactional outbox and publishes them to the message broker. It must restart safely and be monitored for lag or backlog. |
| p95 latency | The 95th-percentile response time, meaning 95% of requests are faster. Checkout p95 latency above 800 ms for 10 minutes is a rollback trigger. |
| reconciliation | Repeated checking that records in different systems agree, such as row counts, order totals, reservations against stock, and payment captures against orders. It is a gate before and after cutover. |
| request IDs | Correlated identifiers carried through the routing layer, service calls, events, and logs. They let operators trace one shopper action across migrated and unmigrated paths. |
| rollback trigger | A measurable condition that causes traffic to return to the monolith. This migration uses an error rate above 1% for 5 minutes or checkout p95 latency above 800 ms for 10 minutes. |
| routing layer | A component in front of the monolith and services that decides which backend handles each request. It is the primary control point for gradual traffic shifting and rollback. |
| service template | The reusable engineering pattern a new service must follow, including health checks, logs, tracing, migration scripts, and CI/CD settings. It keeps operational behaviour consistent across the eight services. |
| shadow mode | A migration state where the new service processes replicated requests or renders messages without affecting customer outcomes, and results are compared with the monolith. |
| strangler fig | The migration pattern used here, where a routing layer gradually sends extracted capabilities from the monolith to services while the monolith continues to serve remaining traffic. |
| table ownership | The mapping of every table to one authoritative owner, such as Catalog, Inventory, Orders, or the monolith. It prevents direct cross-service table access after a service becomes authoritative. |
| transactional outbox | A pattern where a service writes domain data and an outbox event record in the same database transaction, and a relay publishes the event later. It prevents dual writes to a database and a message broker. |
