output.text:
## 1. Summary

This proposal requests funding for an 18-month field experiment with Calloway Mutual, an insurance company with approximately 6,000 office staff. The study tests whether a “Remote-first” work arrangement changes employee productivity, wellbeing, collaboration, and voluntary turnover relative to a “Hybrid” arrangement. Hybrid means three fixed office days per week. Remote-first means office attendance is optional but limited to at most one day per week. The primary comparison is Remote-first against Hybrid.

The study is a parallel two-arm field experiment in which whole teams are randomised, not individual employees. This is necessary because work arrangements are set at team level, and because assigning individuals within the same team to different office-day rules would create contamination, fairness problems, and practical instability. Teams have about eight members on average. The intervention runs for nine months, after a two-month baseline period.

Because individual participation is voluntary, a team can enter the study if its manager agrees and at least six team members consent. Employees can decline or withdraw without penalty. This voluntary design protects autonomy but introduces selection and consent limitations, which are addressed through recruitment, measurement, sensitivity analysis, and transparent reporting.

The primary outcome is individual productivity, measured as the number of completed work items per week recorded in the company’s task-tracking system. This outcome is standardised within job family so that, for example, claims work, underwriting, policy servicing, actuarial work, and technology operations are compared on a comparable scale. Secondary outcomes are wellbeing measured monthly with the WHO-5 Wellbeing Index, collaboration measured as the number of distinct colleagues with whom each person exchanges work messages each month using metadata only and never message content, and voluntary staff turnover recorded through human-resources records.

The primary hypothesis is that Remote-first increases individual productivity. The secondary hypotheses are that Remote-first increases wellbeing and reduces voluntary turnover. Collaboration is measured as an important secondary outcome but is analysed exploratorily because its likely direction is theoretically ambiguous: remote-first may reduce face-to-face coordination or may expand digital communication networks.

The study requires 608 enrolled employees, achieved by randomising 38 teams per arm and assuming an average of eight enrolled employees per team. The sample-size calculation accounts for clustering within teams and anticipated attrition. The analysis plan is pre-specified. The primary analysis is intention-to-treat using a mixed-effects model with a random intercept for team. Missing data will be handled using multiple imputation and sensitivity analyses. Secondary outcomes will be handled using pre-specified models and multiplicity adjustment for the two directional secondary hypotheses.

The study contributes causal, team-based evidence about remote and hybrid work in a real organisation. It is relevant to organisational psychology, economics, management, and the foundation’s board because it tests policy-relevant questions using objective productivity data, employee-reported wellbeing, administrative metadata, and turnover outcomes. The expected output is not a single verdict on remote work, but a nuanced account of the conditions under which flexibility affects performance, human outcomes, and organisational coordination.

## 2. Background and Rationale

The central organisational question is no longer whether employees can work remotely. For many knowledge and administrative roles, they can. The harder question is what work-location policy produces when productivity, wellbeing, collaboration, and retention are considered together. Different disciplines frame this question in complementary ways.

From an organisational psychology perspective, work location affects autonomy, recovery, distraction, social connection, role clarity, and psychological contract. A policy that gives employees more control over their time may reduce commuting strain and increase motivation, but it may also reduce access to informal support, weaken social ties, or make it harder to know when one is genuinely “off work.” These effects may differ by job family, caring responsibilities, tenure, prior remote experience, and team norms.

From an economics perspective, remote and hybrid work change the time and cost of work, the division between office and home resources, the value of local labour markets, and the efficiency of task allocation. Office attendance may create positive externalities for coordination and supervision, but it may also impose travel costs and reduce flexibility. A field experiment can reveal net effects when these mechanisms operate together rather than in isolation.

From a management perspective, work arrangements are a control instrument. They can support performance management, team cohesion, mentoring, and client service, but they can also reduce autonomy, increase absenteeism, or harm retention if they are perceived as unfair or inflexible. Organisations need evidence about which policies sustain performance without damaging the human infrastructure that supports future performance.

Existing evidence on remote and hybrid work is difficult to use for policy because it is often observational. Employees who choose remote work may differ systematically from those who do not. Teams that adopt remote-first policies may differ in leadership quality, task type, technology maturity, or labour-market position. Companies may introduce flexibility during labour shortages, after successful pilots, or as part of wider organisational changes. These confounders make it hard to distinguish the effect of location policy from other factors. A randomised field experiment can reduce this ambiguity by assigning teams to policy arms before outcomes are known.

The present study uses a field experiment rather than a survey-based cross-sectional study because it needs causal evidence. The two selected arms are meaningful and policy-relevant. Hybrid, with three fixed office days, represents a common moderate flexibility model. Remote-first, with optional attendance capped at one day, tests a stronger flexibility model in which remote work is the default. This comparison is useful because organisations are not only asking whether flexibility helps, but how much flexibility may be appropriate when the organisation still wants an office presence.

A three-arm design that also included fully on-site work could be informative, but it would require more teams, more operational disruption, and stronger ethical justification for assigning people to stricter office attendance. A two-arm comparison of Hybrid and Remote-first is more realistic because both arms involve substantial flexibility and both are plausible near-term policies for Calloway Mutual. It also allows the study to ask the more difficult marginal question: does a stronger remote-first policy differ from a hybrid norm?

The study randomises by team rather than by individual. This is essential. If two members of the same team were assigned different office-day rules, the comparison would be contaminated by shared meetings, shared workloads, shared office space, and managerial enforcement difficulties. Team-level assignment also matches the decision-making unit: the company’s scheduling and operational systems are organised around teams. Randomising at team level does require the analysis to account for clustering, and the sample-size plan explicitly does this.

Other designs were considered and rejected. Individual randomisation would be cleaner statistically for the primary employee-level outcome, but it is incompatible with team-level work arrangements and would create within-team inequity. A crossover design, where teams later switch arms, could increase power, but it risks carryover effects, learning, and long-term adaptation that make the first and second periods different. A stepped-wedge design, in which teams gradually move from Hybrid to Remote-first, may be practical in some contexts, but it can confound time trends with treatment and may delay exposure for some teams. A purely observational study would be cheaper and more scalable, but it would not adequately support causal inference. A concurrent no-treatment control arm was not chosen because both Hybrid and Remote-first are plausible operational policies; comparing Remote-first against Hybrid gives a directly policy-relevant contrast.

Calloway Mutual is a suitable context because it has a large office workforce, structured teams, administrative and knowledge-work roles, and digital task-tracking systems that allow productivity measurement without asking employees to self-report effort. The insurance sector also provides an important test because work is not purely discretionary: there are service standards, compliance requirements, and customer-facing obligations. If remote-first affects productivity or coordination, it is likely to matter for both employees and the organisation.

The study is not designed to prove that remote-first is universally better or worse. Its rationale is to generate a defensible estimate of the average effect of Remote-first relative to Hybrid in a defined organisational context, and to examine how that effect relates to wellbeing, collaboration, and turnover. These are different domains with different time horizons. Productivity may change quickly; turnover and wellbeing may evolve more slowly; collaboration patterns may change in ways that are not captured by a single count of distinct colleagues. The design therefore combines objective administrative measures with survey data and metadata measures, while avoiding intrusive content surveillance.

## 3. Research Questions and Hypotheses

The research questions are organised around the primary productivity comparison and two secondary human-outcome comparisons. Collaboration is treated as an additional secondary outcome, but not as a directional hypothesis, because the expected direction of effect is theoretically ambiguous.

Research question 1: Compared with Hybrid, does Remote-first increase individual productivity among enrolled office employees?

Research question 2: Compared with Hybrid, does Remote-first improve employee wellbeing?

Research question 3: Compared with Hybrid, does Remote-first reduce voluntary staff turnover?

An exploratory secondary question is: Compared with Hybrid, does Remote-first change the number of distinct colleagues with whom employees exchange work messages each month?

The hypotheses are as follows.

H1: Employees assigned to teams in the Remote-first arm will have higher mean individual productivity during the nine-month intervention period than employees assigned to teams in the Hybrid arm, measured as weekly completed work items standardised within job family.

H2: Employees assigned to teams in the Remote-first arm will have higher mean wellbeing during the intervention period than employees assigned to teams in the Hybrid arm, measured by the WHO-5 Wellbeing Index.

H3: Employees assigned to teams in the Remote-first arm will have lower voluntary staff turnover during the intervention period than employees assigned to teams in the Hybrid arm.

H1 is the primary hypothesis. It tests whether removing most office mandates increases or decreases completed work output. The direction is stated as an increase because flexibility may reduce commuting, support better recovery and scheduling, and allow employees to work during their most productive hours. However, this is not assumed to be certain. Distractions, childcare demands, home-work boundary problems, and reduced informal coordination could offset or reverse the effect. The study is therefore designed to detect an effect in either direction, even though the hypothesis is directional.

H2 is directional because wellbeing is expected to benefit from reduced commuting and increased autonomy. It is also possible that Remote-first harms wellbeing by reducing social contact or increasing workload spillover, so the analysis will test the stated hypothesis and also report effects in the opposite direction.

H3 is directional because flexibility is often expected to improve retention, especially in labour markets where employees value control over location. However, if Remote-first weakens social integration or career visibility, it could increase turnover. The analysis will therefore examine voluntary resignations as defined by human-resources records and will report uncertainty around the direction.

Collaboration, operationalised as the number of distinct colleagues with whom an employee exchanges work messages each month, is theoretically ambiguous. Remote-first may reduce the number of colleagues someone interacts with if work becomes more locally embedded or if fewer face-to-face encounters are converted into digital communication. It may also increase the number of distinct colleagues if employees use digital channels to maintain a wider network while avoiding commuting. Because the count does not measure message quality, relationship strength, or whether interactions are substantive, collaboration will be analysed exploratorily rather than tested as a directional hypothesis.

## 4. Study Design

The study is a parallel, two-arm, cluster-randomised field experiment. The cluster unit is the team. Each eligible team that meets the recruitment threshold is randomised to one of two policy arms: Hybrid or Remote-first. Employees within those teams may consent to participate in the research. The intervention period lasts nine months and follows a two-month baseline measurement period.

The Hybrid arm requires employees in the assigned team to work in the office on three fixed office days each week. The three days are agreed by the team and recorded as the team’s scheduled office pattern. For example, a team may choose Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday as its fixed office days. The key requirement is stability: the same three office days are used each week during the intervention unless a documented operational exception occurs.

The Remote-first arm treats remote work as the default and office attendance as optional, with a maximum of one office day per week. Employees may choose to attend no office days or one office day. This is not a fully remote policy in the sense that remote attendance is mandated; rather, it is remote-first because the organisation expects the team to operate with minimal office attendance.

The nine-month intervention period is intended to allow employees and managers to adapt to the policy, for productivity patterns to stabilise, and for turnover and wellbeing trends to emerge. A shorter period would risk capturing novelty effects or temporary adjustment costs. A longer period would improve external validity but would increase attrition, operational drift, and cost. Two months of baseline data provide a person-level pre-intervention benchmark for productivity and initial collaboration patterns. Baseline wellbeing is also collected before randomisation where feasible, although the primary wellbeing analysis can use baseline as a covariate if the first monthly survey occurs at or shortly after baseline.

Eligible teams are office-based teams with about eight members and active use of the task-tracking system. Teams are selected through a stratified random sampling approach from eligible teams across Calloway Mutual. Stratification will include site or office location, job family, and a proxy for baseline team productivity where available. This reduces the risk that the randomised teams are concentrated in one function, one office, or one performance profile. Because the company has about 6,000 office staff and the study needs only a subset of teams, random sampling from eligible teams improves the relevance of the comparison within the organisation.

Before randomisation, team managers must agree that the team can participate. Employees then receive study information and are invited to consent individually. A team enters the study if at least six team members consent. This threshold is not intended to override individual autonomy. Non-consenting employees are not enrolled as research participants, and their individual records are not used for the research analysis. Because work arrangements are set at team level, non-consenting employees may nevertheless be influenced by the team’s operational pattern. This is acknowledged as a limitation. The design protects research autonomy while recognising organisational constraints: if a team cannot operate under the assigned pattern because too few members consent, it is replaced.

Randomisation occurs after teams have met the participation threshold. This protects individuals from being enrolled or analysed before consent, but it introduces a potential team-level self-selection issue. Teams that reach the consent threshold may differ from teams that do not. We will measure and report consent rates, team-level participation, and characteristics of participating and non-participating eligible teams. The causal interpretation is strongest for the enrolled employee sample; the organisational generalisability is limited to teams willing to participate under the stated conditions.

Teams are randomised using permuted-block randomisation within stratification groups. An independent statistician not involved in day-to-day data collection will generate the allocation sequence. Teams will be assigned arm labels using a numeric code rather than the words Hybrid or Remote-first during early data assembly. Outcome analysts will be masked to arm labels until the analysis code and data-checking plan are locked. Employees, managers, and operational staff will necessarily know the assigned policy once it begins, because this is an open field experiment rather than a blinded clinical trial.

The intervention is implemented through ordinary operational systems. Assigned teams are instructed to follow the relevant work pattern. Office attendance compliance will be measured through badge-entry logs where available and through brief monthly attendance check-ins. Compliance is not required for primary analysis because the primary analysis is intention-to-treat. If a team or employee does not follow the assigned pattern, that individual or team remains analysed in the arm to which the team was assigned. Compliance will be used to describe fidelity, conduct sensitivity analyses, and explore whether effects differ among compliant teams.

Contamination is possible through several routes. Employees from different teams meet in the same office, managers oversee multiple teams, and cross-team tasks may create pressure to deviate from assigned schedules. The protocol reduces contamination by assigning whole teams to arms, using fixed Hybrid office days, limiting Remote-first attendance to one day, and communicating expectations to managers. However, the field context cannot eliminate all cross-arm influence. The analysis will report the proportion of enrolled employees observed in the office in ways that exceed the Remote-first cap or fall below the Hybrid expectation, and it will assess whether such variation changes estimated effects.

The study design is intentionally pragmatic. It asks what happens when a real company sets team-level policies, not what happens under ideal laboratory conditions. This increases relevance for policy but introduces uncertainty from organisational variation. The analysis plan therefore controls for job family, site, baseline productivity, time trends, and team-level clustering, and treats the intervention effect as an average effect within the enrolled organisation.

## 5. Participants and Recruitment

The target population is Calloway Mutual’s office staff, about 6,000 employees. Eligible employees are those employed at baseline, assigned to a regular office-based team, and working in a role that uses the task-tracking system to record completed work items. Employees who are absent for the baseline period, on extended leave, or in temporary roles that do not generate standard task-tracking records are not eligible. The exact eligibility rules will be agreed with the company before sampling.

The team is the randomisation unit, but the employee is the primary unit of productivity measurement and survey response. A team becomes eligible for randomisation if: first, the team is operationally stable enough to follow a work-location policy for nine months; second, the team manager agrees to the study; third, at least six team members give individual consent; and fourth, team-level data can be pseudonymised. Team size is assumed to average eight members, but actual eligible teams may vary from six to eight or slightly more if replacement teams are needed.

Recruitment will begin with a list of eligible teams provided by the company. The research team will identify a stratified random sample of teams sufficient to reach the target number of enrolled employees. The plan is to randomise 38 teams per arm, producing 76 randomised teams and, if eight employees consent per team, 608 enrolled employees. In practice, teams may enter only when at least six employees consent. If teams average fewer than eight consented employees, additional teams may be recruited to preserve the employee-level power target. The sample-size table states the planned number under the average team-size assumption; the recruitment plan prioritises achieving at least 608 enrolled employees.

Individual employees will receive a plain-language information sheet. It will explain the purpose of the study, the assigned work patterns, what data will be collected, how productivity and collaboration metadata are pseudonymised, the voluntary nature of participation, and the right to withdraw. Employees will be told that participation does not affect performance evaluation, promotion, or employment terms, and that no individual research results will be shared with the employer. A consent form will be separate from the information sheet and may be completed electronically. Employees may decline without giving a reason. If an employee declines, the team may still qualify if at least six other members consent; the declined employee is not enrolled and is not included in the research dataset.

Manager consent is operational rather than proxy consent for employees. A manager may agree that the team can participate, but cannot consent on behalf of employees. This distinction is important because the study tests organisational policy but protects individual autonomy. The company will be informed that managers must not pressure employees to consent or participate. A neutral contact point, separate from the direct line-management chain, will be available for employees who have questions about the voluntariness of participation.

The study will use a small incentive of €40 per enrolled employee. The incentive is modest and is intended to compensate for survey time and attention. It is not contingent on productivity, wellbeing, attendance, or staying in the study. To avoid coercion, employees who withdraw will be paid for completed parts of the study up to the point of withdrawal where practicable, and the incentive structure will be explained clearly in the consent process.

Recruitment will continue until the target number of teams and employees is reached. Replacement teams will be randomly selected from the eligible team pool when a sampled team fails the consent threshold, loses manager agreement, or becomes ineligible. The research team will record reasons for non-participation at the team and employee levels, including administrative exclusions and non-consent. This will support an assessment of selection bias and will help interpret whether enrolled teams resemble the wider workforce.

## 6. Measures

The primary outcome is individual productivity measured weekly during the nine-month intervention period. The measure is the number of completed work items per week recorded in Calloway Mutual’s task-tracking system. Because different job families complete different types of work items, productivity is standardised within job family before analysis. Job family categories may include, for example, claims, underwriting, policy servicing, actuarial and financial analysis, customer service operations, and technology or administrative support. The exact categories will be agreed with the company and will be broad enough to preserve privacy and comparability.

Standardisation is conducted using a pre-specified job-family reference distribution, primarily based on the baseline period and stable role information. Each employee’s weekly completed item count is converted into a job-family-specific standardised score. This allows employees doing similar work to be compared on a common scale while avoiding direct comparison of fundamentally different task systems. The primary productivity endpoint will be the mean standardised weekly completed-item score over the intervention period, adjusted for baseline productivity and relevant covariates. Weekly observations will also be used in repeated-measures models to capture within-person variation and time trends.

The measure has strengths and weaknesses. Its strength is that it is administrative, repeated, and independent of self-report. Its weakness is that completed items may not fully capture quality, complexity, innovation, or important collaborative work that is not recorded in the task-tracking system. The protocol will therefore treat productivity as “quantity of recorded completed work items,” not as a complete measure of organisational value. Sensitivity analyses will use raw item counts and will examine whether results are sensitive to employees with extreme values. Where task-system downtime, leave, or role changes create missing weeks, the analysis will account for these conditions.

Wellbeing is measured using the WHO-5 Wellbeing Index, administered monthly during the baseline and intervention periods. The survey will be collected through a secure survey platform and linked to the research ID rather than to a name visible to the company. The primary wellbeing endpoint will be the mean monthly WHO-5 score during the intervention period. Monthly scores will also be analysed to examine whether any effects appear early or develop over time. The survey will be brief to reduce burden. Employees will be able to skip items, and support resources will be listed in the survey materials because wellbeing questions can sometimes prompt reflection on personal distress.

Collaboration is measured as the number of distinct colleagues with whom each person exchanges work messages each month. Data are taken from corporate messaging or email metadata, not from message content. The system provides pseudonymised counts of unique colleagues contacted by each employee in a given month. No subject lines, message bodies, attachments, or content classifications are collected. This measure captures breadth of digital collaboration but not depth, tone, influence, or quality. It is useful because it provides an objective, repeated indicator of communication networks, but it cannot tell whether collaboration is effective or satisfying. The primary collaboration endpoint will be the average monthly number of distinct colleagues during the intervention period, with analyses conducted on a log-transformed or count-based scale as appropriate.

Voluntary staff turnover is measured using human-resources records. The outcome is an employee-initiated separation during the nine-month intervention period, based on human-resources classification. Involuntary termination, redundancy, retirement, end of fixed-term contract, and organisational restructuring will not be counted as voluntary turnover unless the company’s classification codes identify the employee as having initiated a resignation or comparable employee-led separation. The primary turnover endpoint is the proportion of enrolled employees who voluntarily leave during the intervention period. Time-to-event analysis will be used as the main robustness approach, treating the start of the intervention as time zero and censoring employees who remain employed at the end of the intervention period or who leave for non-voluntary reasons.

Baseline and covariate data will be collected from administrative systems where permitted and from the consent process. Relevant covariates include job family, site, team identifier, role tenure, employment status, part-time or full-time status, and pre-intervention productivity. Baseline wellbeing and baseline collaboration may also be included where available. Additional contextual controls include week number, public holidays, known system outages, and business-season markers. These controls are intended to reduce noise and account for systematic external events rather than to adjust for factors that are consequences of the intervention.

Attendance and fidelity data will be collected but will not be used for the primary intention-to-treat estimate. Office attendance will be measured through badge-entry logs where available and supplemented by brief monthly check-ins. The fidelity measures will record whether Hybrid teams followed three fixed office days and whether Remote-first teams exceeded the one-day cap. These data will help interpret whether the intervention was delivered as intended and whether deviations diluted or amplified estimated effects.

## 7. Sample Size and Power

The sample size is based on the primary continuous productivity outcome. The desired effect size is a standardised Cohen’s d of 0.3. The significance level is two-sided at 0.05, corresponding to a z value of 1.96. Power is 0.80, corresponding to a z value of 0.84. Because randomisation is by team, the individual-level sample size must be adjusted for clustering. The intra-class correlation within teams is assumed to be 0.05, and the average team size is assumed to be eight employees. Attrition over the study is assumed to be 20%.

The starting point is the per-group sample size for individual randomisation:

n = 2 × (z₁ + z₂)² / d²  
n = 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² / 0.3²  
n = 2 × (2.80)² / 0.09  
n = 2 × 7.84 / 0.09  
n = 15.68 / 0.09  
n = 174.22  

Rounded up to the next whole person, this gives 175 employees per group.

The design effect for cluster randomisation is:

Design effect = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC  
Design effect = 1 + (8 − 1) × 0.05  
Design effect = 1 + 0.35  
Design effect = 1.35

Applying the design effect to the per-group individual sample size gives:

175 × 1.35 = 236.25

Rounded up, this gives 237 employees per group after the clustering adjustment.

Allowing for 20% attrition means dividing by 0.8:

237 / 0.8 = 296.25

Rounded up, this gives 297 employees per group after attrition.

Dividing by the average team size of eight gives the number of teams per group:

297 / 8 = 37.125

Rounded up, this gives 38 teams per group.

The planned total number of enrolled employees is therefore:

38 teams × 2 arms × 8 employees per team = 608 employees.

This calculation is a planning calculation for the primary outcome. It does not build additional power into all secondary outcomes. The primary hypothesis H1 is the basis for the confirmatory sample-size target. The secondary hypotheses H2 and H3 are tested with appropriate adjustment, but the study is not independently powered to detect small effects in wellbeing or turnover as though they were the only outcomes. The sample-size calculation also assumes that productivity is measured repeatedly over time. Repeated measurements and baseline adjustment can increase efficiency, but the sample size has not been reduced to rely on those additional gains. If the actual intra-class correlation is higher than 0.05, if teams are smaller than eight on average, or if the true productivity effect is smaller than d = 0.3, the study will have less power than planned.

| Step | Value |
|---|---:|
| Per-group sample size, individual randomisation | 175 |
| Design effect | 1.35 |
| Per-group sample size after design effect | 237 |
| Per-group sample size after attrition | 297 |
| Teams per group | 38 |
| Total employees enrolled | 608 |

## 8. Analysis Plan

The primary analysis is intention-to-treat. In a cluster-randomised field experiment with voluntary individual participation, intention-to-treat is defined at the team level: all randomised teams are included according to their assigned arm, and outcomes are analysed for enrolled employees within those teams regardless of observed compliance. An employee who attends the office more often than expected in the Remote-first arm, or fewer days than expected in the Hybrid arm, remains analysed in the assigned arm. This preserves the random assignment contrast and avoids bias from excluding non-compliant participants.

Because individual consent is required, the employee-level analysis is a modified intention-to-treat analysis in the sense that it can only include employees who consented to participate. All randomised teams are retained, and all enrolled employees are retained according to assigned arm, but employees who declined individual consent are outside the analysed research dataset. This is a limitation, and the balance tables and sensitivity analyses will assess whether consent-related selection could have influenced the estimates.

The primary outcome is weekly standardised completed work items during the nine-month intervention period. The pre-specified primary model is a linear mixed-effects model:

Y_itw = β₀ + β₁RemoteFirst_it + β₂BaselineProductivity_it + β₃X_itw + u_t + v_i + ε_itw

Here, Y_itw is employee i in team t in week w. β₁ is the estimated effect of Remote-first relative to Hybrid. BaselineProductivity is the employee’s mean baseline weekly standardised completed-item score. X_itw includes fixed covariates such as job family, site, part-time or full-time status, role tenure, and week or month indicators. u_t is a random intercept for team. v_i is a random intercept for employee nested within team. ε_itw is the residual error. The model will include a random intercept for team as required and may include a random slope for time by team if preliminary checks indicate substantial team-specific trends.

The primary estimate is the coefficient β₁, with the comparison direction Remote-first minus Hybrid. Positive β₁ indicates higher productivity under Remote-first, consistent with H1. The model will be fitted using restricted maximum likelihood, with confidence intervals and p-values calculated using small-sample methods appropriate for the number of teams, such as Kenward-Roger or Satterthwaite approaches. Because the unit of randomisation is the team, the model must account for team-level clustering. In sensitivity analysis, team-cluster-robust standard errors will be used to verify that inference is not dependent on the mixed-model specification.

Missing data will be handled under the assumption that data are missing at random, conditional on observed variables, unless evidence suggests otherwise. For the primary weekly productivity outcome, linear mixed models can accommodate intermittent missing weeks without requiring complete weekly records, but the model assumes that missingness can be explained by included covariates and random effects. If missingness is substantial, particularly at the end of the study, multiple imputation by chained equations will be used. The imputation model will include team, job family, site, week, prior weekly productivity, baseline productivity, employment status, part-time status, and baseline wellbeing where relevant. Multiple imputation will produce pooled point estimates and confidence intervals using standard combining rules. Sensitivity analyses will include complete-case analysis, worst-case imputation for employees lost in the Remote-first arm, and control-group-based imputation for employees lost after randomisation. The goal is not to hide missing data but to test whether the primary conclusion depends on untestable missing-data assumptions.

For H2, wellbeing is analysed as a linear mixed-effects model on the mean WHO-5 score during the intervention period, adjusted for baseline WHO-5 score and the same clustering structure. A random intercept for team will be included. If monthly repeated measures are analysed, week or month fixed effects and random employee intercepts will be included. The primary confirmatory secondary endpoint is the intervention-period mean wellbeing, not a series of individual monthly comparisons. This reduces multiplicity and avoids selectively reporting the month with the strongest result.

For H3, voluntary turnover is a binary time-to-event outcome. The primary analysis will use logistic mixed-effects regression on voluntary turnover by the end of the nine-month intervention period, with a random intercept for team. This estimates the odds of voluntary separation under Remote-first relative to Hybrid. Because the number of events may be small, time-to-event analysis using a Cox model with team-level frailty or random effects will be used as a robustness check. If frailty models are unstable because of few events, standard errors will be treated cautiously and confidence intervals will be emphasised over binary significance statements.

Multiple secondary outcomes will be handled hierarchically. H1 is the single primary hypothesis. H2 and H3 are directional confirmatory secondary hypotheses. H2 and H3 will be tested using the Holm adjustment to control the familywise error rate across the two secondary directional tests. The collaboration outcome is exploratory. It will be analysed using a mixed Poisson or negative binomial model with a random intercept for team, depending on overdispersion. If the number of distinct colleagues is zero for some employees, zero-inflated or hurdle models may be considered. Because collaboration has no directional hypothesis and may have multiple plausible interpretations, results will be reported as descriptive effects with confidence intervals, and no confirmatory claim will be made. If several exploratory secondary analyses are conducted, including heterogeneity by job family or site, a false-discovery-rate procedure or conservative threshold may be used, but such findings will be labelled exploratory.

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses will include: excluding weeks with known task-system outages; winsorising productivity at extreme percentiles; using raw unstandardised item counts with job-family fixed effects; excluding teams with very low compliance; and estimating a team-level difference in team mean productivity as a simpler robustness check. Balance tables will compare baseline characteristics across arms at the team and employee levels. Because randomisation is at team level and the number of teams is limited, small baseline imbalances are possible even when randomisation is correct; covariate adjustment will be used, but the unadjusted model will remain the primary comparison.

The analysis code will be version-controlled. Before unmasking the arm labels, the research team will lock the data-processing script, variable definitions, exclusion rules, and model specification. After unmasking, changes to the analysis plan will be documented as post-specified and clearly separated from the primary plan. This strengthens credibility and protects against selective analysis.

## 9. Ethics and Data Protection

The study involves organisational policy, employee wellbeing, administrative performance data, and communication metadata. These raise important ethical and data-protection questions. The guiding principle is that the research should generate useful evidence without exposing employees to disproportionate surveillance, coercion, or performance risk.

Individual employees provide informed consent. The consent process will use plain language and will clearly state that participation is voluntary. Employees can decline to participate and can withdraw after joining without penalty. Managers will be trained not to present participation as optional in words while implying it is mandatory in practice. A study contact point outside the employee’s direct line-management chain will be available for concerns about voluntariness or pressure.

Manager agreement is necessary because the team must operate under an assigned work pattern, but manager agreement does not substitute for employee consent. If fewer than six employees in a team consent, the team will not be included as an analysed research team and will be replaced. Non-consenting employees are not enrolled and are not included in the research dataset. The employer will be asked to ensure that non-participation does not lead to adverse assignment, exclusion from routine tasks, or reduced access to normal work opportunities.

The right to withdraw will be honoured. Employees may withdraw from the wellbeing survey and from further study contact. If they withdraw, their future survey responses will not be collected. For administrative and metadata outcomes, employees will be asked at consent to specify how far their data may be used. As far as technically feasible, data will be removed from the analysis dataset if withdrawal occurs before the agreed database lock. Data already aggregated in a way that cannot be traced back to an individual cannot usually be unaggregated, so the consent materials will explain this practical limit. The employer will be informed that research withdrawal is not a performance issue.

Productivity data and message metadata will be pseudonymised. The company’s secure analytics environment will assign each employee a study-specific research identifier. Names, national identifiers, and other direct identifiers will not be transferred to the research team. The mapping between research identifiers and employee records will be held by an independent or restricted-access data steward under a written agreement. Team identifiers will also be recoded into non-meaningful numeric IDs. Job family will be recorded in broad categories sufficient for analysis but not so detailed that a person is identifiable through role combination. Collaboration metadata will include only counts of distinct colleagues exchanged with in a given month. It will never include message content, subject lines, attachments, recipient identity beyond the aggregated count, or any keyword classification. This is essential because message content could reveal health, personal relationships, or sensitive personal matters.

The primary data flow is: the company extracts pseudonymised records from its systems; the research team analyses only pseudonymised records; the research team reports results in aggregate; and the employer receives only aggregated findings. The research team may see pseudonymised individual-level records for analysis, but it will not attempt to re-identify employees. Re-identification will be prohibited under the data-processing agreement. If small cell sizes create a risk of identification, results will be suppressed or aggregated further.

Team-level results will be visible only to the research team and to a small, pre-specified group within the employer, limited to senior human-resources or employee-experience leaders and, if required by governance, an employee representative or privacy officer. Team-level results will be provided using pseudonymised team codes and will not include team names, manager names, sites in combination with job family, or other details that could identify a team. Line managers will not receive research results for their own teams or for any individual employee. No individual employee results will ever be shared with the employer. The company will be informed that individual productivity, wellbeing, attendance, or turnover status will not be disclosed to managers for performance-management purposes.

The study will follow data-minimisation and privacy-by-design principles. Only variables needed for the hypotheses will be collected. Data will be stored on secure systems with access controls, encryption, and logging where feasible. Personal data will be retained only for the period needed for the research, audit, and legal obligations. The final public report and any publications will present aggregated, non-identifying results. The research team will conduct a data-protection impact assessment before data extraction begins, covering the productivity system, wellbeing surveys, badge-entry logs where used, messaging metadata, HR records, and pseudonymisation procedures.

Potential risks to employees include performance anxiety from productivity measurement, discomfort with communication metadata, stress from wellbeing questions, and possible concerns about fairness if team policies differ. Mitigations include transparency, voluntary consent, aggregate-only reporting, prohibition on individual feedback to managers, no performance-linked use of research data, a clear opt-out, and access to employee wellbeing resources. The study will also avoid assigning employees to stricter office attendance than they would ordinarily experience, because both arms already involve flexibility relative to a fully office-based regime.

## 10. Timeline

| Phase | Months |
|---|---|
| Preparation, contracts, and ethics approval | Month 1 to Month 2 |
| Team recruitment and employee consent | Month 3 to Month 4 |
| Baseline measurement | Month 5 to Month 6 |
| Intervention | Month 7 to Month 15 |
| Data preparation and analysis | Month 16 to Month 17 |
| Reporting and dissemination | Month 18 to Month 18 |

## 11. Budget

| Item | Amount (€) | Basis |
|---|---:|---|
| Research assistant | 36,000 | 0.5 FTE × 18 months × €4,000 per FTE-month |
| Data platform licence | 6,000 | Annual licence for secure research data environment |
| Participant incentives | 24,320 | 608 enrolled employees × €40 per enrolled employee |
| Statistician | 18,000 | 30 days × €600 per day |
| Open-access publication fees | 3,000 | One article-level publication charge |
| Travel to Calloway Mutual sites and one conference | 4,500 | Site visits and one conference presentation |
| Total | 91,820 | Sum of all budget items |

## 12. Limitations

The study has several limitations. First, it is a single-organisation field experiment. Calloway Mutual is a large insurance company with office-based teams, but its job mix, culture, customer obligations, and management practices are specific. Results may not generalise to smaller firms, manufacturing, healthcare, education, creative work, or organisations with different labour markets. The study therefore supports evidence about this context and about the mechanisms tested, not a universal claim about remote-first work.

Second, randomisation occurs at team level but consent is individual. This protects autonomy but creates a modified intention-to-treat structure at the employee level. If teams that reach the six-consent threshold differ systematically from teams that do not, or if employees who consent differ from employees who do not, the estimated effects apply to a self-selected subset of teams and employees within the organisation. The study will measure participation rates and baseline differences, but it cannot fully observe the opinions or outcomes of employees who decline.

Third, the intervention may be contaminated or imperfectly delivered. Teams interact across arms, managers may interpret policies differently, badge logs may be incomplete, and employees may work from home during Hybrid office days or attend the office more than once in Remote-first teams. Intention-to-treat analysis preserves the randomised contrast but may dilute the estimated policy effect if compliance is imperfect. Fidelity data will help interpret this, but they cannot fully solve the problem.

Fourth, the primary productivity measure is a count of completed work items standardised within job family. This is useful and objective, but it does not measure quality, customer satisfaction, innovation, ethical care, risk control, or collaboration. If remote-first increases speed but reduces quality, or reduces completed items but improves outcomes through better coordination, the productivity endpoint may be misleading. The study does not include a full quality outcome and therefore should not be read as a complete assessment of organisational performance.

Fifth, the collaboration measure is a count of distinct colleagues exchanged with in work messages each month. It captures network breadth but not relationship strength, message depth, meeting quality, or whether communication was necessary. Remote-first may change the mix of communication channels, reduce in-person contact without reducing digital contact, or convert informal communication into fewer structured messages. A change in distinct colleague count may therefore be difficult to interpret.

Sixth, voluntary turnover is sensitive to external labour-market conditions. If employees can easily move to another employer, flexibility may have a different retention effect than if labour-market conditions are tight. Turnover may also lag the intervention period. A nine-month window may miss later retention effects. Time-to-event analysis will help, but the study is not powered for large effects beyond the intervention period.

Seventh, the sample-size calculation is based on a primary productivity effect of d = 0.3, an intra-class correlation of 0.05, an average team size of eight, and 20% attrition. If the true intra-class correlation is higher, teams are smaller, compliance is very uneven, or the true effect is smaller than d = 0.3, the study may be underpowered for the primary outcome. Repeated measures and baseline covariates may improve efficiency, but they are not relied upon to reduce the sample size. The study may be better positioned to detect medium or large effects than small effects.

Eighth, the study is open-label in the sense that employees and managers know the assigned work pattern. This can produce expectation effects. Employees assigned to Remote-first may feel more positively treated, while employees assigned to Hybrid may feel monitored or restricted. This is part of the real policy effect but makes it difficult to separate psychological expectations from the material consequences of office attendance. The design mitigates this by comparing two plausible policies rather than a policy against no policy, but expectation effects remain.

Ninth, privacy concerns may influence behaviour. Even if only counts are collected, employees may worry about productivity measurement or metadata monitoring. This may make responses more guarded or may affect cooperation. The protocol minimises content collection, prohibits individual results, and uses pseudonymisation, but perceived surveillance cannot be fully eliminated when administrative data are used.

Finally, the study compares Remote-first with Hybrid, not with full office work or full remote work. It therefore answers an important marginal question, but not every possible policy question. If Hybrid itself has changed productivity or collaboration relative to earlier office norms, the comparison between Remote-first and Hybrid describes the effect of an additional step away from office mandates, not the effect of remote-first relative to an office-only baseline. This limitation is also a strength: the comparison is directly relevant to organisations already using hybrid norms and deciding how far to move toward remote-first flexibility.

## How to Use These Playbooks Use these playbooks during a live incident. Each playbook is complete on its own and should be followed step by step. Start every incident in the “SEC-INC” ticket queue. Keep one ticket open until post-incident review closes.
SEV1: customer-facing outage, active attacker, or confirmed exposure of customer data; all-hands response, leadership informed within 30 minutes.
SEV2: contained compromise of one account or system, or a suspected data exposure; response in working hours plus on-call.
SEV3: low-impact event with no evidence of compromise; next working day.
Roles: - Incident Commander (the on-call security engineer, until handed over) - Communications Lead (Head of Customer Service) - Technical Lead (on-call platform engineer) - Data Protection Officer - Executive Sponsor (the COO) Evidence rule: take memory and disk images before rebuilding any machine. Never power off a machine suspected of ransomware infection; isolate it from the network instead. Backups run nightly, keep for 35 days, include a weekly offline copy, and restores are tested quarterly. Customer communications only go out after approval by the Communications Lead and the Executive Sponsor. ## Ransomware on a File Server Default severity: SEV1 Typical triggers: EDR alert on file server, unexpected file encryption, file-renaming pattern, ransom note, sudden file-write spikes, or failed backup access. ### Detection 1. Incident Commander: Open a new ticket in the SEC-INC queue. Include time, file server name, share paths, warehouse, and alert text. Done when ticket ID exists and alert links are attached. 2. Incident Commander: Appoint yourself as Incident Commander. Name Technical Lead, Communications Lead, Data Protection Officer, and Executive Sponsor in ticket. Done when roles are recorded and acknowledged. 3. Incident Commander: Classify as SEV1. Declare all-hands response and ensure leadership is informed within 30 minutes. Done when severity decision and leadership notification time are logged. 4. Technical Lead: Confirm ransomware indicators from EDR, SIEM, file auditing, and server monitoring. Check process tree, encrypted file extensions, ransom note, and service account behavior. Done when indicator evidence is saved in ticket. 5. Technical Lead: Identify scope: affected file server, shares, connected warehouses, web shop integrations, service accounts, and users accessing data. Done when affected systems, users, and data types are listed. 6. Technical Lead: Begin evidence preservation. Capture memory and disk images before any rebuild. Preserve EDR logs, Windows event logs, SIEM events, snapshots, and file-server logs. Done when evidence location and hashes are recorded. 7. Incident Commander: Ensure suspected ransomware machines are not powered off. Isolate them from the network at host, switch, firewall, or VPC level. Done when isolation is verified and no further spread is observed. 8. Data Protection Officer: Perform preliminary personal-data assessment. Determine whether customer, employee, supplier, or order data is on affected shares. Done when DPO assessment is recorded and 72-hour clock is noted. 9. Incident Commander: Brief Executive Sponsor, Head of Customer Service, and warehouse operations. State facts, unknowns, containment steps, and next update time. Done when leadership acknowledgement is logged. ### Containment 1. Technical Lead: Isolate the file server from internal network access. Block SMB, RDP, file sync, backup traffic, and lateral movement paths. Done when connection tests fail and monitoring confirms isolation. 2. Technical Lead: Isolate additional servers or workstations showing the same process, file, or authentication indicators. Done when list of isolated machines is complete in ticket. 3. Technical Lead: Disable service accounts, scheduled tasks, and mapped drives connected to the file server. Done when account and task status changes are logged. 4. Technical Lead: Block malicious file hashes, process names, domains, and IP addresses in endpoint protection, firewall, CDN, and DNS controls. Done when blocklist changes are approved and active. 5. Technical Lead: Reset credentials for any accounts that accessed the file server after suspicious activity began. Done when password and secret rotation evidence is saved. 6. Incident Commander: Suspend affected warehouse integrations, order syncs, and automated jobs. Done when job scheduler shows jobs stopped and errors handled. 7. Technical Lead: Preserve volatile evidence: memory dump, open files, network connections, and current process list. Done when evidence is stored in the evidence repository with hashes. 8. Incident Commander: Confirm containment complete. Done when ransomware movement stops, no new files are encrypted, evidence is captured, and ticket records containment state. ### Eradication 1. Technical Lead: Identify entry vector: phishing, stolen credential, vulnerable service, exposed remote access, or unpatched software. Done when timeline, evidence, and confidence level are written. 2. Technical Lead: Remove malicious files, processes, scheduled tasks, services, registry persistence, and malicious user accounts. Done when EDR and manual scans show no known malware. 3. Technical Lead: Close the exploited path. Patch system, disable exposed port, revoke trusted application, or fix authentication weakness. Done when remediation evidence is recorded. 4. Technical Lead: Prepare clean rebuild only after memory and disk images are preserved. Document original configuration before wiping. Done when image verification and rebuild plan are approved. 5. Technical Lead: Rebuild the file server from known-good image or approved baseline. Do not reuse unverified binaries or scripts. Done when rebuilt server configuration matches secure baseline. 6. Technical Lead: Select restore source. Use nightly backup if clean; otherwise use weekly offline backup within the 35-day retention window. Done when backup date, integrity test, and approval are logged. 7. Technical Lead: Verify eradication. Monitor file writes, EDR alerts, authentication logs, and network traffic for abnormal patterns. Done when monitoring shows clean state for agreed review period. ### Recovery 1. Technical Lead: Restore data to an isolated validation environment first. Confirm files open and application logs are clean. Done when restoration report and test results are attached. 2. Technical Lead: Validate restored content with warehouse staff, Customer Service, and data owners. Check orders, contracts, manifests, and customer records. Done when business owners sign off on sampled files. 3. Technical Lead: Bring file server back online in a restricted segment. Re-enable shares gradually with logging enabled. output.text:
## Overview

### Base URL

The Parcelpoint public API is served from a single base URL:

`https://api.parcelpoint.example/v1`

All endpoints documented in this reference are relative to that base URL. For example, the shipments collection is requested as:

`https://api.parcelpoint.example/v1/shipments`

The API is available only over HTTPS. Plaintext HTTP requests are not supported.

Requests that send a body and responses that return a body use JSON. The media type is:

`Content-Type: application/json`

Some endpoints accept a body, some endpoints do not accept a body, and successful `DELETE /pickups/{pickup_id}` responses return no body. For methods that send a body, the body must be valid JSON. For endpoints that return a body, the body is valid JSON.

### Authentication

Every request must send an API key in the `X-Api-Key` header.

Example header:

`X-Api-Key: pp_test_your_api_key`

API keys have environment-specific prefixes:

- Keys that start with `pp_test_` work in the sandbox.
- Keys that start with `pp_live_` work in production.

A request that omits `X-Api-Key`, or that sends an invalid or unauthorized key, returns:

- HTTP status `401`
- Error code `unauthorized`

### Rate Limits

The API is rate limited to 600 requests per minute per API key.

Every response includes the following rate limit headers:

- `X-RateLimit-Limit`
  - The total request limit allowed in the current minute.
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining`
  - The number of requests remaining in the current minute.
- `X-RateLimit-Reset`
  - The Unix timestamp, in seconds, when the rate limit window resets.

If a client exceeds the limit, the API returns:

- HTTP status `429`
- Error code `rate_limited`

Rate limit headers are omitted from the response examples below for readability. They are still present on all real API responses.

### Pagination

List endpoints use cursor-based pagination.

List requests may provide the following query parameters:

- `limit`
  - Page size.
  - Must be an integer between `1` and `100`.
  - Defaults to `20`.
- `cursor`
  - Optional pagination cursor.
  - Use the value returned as `next_cursor` from a previous page.

List responses contain:

- `data`
  - Array of result objects.
- `next_cursor`
  - String cursor for the next page, or `null` when there is no next page.

When `next_cursor` is `null`, the response represents the last page.

### Idempotency

POST requests may include an idempotency key to avoid creating duplicate resources after retries.

Send the header:

`Idempotency-Key: your-unique-key`

If the same API key repeats a POST request with the same idempotency key within 24 hours, Parcelpoint returns the original response.

### Data Formats

Timestamps are ISO 8601 timestamps in UTC.

Example timestamp:

`2025-01-15T09:30:00Z`

Weights are represented in grams.

Dimensions are represented in centimetres.

Money is represented as a JSON object with two fields:

```json
{
  "amount": "12.40",
  "currency": "EUR"
}
```

- `amount` is a decimal string.
- `currency` is the currency code.

### Errors

Error responses use the following JSON body:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_failed",
    "message": "country is required",
    "field": "country"
  }
}
```

The `field` property is present only for validation errors.

The following table lists the supported error status codes and error codes.

| Status | Error Code | Description |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 400 | invalid_request | The request is malformed, for example invalid JSON or an invalid request structure. |
| 401 | unauthorized | Authentication failed because `X-Api-Key` is missing or invalid. |
| 403 | forbidden | The request is authenticated but not allowed for the API key. |
| 404 | not_found | The requested resource does not exist. |
| 409 | conflict | The request conflicts with the current state of the resource. |
| 422 | validation_failed | The request is well formed but failed validation. A `field` may be returned. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The API key has exceeded the rate limit. |
| 500 | internal_error | Parcelpoint encountered an unexpected internal error. |

## Objects

### Shipment

A shipment represents a parcel or group of parcels to be shipped from one address to another.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | Yes | Unique shipment identifier. Always starts with `shp_`. |
| `status` | string | Yes | Current shipment status. One of `draft`, `label_purchased`, `in_transit`, `delivered`, or `cancelled`. |
| `from_address` | Address | Yes | Sender address. |
| `to_address` | Address | Yes | Delivery address. |
| `parcels` | array of Parcel | Yes | Parcels included in the shipment. |
| `carrier` | string or null | Yes | Selected carrier. `null` when no label has been purchased. |
| `service` | string or null | Yes | Selected carrier service. `null` when no label has been purchased. |
| `reference` | string | Optional | Optional merchant reference. Maximum length is 64 characters. |
| `label_url` | string or null | Yes | URL to the purchased label. `null` when no label has been purchased. |
| `tracking_number` | string or null | Yes | Carrier tracking number. `null` when no tracking number is available. |
| `created_at` | timestamp string | Yes | Shipment creation timestamp in ISO 8601 UTC format. |
| `updated_at` | timestamp string | Yes | Shipment last update timestamp in ISO 8601 UTC format. |

### Address

An address is used for shipment senders, shipment delivery recipients, pickup locations, and address validation requests.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | Yes | Recipient or contact name. |
| `company` | string | Optional | Company name. |
| `line1` | string | Yes | Primary street line. |
| `line2` | string | Optional | Secondary street line, apartment, floor, suite, or similar detail. |
| `city` | string | Yes | City. |
| `postal_code` | string | Yes | Postal or ZIP code. |
| `country` | string | Yes | ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code. |
| `phone` | string | Optional | Phone number. |
| `email` | string | Optional | Email address. |

### Parcel

A parcel describes one physical package in a shipment.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `weight_g` | integer | Yes | Weight in grams. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `30000`. |
| `length_cm` | integer | Yes | Length in centimetres. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `150`. |
| `width_cm` | integer | Yes | Width in centimetres. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `150`. |
| `height_cm` | integer | Yes | Height in centimetres. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `150`. |

### Rate

A rate is a shipping price returned for a draft shipment.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `carrier` | string | Yes | Carrier identifier. |
| `service` | string | Yes | Carrier service identifier. |
| `price` | money object | Yes | Price as a money object containing `amount` and `currency`. |
| `estimated_days` | integer | Yes | Estimated delivery time in days. |

### Pickup

A pickup schedules a carrier to collect one or more shipments from an address.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | Yes | Unique pickup identifier. Always starts with `pck_`. |
| `carrier` | string | Yes | Carrier that will perform the pickup. |
| `address` | Address | Yes | Pickup address. |
| `date` | string | Yes | Pickup date in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. |
| `window_start` | string | Yes | Pickup window start time in `HH:MM` format. |
| `window_end` | string | Yes | Pickup window end time in `HH:MM` format. |
| `shipment_ids` | array of string | Yes | Shipment identifiers included in the pickup. |
| `status` | string | Yes | Pickup status. One of `scheduled` or `cancelled`. |

### Webhook

A webhook sends event notifications to an HTTPS endpoint you control.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | Yes | Unique webhook identifier. Always starts with `whk_`. |
| `url` | string | Yes | HTTPS URL that receives webhook deliveries. |
| `events` | array of string | Yes | Subscribed events. Allowed values are `shipment.updated`, `tracking.updated`, and `pickup.updated`. |
| `secret` | string | Yes | Signing secret. Returned only when the webhook is created. |
| `created_at` | timestamp string | Yes | Webhook creation timestamp in ISO 8601 UTC format. |

Webhook deliveries are signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw delivery body using the webhook `secret`. The signature is included in the `Parcelpoint-Signature` header.

## POST /webhooks

Registers a webhook.

A webhook sends event notifications to an HTTPS URL. Parcelpoint supports these events:

- `shipment.updated`
- `tracking.updated`
- `pickup.updated`

When a webhook is created successfully, the response includes the `secret` field. The `secret` is returned only on creation. Store it securely.

Webhook deliveries are signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw delivery body using the webhook `secret`. The signature is included in the `Parcelpoint-Signature` header.

### Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | body | string | Yes | HTTPS URL that will receive webhook deliveries. |
| `events` | body | array of string | Yes | Events to subscribe to. Allowed values are `shipment.updated`, `tracking.updated`, and `pickup.updated`. |

```bash

  --header "X-Api-Key: pp_test_your_api_key" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "url": "https://example.com/webhooks/parcelpoint",
    "events": [
      "shipment.updated",
      "tracking.updated",
      "pickup.updated"
    ]
  }'
```

```json
    "tracking.updated",
    "pickup.updated"
  ],
  "secret": "s3cr3t",

}
```

| 422 | validation_failed | `url` is invalid or not HTTPS, or `events` contains an unsupported event name. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The API key has exceeded 600 requests per minute. |

output.text:
## Overview

### Base URL

The Parcelpoint v2 public API is served from a single base URL:

`https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2`

All v2 endpoints documented in this reference are relative to that base URL. For example, the shipments collection is requested as:

`https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2/shipments`

The API is available only over HTTPS.

For Parcelpoint API endpoints under this base URL, request bodies and response bodies are JSON:

`Content-Type: application/json`

Some endpoints do not send a body. A successful `DELETE /pickups/{pickup_id}` response and a successful `DELETE /webhooks/{webhook_id}` response return no body. The OAuth token endpoint documented below sends a form-encoded request body.

### Authentication

Parcelpoint v2 uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials.

Obtain an access token by sending a form-encoded `POST` request to:

`https://auth.parcelpoint.example/oauth/token`

The token request body must include:

- `grant_type=client_credentials`
- `client_id`
- `client_secret`
- `scope`

The `scope` value is a space-separated list of scopes. The available scopes are:

- `shipments:read`
- `shipments:write`
- `pickups:write`
- `webhooks:manage`

Example token request:

```bash
curl --request POST "https://auth.parcelpoint.example/oauth/token" \
  --data "grant_type=client_credentials" \
  --data-urlencode "client_id=your_client_id" \
  --data-urlencode "client_secret=your_client_secret" \
  --data-urlencode "scope=shipments:read shipments:write"
```

Example token response:

```json
{
  "access_token": "...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "scope": "shipments:read shipments:write"
}
```

Send the access token on every API request as a bearer token:

`Authorization: Bearer <token>`

Access tokens last `3600` seconds. There are no refresh tokens. When a token expires, request a new token using the same client credentials grant.

A request whose token lacks the required scope receives:

- HTTP status `403`
- Error code `forbidden`

The legacy `X-Api-Key` header continues to work on v2 until 31 March 2027. After that date, requests that rely on `X-Api-Key` instead of an OAuth bearer token return `401 unauthorized`.

### Rate Limits

The API is rate limited to 600 requests per minute per key.

Every response includes the following rate limit headers:

- `X-RateLimit-Limit`
  - The total request limit allowed in the current minute.
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining`
  - The number of requests remaining in the current minute.
- `X-RateLimit-Reset`
  - The Unix timestamp, in seconds, when the rate limit window resets.

If a client exceeds the limit, the API returns:

- HTTP status `429`
- Error code `rate_limited`

Rate limit headers are omitted from the response examples below for readability. They are still present on all real API responses.

### Pagination

List endpoints use cursor-based pagination.

List requests may provide the following query parameters:

- `limit`
  - Page size.
  - Must be an integer between `1` and `100`.
  - Defaults to `20`.
- `cursor`
  - Optional pagination cursor.
  - Use the value returned as `next_cursor` from a previous page.

List responses contain:

- `data`
  - Array of result objects.
- `next_cursor`
  - String cursor for the next page, or `null` when there is no next page.

When `next_cursor` is `null`, the response represents the last page.

### Idempotency

POST requests may include an idempotency key to avoid creating duplicate resources after retries.

Send the header:

`Idempotency-Key: your-unique-key`

If the same key repeats a POST request with the same idempotency key within 24 hours, Parcelpoint returns the original response.

### Data Formats

Timestamps are ISO 8601 timestamps in UTC.

Example timestamp:

`2025-01-15T09:30:00Z`

Weights are represented in grams.

Dimensions are represented in centimetres.

Money is represented as a JSON object with two fields:

```json
{
  "amount": "12.40",
  "currency": "EUR"
}
```

- `amount` is a decimal string.
- `currency` is the currency code.

### Errors

Error responses use the following JSON body:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_failed",
    "message": "country is required",
    "field": "country"
  }
}
```

The `field` property is present only for validation errors.

The following table lists the supported error status codes and error codes.

| Status | Error Code | Description |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 400 | invalid_request | The request is malformed, for example invalid JSON or an invalid request structure. |
| 401 | unauthorized | Authentication failed because the bearer token is missing, invalid, expired, or a legacy `X-Api-Key` was used after its sunset date. |
| 403 | forbidden | The request is authenticated but not allowed for the token, for example when the token lacks the required scope. |
| 404 | not_found | The requested resource does not exist. |
| 409 | conflict | The request conflicts with the current state of the resource. |
| 422 | validation_failed | The request is well formed but failed validation. A `field` may be returned. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The key has exceeded the rate limit. |
| 500 | internal_error | Parcelpoint encountered an unexpected internal error. |

## Objects

### Shipment

A shipment represents a parcel or group of parcels to be shipped from one address to another.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | Yes | Unique shipment identifier. Always starts with `shp_`. |
| `status` | string | Yes | Current shipment status. One of `draft`, `label_purchased`, `in_transit`, `delivered`, or `cancelled`. |
| `from_address` | Address | Yes | Sender address. |
| `to_address` | Address | Yes | Delivery address. |
| `parcels` | array of Parcel | Yes | Parcels included in the shipment. |
| `carrier` | string or null | Yes | Selected carrier. `null` when no label has been purchased. |
| `service` | string or null | Yes | Selected carrier service. `null` when no label has been purchased. |
| `reference` | string | Optional | Optional merchant reference. Maximum length is 64 characters. |
| `label_url` | string or null | Yes | URL to the purchased label. `null` when no label has been purchased. |
| `tracking_number` | string or null | Yes | Carrier tracking number. `null` when no tracking number is available. |
| `tracking_events` | array of tracking events | Yes | Array of tracking events. Each event contains `status`, `description`, `location` (`string` or `null`) and `occurred_at`. |
| `created_at` | timestamp string | Yes | Shipment creation timestamp in ISO 8601 UTC format. |
| `updated_at` | timestamp string | Yes | Shipment last update timestamp in ISO 8601 UTC format. |

### Address

An address is used for shipment senders, shipment delivery recipients, pickup locations, and address validation requests.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | Yes | Recipient or contact name. |
| `company` | string | Optional | Company name. |
| `line1` | string | Yes | Primary street line. |
| `line2` | string | Optional | Secondary street line, apartment, floor, suite, or similar detail. |
| `city` | string | Yes | City. |
| `postal_code` | string | Yes | Postal or ZIP code. |
| `country` | string | Yes | ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code. |
| `phone` | string | Optional | Phone number. |
| `email` | string | Optional | Email address. |

### Parcel

A parcel describes one physical package in a shipment.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `weight_g` | integer | Yes | Weight in grams. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `30000`. |
| `length_cm` | integer | Yes | Length in centimetres. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `150`. |
| `width_cm` | integer | Yes | Width in centimetres. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `150`. |
| `height_cm` | integer | Yes | Height in centimetres. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `150`. |

### Rate

A rate is a shipping price returned for a draft shipment.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `carrier` | string | Yes | Carrier identifier. |
| `service` | string | Yes | Carrier service identifier. |
| `price` | money object | Yes | Price as a money object containing `amount` and `currency`. |
| `estimated_days` | integer | Yes | Estimated delivery time in days. |

### Pickup

A pickup schedules a carrier to collect one or more shipments from an address.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | Yes | Unique pickup identifier. Always starts with `pck_`. |
| `carrier` | string | Yes | Carrier that will perform the pickup. |
| `address` | Address | Yes | Pickup address. |
| `date` | string | Yes | Pickup date in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. |
| `window_start` | string | Yes | Pickup window start time in `HH:MM` format. |
| `window_end` | string | Yes | Pickup window end time in `HH:MM` format. |
| `shipment_ids` | array of string | Yes | Shipment identifiers included in the pickup. |
| `status` | string | Yes | Pickup status. One of `scheduled` or `cancelled`. |

### Webhook

A webhook sends event notifications to an HTTPS endpoint you control.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | Yes | Unique webhook identifier. Always starts with `whk_`. |
| `url` | string | Yes | HTTPS URL that receives webhook deliveries. |
| `events` | array of string | Yes | Subscribed events. Allowed values are `shipment.updated`, `tracking.updated`, and `pickup.updated`. |
| `secret` | string | Creation only | Signing secret. Returned only when the webhook is created. |
| `created_at` | timestamp string | Yes | Webhook creation timestamp in ISO 8601 UTC format. |

Webhook deliveries are signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw delivery body using the webhook `secret`. The signature is included in the `Parcelpoint-Signature` header.
