## POST /pickups

Scope: `pickups:write`

Schedules a carrier pickup for one or more shipments.

All of the following fields are required:

- `carrier`
- `address`
- `date`
- `window_start`
- `window_end`
- `shipment_ids`

Every shipment identifier in `shipment_ids` must refer to a shipment that:

1. exists,
2. is in `label_purchased` status, and
3. is associated with the same `carrier` specified in the pickup request.

The endpoint returns a `Pickup` object in `scheduled` status.

### Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `carrier` | body | string | Yes | Carrier that will collect the shipment. |
| `address` | body | Address | Yes | Pickup address. See the Address object. |
| `date` | body | string | Yes | Pickup date in `YYYY-MM-DD` format. |
| `window_start` | body | string | Yes | Pickup window start time in `HH:MM` format. |
| `window_end` | body | string | Yes | Pickup window end time in `HH:MM` format. |
| `shipment_ids` | body | array of string | Yes | Shipment identifiers to pick up. Each shipment must be in `label_purchased` status with the same carrier. |

### Example request

```bash
curl --request POST "https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2/pickups" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "carrier": "pp_express",
    "address": {
      "name": "Alice Example",
      "company": "Example Shop",
      "line1": "1 Example Street",
      "line2": "Loading Dock",
      "city": "Berlin",
      "postal_code": "10115",
      "country": "DE",
      "phone": "+493012345678",
      "email": "logistics@example.com"
    },
    "date": "2025-01-20",
    "window_start": "09:00",
    "window_end": "11:00",
    "shipment_ids": [
      "shp_123456"
    ]
  }'
```

### Example response

`201 Created`

```json
{
  "id": "pck_987654",
  "carrier": "pp_express",
  "address": {
    "name": "Alice Example",
    "company": "Example Shop",

| Status | Error Code | When This Happens |

| 401 | unauthorized | The bearer token is missing, invalid, expired, or a legacy `X-Api-Key` was used after its sunset date. |
| 403 | forbidden | The token lacks the required scope `pickups:write`. |
| 409 | conflict | One or more shipments are not in `label_purchased` status with the requested carrier, or the pickup cannot be scheduled because of conflicting resource state. |
| 422 | validation_failed | `carrier`, `address`, `date`, `window_start`, `window_end`, or `shipment_ids` failed validation. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The key has exceeded 600 requests per minute. |

## DELETE /pickups/{pickup_id}

Scope: `pickups:write`

Cancels a scheduled pickup.

A pickup can be cancelled up to 2 hours before its `window_start` time.

A successful deletion returns HTTP status `204 No Content` and no response body.

### Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pickup_id` | path | string | Yes | Pickup identifier. Always starts with `pck_`. |

### Example request

```

`204 No Content`

No response body.

### Errors

| Status | Error Code | When This Happens |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 401 | unauthorized | The bearer token is missing, invalid, expired, or a legacy `X-Api-Key` was used after its sunset date. |
| 403 | forbidden | The token lacks the required scope `pickups:write`. |
| 404 | not_found | No pickup exists with the requested `pickup_id`. |
| 409 | conflict | The pickup cannot be cancelled, for example because it is within 2 hours of `window_start`. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The key has exceeded 600 requests per minute. |

## GET /pickups/{pickup_id}

Scope: `pickups:write`

Retrieves a single pickup by pickup identifier.

### Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Description |

## POST /webhooks

Scope: `webhooks:manage`

Registers a webhook.

A webhook sends event notifications to an HTTPS URL. Parcelpoint supports these events:

- `shipment.updated`
- `tracking.updated`
- `pickup.updated`

When a webhook is created successfully, the response includes the `secret` field. The `secret` is returned only on creation. Store it securely.

Webhook deliveries are signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw delivery body using the webhook `secret`. The signature is included in the `Parcelpoint-Signature` header.

### Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | body | string | Yes | HTTPS URL that will receive webhook deliveries. |
| `events` | body | array of string | Yes | Events to subscribe to. Allowed values are `shipment.updated`, `tracking.updated`, and `pickup.updated`. |

### Example request

```bash
curl --request POST "https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2/webhooks" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "url": "https://example.com/webhooks/parcelpoint",
    "events": [
      "shipment.updated",
      "tracking.updated",
      "pickup.updated"
    ]
  }'
```

### Example response

`201 Created`

```json
{
  "id": "whk_456789",
  "url": "https://example.com/webhooks/parcelpoint",
  "events": [
    "shipment.updated",
    "tracking.updated",
    "pickup.updated"
  ],
  "secret": "s3cr3t",
  "created_at": "2025-01-15T11:00:00Z"
}
```

### Errors

| Status | Error Code | When This Happens |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 400 | invalid_request | The request body is not valid JSON or is not a valid request structure. |
| 401 | unauthorized | The bearer token is missing, invalid, expired, or a legacy `X-Api-Key` was used after its sunset date. |
| 403 | forbidden | The token lacks the required scope `webhooks:manage`. |
| 422 | validation_failed | `url` is invalid or not HTTPS, or `events` contains an unsupported event name. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The key has exceeded 600 requests per minute. |

## GET /webhooks

Scope: `webhooks:manage`

Lists webhooks.

This endpoint is paginated with `limit` and `cursor`. The webhook `secret` is never returned by this endpoint.

### Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `limit` | query | integer | No | Page size. Minimum is `1`. Maximum is `100`. Defaults to `20`. |
| `cursor` | query | string | No | Pagination cursor returned by a previous response as `next_cursor`. |

### Example request

```bash
curl --request GET "https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2/webhooks?limit=20" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
```

### Example response

`200 OK`

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "whk_456789",
      "url": "https://example.com/webhooks/parcelpoint",
      "events": [
        "shipment.updated",
        "tracking.updated",
        "pickup.updated"
      ],
      "created_at": "2025-01-15T11:00:00Z"
    }
  ],
  "next_cursor": null
}
```

### Errors

| Status | Error Code | When This Happens |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 401 | unauthorized | The bearer token is missing, invalid, expired, or a legacy `X-Api-Key` was used after its sunset date. |
| 403 | forbidden | The token lacks the required scope `webhooks:manage`. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The key has exceeded 600 requests per minute. |

## DELETE /webhooks/{webhook_id}

Scope: `webhooks:manage`

Deletes a webhook.

A successful deletion returns HTTP status `204 No Content` and no response body.

### Parameters

| Name | In | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `webhook_id` | path | string | Yes | Webhook identifier. Always starts with `whk_`. |

### Example request

```bash
curl --request DELETE "https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2/webhooks/whk_456789" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
```

### Example response

`204 No Content`

No response body.

### Errors

| Status | Error Code | When This Happens |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| 401 | unauthorized | The bearer token is missing, invalid, expired, or a legacy `X-Api-Key` was used after its sunset date. |
| 403 | forbidden | The token lacks the required scope `webhooks:manage`. |
| 404 | not_found | No webhook exists with the requested `webhook_id`. |
| 429 | rate_limited | The key has exceeded 600 requests per minute. |

## Migrating from v1 to v2

1. Change all API request URLs from `https://api.parcelpoint.example/v1` to `https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2`.
2. Replace API-key authentication with OAuth 2.0 client credentials by requesting a token from `https://auth.parcelpoint.example/oauth/token` using `grant_type=client_credentials`, `client_id`, `client_secret`, and the required scopes.
3. Send the access token on every v2 API request as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, refresh your integration to request a new token after the token expires after `3600` seconds, and treat `403 forbidden` as a scope problem.
4. Add the required scope for each operation: `shipments:read` for shipment, rate, and tracking reads; `shipments:write` for shipment creation, update, cancellation, label purchase, and address validation; `pickups:write` for pickup operations; and `webhooks:manage` for webhook operations.
5. Update tracking integrations to use the `tracking_events` field returned by `GET /shipments/{shipment_id}` or the `tracking.updated` webhook, because `GET /shipments/{shipment_id}/tracking` is deprecated and will be removed on 30 June 2027.
6. Replace `POST /addresses/validate` by creating shipments with `"validate_addresses": true`, handle `422 validation_failed` with `field` set to `to_address` or `from_address`, and add support for `GET /pickups/{pickup_id}`, `GET /webhooks`, and `DELETE /webhooks/{webhook_id}`.

| Area | v1 | v2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base URL | `https://api.parcelpoint.example/v1` | `https://api.parcelpoint.example/v2` |
| Primary authentication | `X-Api-Key` header | OAuth 2.0 bearer token in `Authorization` header |
| Token expiry | Not applicable | Access tokens last `3600` seconds |
| Scope errors | Not applicable | `403 forbidden` when the token lacks the required scope |
| Legacy authentication | `X-Api-Key` was standard | `X-Api-Key` works only until 31 March 2027 |
| Tracking retrieval | `GET /shipments/{shipment_id}/tracking` | `tracking_events` in the Shipment response or `tracking.updated` webhook |
| Address validation | `POST /addresses/validate` | `POST /shipments` with `"validate_addresses": true` |
| Pickup retrieval | Not available | `GET /pickups/{pickup_id}` |
| Webhook listing | Not available | `GET /webhooks` |
| Webhook deletion | Not available | `DELETE /webhooks/{webhook_id}` |

# 1. Executive Summary

Bramblewood Payroll Services can achieve Kestrel Data Security Standard (KDSS) certification within 12 months only with a structured remediation program. Based solely on the facts provided, the company has Met 3 controls, Partially met 7 controls, and Not met 5 controls. The controls already Met are endpoint protection, security awareness training, and secure development. Those are valuable strengths, but they do not offset major gaps in inventory, resilience, logging, supplier assurance, access hygiene, and incident response.

The most serious current-state risks are: there is no asset inventory or named asset owners; four leaver accounts remain active; server critical patches are applied far outside a 14-day window; administrator accounts lack MFA; backups have never been restore tested; security logs are kept only 30 days and reviewed only when something goes wrong; and there is no incident response plan, business continuity plan, supplier due diligence process, or information-security risk assessment. Client data encryption is partly evidenced, but the facts do not show that all client data stores and backup copies are encrypted.

Because the largest client will require certification in 12 months, the company should start with actions that reduce immediate exposure and create the evidence trail needed for certification. Some controls cannot be made compliant quickly if remediation starts late: 12-month log retention and annually tested continuity require time. Others, such as admin MFA and policy review, can be corrected quickly and should be treated as urgent.

The company needs leadership approval for a program led by a named owner, with IT, HR, operations, payroll, developers, and finance working together. The work is feasible, but it cannot be absorbed as an IT side task. The budget should cover process design, tooling or configuration changes, staff time, supplier assessment costs, testing, and independent review where appropriate.

1. Disable the four active leaver accounts, enforce MFA on the four administrator accounts, and start a formal access request, review, and daily leaver process.
2. Establish interim asset and system lists immediately, then complete a full asset inventory with named owners, because inventory underpins patching, logging, encryption, backup, and risk decisions.
3. Start 12-month security log retention, document an incident response plan, and implement a 14-day critical patch process for servers and network systems now.

# 2. Scope and Method

This gap analysis evaluates Bramblewood Payroll Services against the fifteen KDSS controls provided. It is based only on the current-state facts supplied by the operations director. It does not assume the presence of additional controls, evidence, contracts, systems, policies, procedures, ownership arrangements, monitoring tools, external reports, or historical test results unless those items are explicitly stated in the facts. Where a control requirement is not fully demonstrated by the facts, the control is not treated as Met.

The assessment applies the required status definitions exactly:

- **Met**: everything the control requires is in place today.
- **Partially met**: some, but not all, of the required elements are in place.
- **Not met**: none of the required elements is in place.

For controls already Met, this report does not invent gaps merely to fill the analysis. However, Met status means that the facts provided are sufficient to conclude that the control is currently satisfied. It does not guarantee that an auditor will accept all evidence without request for documentation, because an auditor may ask for records of review, test evidence, monitoring logs, approvals, or ownership confirmation that were not included in the facts.

Effort categories are applied as requested:

- **S**: up to 5 person-days.
- **M**: 6 to 20 person-days.
- **L**: more than 20 person-days.

For controls that are already Met, the effort column is shown as **S** to keep the findings within the defined effort categories. For those controls, **S** represents routine maintenance or evidence maintenance rather than remediation of a current gap. For controls that are not Met, effort represents the approximate work required to bring the control to a Met position based on the facts provided.

Several controls interact closely with others. In particular, C-02 asset inventory is foundational to C-03 access management, C-05 encryption, C-06 backups, C-07 patch management, C-09 logging and monitoring, C-13 secure development, C-14 business continuity, and C-15 risk assessment. The lack of an asset inventory is not only a gap against C-02; it also weakens the company’s ability to prove that other controls cover all relevant systems, data, and people.

This report treats payroll data as sensitive client data because Bramblewood runs payroll for about 300 small businesses, but it does not assume details beyond the facts provided. It does not assume that backup copies are encrypted, that laptop data is encrypted, that all servers are known, that suppliers have security certifications, that incident response steps exist in any written form, that continuity arrangements exist in any written form, or that risk treatment actions are being tracked. Those points are treated as unknown and therefore not Met unless the facts specifically state them.

# 3. Summary of Findings

| Control | Status | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| C-01 Information security policy | Partially met | S |
| C-02 Asset inventory | Not met | L |
| C-03 Access management | Partially met | M |
| C-04 Multi-factor authentication | Partially met | S |
| C-05 Encryption | Partially met | M |
| C-06 Backups | Partially met | M |
| C-07 Patch management | Partially met | M |
| C-08 Endpoint protection | Met | S |
| C-09 Logging and monitoring | Partially met | L |
| C-10 Incident response | Not met | M |
| C-11 Supplier security | Not met | M |
| C-12 Security awareness training | Met | S |
| C-13 Secure development | Met | S |
| C-14 Business continuity | Not met | L |
| C-15 Risk assessment | Not met | M |

Met: 3. Partially met: 7. Not met: 5.

# 4. Control-by-Control Analysis

### C-01: Information security policy

Status: Partially met

Gap: A four-page information security policy exists and was approved by the board two years ago, which satisfies the existence of a written policy with leadership approval. However, the control requires review every year, and the facts state that the policy has not been reviewed since approval. Therefore, the annual review requirement is not met. The facts also do not show that the policy was reviewed after the board approval two years ago, and they do not show whether the policy content has been updated to reflect current systems, risks, roles, or certification requirements.

Remediation:
- Assign an accountable owner for policy maintenance, likely the person who leads the certification program or IT/operations leadership.
- Schedule an immediate policy review with leadership and relevant operational owners.
- Review the policy against all fifteen KDSS controls and confirm that it states responsibilities, asset ownership, access management, MFA, encryption, backups, patching, endpoint protection, logging, incident response, supplier security, training, secure development, continuity, and risk assessment.
- Update the policy to reflect current systems, current roles, and current certification expectations.
- Obtain board approval for the updated policy.
- Set a recurring annual review date and create a simple review log showing date reviewed, reviewer, changes, and approver.

Effort: S

### C-02: Asset inventory

Status: Not met

Gap: The facts state that there is no asset inventory of any kind: nobody records hardware, software, or data stores, and assets have no named owners. This means none of the control’s required elements is in place today: there is no inventory of hardware, no inventory of software, no inventory of data stores, no named owner for assets, and no up-to-date inventory. The absence of this control is a major gap because many other controls depend on knowing what assets and data stores exist and who owns them.

Remediation:
- Define inventory categories at a minimum: laptops, servers, network devices, cloud applications, payroll systems, client portal, backup systems, file shares, email systems, client file-transfer systems, databases, and data stores containing client payroll data.
- Create interim lists from known administrative sources, including email/VPN accounts, admin server accounts, IT devices, backup systems, application access lists, developer tooling, and HR employee lists.
- Record each asset with at least: asset name, type, location, criticality, data handled, technology owner, and business owner.
- Assign a named owner to every asset and data store.
- Define what “up-to-date” means, such as updates when devices are deployed, retired, migrated, or when owners change.
- Store the inventory in a controlled location accessible to authorized staff and protected from unauthorized changes.
- Establish a periodic review cadence, at least quarterly during remediation and at least annually after stabilization.

Effort: L

### C-03: Access management

Status: Partially met

Gap: Some elements of access management exist. New access is requested by email to IT and approved by the requester’s manager, which provides a form of approval. However, the control also requires access to be reviewed at least every 6 months and removed within 1 working day of a leaver’s departure. The facts state that access has never been reviewed, and although accounts are usually disabled on the leaver’s last day, an internal check last month found 4 active accounts belonging to people who left more than a month ago. Therefore, the current state cannot be considered Met.

Remediation:
- Immediately investigate and disable the 4 active accounts belonging to people who left more than a month ago.
- Perform a full leaver reconciliation against HR records and all known access points, including email, VPN, servers, payroll database, file shares, client portal, administrative accounts, and file-transfer access.
- Create a joiner, mover, and leaver process using a request form or ticket that records requester, requester’s manager, approver, required system, role, date approved, date provisioned, and date removed.
- Require manager approval for access before IT enables it.
- Define access roles for common functions, especially payroll data, server administration, backup administration, and client portal access.
- Perform an immediate full access review across all known systems.
- Establish a recurring access review at least every 6 months with evidence showing scope, reviewer, date, decisions, and remediation of excessive access.
- Require HR to notify IT of leavers on the leaver’s last day and require IT to disable access within 1 working day.
- Create a daily or frequent reconciliation between HR leaver data and active accounts until the process is reliable.

Effort: M

### C-04: Multi-factor authentication

Status: Partially met

Gap: MFA is enforced on email and VPN, which satisfies part of the control. However, the control requires MFA on all remote access, email, and administrative accounts. The facts state that the four administrator accounts on servers do not use MFA. Therefore, administrative accounts do not currently meet the requirement. Because MFA is present on some but not all required areas, the control is Partially met.

Remediation:
- Identify the four administrator accounts named in the current-state facts.
- Enroll those four administrator accounts in MFA.
- Test the login flow to confirm that MFA works for each administrator account without breaking administrative tasks.
- Confirm that no administrator account remains exempt from MFA.
- Document the MFA enforcement policy and confirm it covers email, VPN, remote access, and administrative accounts.
- Add administrative accounts to a periodic review list to confirm MFA remains enabled.
- If any legacy access method cannot use MFA, document it and evaluate whether an alternative approved control exists; do not assume an exception is permitted, because the standard says all administrative accounts.

Effort: S

### C-05: Encryption

Status: Partially met

Gap: Some required encryption is in place. The payroll database and file shares are encrypted at rest. All web traffic uses TLS. Payroll files are exchanged with clients over an encrypted file-transfer service. However, the facts do not demonstrate that all client data is encrypted at rest and in transit. There is no asset inventory or data-store inventory, so the company cannot currently identify every place where client data resides or travels. The facts do not state whether backups, laptop local copies, mobile devices, temporary files, application data stores, print systems, or internal transfers are encrypted. Because full coverage cannot be demonstrated, the control is not fully Met.

Remediation:
- Create a client data-store inventory as part of or alongside C-02.
- For each data store, record whether data at rest is encrypted, what protects it, and who owns it.
- Verify encryption for the payroll database, file shares, client portal data stores, backup media, backup sites, endpoint devices, temporary files, export files, print queues or scanned documents if used, and any other client data stores identified.
- Confirm in-transit protection for web traffic, file-transfer service, internal data movement, and client exchange workflows.
- Enable or strengthen encryption where any client data store or transport path is unprotected.
- Document the encryption approach as evidence that client data is encrypted at rest and in transit.
- Include encryption verification in future asset and risk reviews.

Effort: M

### C-06: Backups

Status: Partially met

Gap: Daily backups of client data to a second site are in place, which satisfies part of the control. However, the control also requires a restore test at least every quarter, and the facts state that nobody has ever tested a restore. Therefore, the backup control is not fully Met. The company also cannot currently show that the backup scope includes all relevant client data because there is no asset or data-store inventory.

Remediation:
- Define which data is included in the client-data backup scope.
- Confirm whether all relevant client data stores, including payroll database, file shares, client portal data, configuration data, and any other client data identified in the asset inventory, are included in daily backups.
- Document the backup process: what is backed up, when, where, how long retained, who monitors it, and how failures are handled.
- Create a restore procedure for a representative full restore and a representative partial file restore.
- Perform the first restore test now and document the result, including start time, end time, data restored, source backup date, target system, verification steps, and issues found.
- Establish quarterly restore tests and record evidence for each test.
- Add backup success monitoring and exception reporting to the IT operations routine.

Effort: M

### C-07: Patch management

Status: Partially met

Gap: Laptops receive patches automatically within a week, which supports the control for laptops. However, the control requires critical security patches to be applied within 14 days of release on all systems. The facts state that servers are patched by hand about every two months and that the last critical patch took 51 days to apply. This exceeds the 14-day requirement. The company also has no asset inventory, so it cannot currently demonstrate complete coverage across all systems. Therefore, patch management is Partially met.

Remediation:
- Create an interim system list for servers, network devices, payroll systems, client portal infrastructure, backup systems, and any other relevant systems.
- Record the owner and patch responsibility for each system.
- Identify any outstanding critical patches that are older than 14 days and remediate them immediately.
- Define what counts as a critical security patch and how release dates are tracked.
- Create a patch process that applies critical security patches within 14 days of release.
- Define maintenance windows, rollback procedures, and emergency change handling for critical patches.
- Maintain evidence for each critical patch, including patch name, release date, deployment date, systems affected, and who approved deployment.
- Add a monthly or more frequent patch compliance report for servers and network systems.

Effort: M

### C-08: Endpoint protection

Status: Met

Gap: No gap has been shown in the facts for this control. The facts state that every laptop and server runs anti-malware, reporting to a central console that IT checks daily. That is sufficient to conclude that anti-malware is present on every laptop and server and that it is centrally monitored. This conclusion is based only on the facts provided and assumes the statement that “every laptop and server” is accurate and current.

Remediation:
- Maintain the current endpoint protection configuration.
- Keep the central console available and ensure daily checks remain documented or evidenced.
- Include endpoint coverage in the future asset inventory so the company can reconcile endpoints against inventory records.
- Confirm that new laptops and servers are automatically enrolled in anti-malware before first use.
- Retain evidence of central console status and monitoring for auditor review.

Effort: S

### C-09: Logging and monitoring

Status: Partially met

Gap: Some logging exists because firewall and server logs are kept, but they are kept for only 30 days. The control requires security logs from key systems to be kept for 12 months and reviewed weekly. The facts state that logs are only looked at when something goes wrong, so weekly review is not in place. The facts also do not show that “key systems” have been defined or that all relevant log sources are being collected. Therefore, the control is Partially met but materially short of the requirement.

Remediation:
- Define key systems for logging, including firewalls, servers, payroll database, client portal, authentication systems, file-transfer service, backup infrastructure, and any other systems that could show security events.
- Determine whether current logs from the 30-day retention are sufficient or whether log sources need to be re-enabled or expanded.
- Implement a log aggregation or logging method that can retain required security logs for 12 months.
- Confirm storage capacity and cost for 12 months of logs.
- Create a weekly review checklist covering failed logins, privileged account changes, configuration changes, backup failures, suspicious server activity, firewall rule changes, and client-data access anomalies.
- Assign a named reviewer for weekly reviews and record who reviewed, what was reviewed, dates covered, findings, and actions taken.
- Start weekly review immediately rather than waiting for full tooling maturity.

Effort: L

### C-10: Incident response

Status: Not met

Gap: There is no incident response plan. Past incidents were handled by the IT manager as they arose. Informal handling does not satisfy the requirement for a documented incident response plan tested at least once a year. Therefore, none of the required elements is currently in place: there is no plan and no evidence of a test.

Remediation:
- Appoint an incident response lead and define support roles.
- Draft an incident response plan covering: incident definitions, severity levels, detection sources, initial triage, containment steps, eradication steps, recovery steps, communication steps, evidence retention, client notification considerations, root-cause analysis, and post-incident review.
- Include scenarios relevant to Bramblewood: credential compromise, payroll data exposure, ransomware, client portal compromise, malicious insider access, vendor compromise, accidental client-data disclosure, and suspected leaver account misuse.
- Define who is contacted at what time, including IT, leadership, HR, payroll operations, legal or external counsel if appropriate, and client contacts when contractually relevant.
- Test the plan through a tabletop exercise and document the scenario, participants, timeline, decisions, gaps found, and remediation actions.
- Schedule annual testing and add the test date to the certification evidence calendar.

Effort: M

### C-11: Supplier security

Status: Not met

Gap: The company has 9 suppliers that handle client data, but the facts state that the company has never assessed their security. The control requires security due diligence on every supplier that handles client data, repeated every year. Because no due diligence has been performed for any of the 9 suppliers, the control is Not met.

Remediation:
- Confirm the list of all 9 suppliers that handle client data.
- Create a supplier security due diligence method, including questionnaire or evidence request covering access controls, data handling, incident reporting, subcontractors, data location if relevant, and security certifications or reports where available.
- Send the due diligence request to all 9 suppliers.
- Review each supplier’s responses and supporting evidence.
- Identify suppliers with material gaps and define follow-up actions, such as additional information, remediation, compensating controls, or replacement considerations.
- Set a repeat cycle of at least annual due diligence for every supplier that handles client data.
- Record supplier assessment results, dates, assessors, findings, and actions in a controlled evidence file.

Effort: M

### C-12: Security awareness training

Status: Met

Gap: No gap has been shown in the facts for this control. The facts state that all staff complete security awareness training when they join and every year after, and that completion last year was 100%. That satisfies the requirement for training at joining and every year. This conclusion is based only on the facts provided and assumes the statement is current and accurate.

Remediation:
- Maintain the current training schedule.
- Keep completion records for new hires and annual refreshers.
- Ensure new hires receive training at joining and that all staff receive annual training.
- Update content if major control changes occur, such as incident response, phishing, password/MFA expectations, supplier security, or client-data handling changes.
- Retain evidence showing course content, completion dates, and employee names for auditor review.

Effort: S

### C-13: Secure development

Status: Met

Gap: No gap has been shown in the facts for this control. Bramblewood builds and maintains a client portal in-house with two developers. The facts state that every change is reviewed by the other developer and checked against a written list of security requirements before release. That satisfies the control requirements for security requirements and code review for in-house software changes. This conclusion is based only on the facts provided and assumes “every change” is accurate and enforced.

Remediation:
- Maintain the requirement that both developers participate in security review and code review before release.
- Keep the written security requirements list available and current.
- Ensure review evidence is retained, including what was reviewed, who reviewed it, and approval for release.
- If development staffing changes, update the process so that code review cannot be bypassed by a single person.
- Include portal changes in asset inventory and risk assessment evidence so the portal is treated consistently with other key systems.

Effort: S

### C-14: Business continuity

Status: Not met

Gap: There is no business continuity plan. The control requires a plan covering loss of the office and loss of key systems, tested every year. Because no plan exists, none of the required elements is currently in place. The lack of a plan is especially significant for a payroll provider serving about 300 small businesses, because office loss, system loss, or data loss could interrupt payroll processing.

Remediation:
- Identify Bramblewood’s key payroll functions and dependencies, including payroll database access, client file-transfer service, client portal, email, telephony if used, backup access, IT administration access, HR systems, and finance/payroll operations.
- Define recovery priorities and objectives, such as which services must be restored first and what tolerable downtime and data loss would be for each.
- Develop scenarios for loss of office and loss of key systems.
- Define alternate workspace arrangements for staff if the office is unavailable.
- Define alternate access methods for critical systems if normal access is unavailable, ensuring those methods still comply with MFA and access controls.
- Document recovery steps, responsible people, contact lists, and communication procedures.
- Define how payroll processing would continue during degraded conditions.
- Test the continuity plan at least once a year using tabletop, functional, or full tests, and document results and corrective actions.

Effort: L

### C-15: Risk assessment

Status: Not met

Gap: No information-security risk assessment has ever been done. The control requires a documented information-security risk assessment updated every year. Because no risk assessment exists, the control is Not met. The absence of an asset inventory also makes a complete risk assessment more difficult, because risks must be assessed against known assets, data stores, dependencies, owners, and business processes.

Remediation:
- Define a simple risk assessment method with consistent scoring for likelihood and impact.
- Define the scope: client data, payroll processing, IT systems, people, suppliers, offices, and external interfaces.
- Use the asset inventory and supplier list as inputs once available.
- Identify risks such as unauthorized access to payroll data, leaver account misuse, admin accounts without MFA, delayed server patching, insufficient log retention, backup restore failure, supplier compromise, office loss, key system loss, and insecure data stores not yet identified.
- Assess current controls, residual risk, and needed treatments.
- Produce a risk register with owner, treatment, due date, and status.
- Obtain leadership approval for the risk assessment and treatment plan.
- Schedule annual updates and add interim updates when major systems, suppliers, or incidents change.

Effort: M

# 5. Remediation Roadmap

The roadmap places every control that is not Met into one of three phases. Controls already Met are not included in the remediation phases, although they will need evidence maintenance. The ordering is based on three priorities: reduce immediate exposure, create evidence that depends on time passing, and build foundational records that support later assurance. Some controls may require interim work before their assigned phase, but each control is assigned to one phase for completion and audit readiness.

## 0–3 months: Immediate exposure and time-sensitive controls

This phase focuses on the highest-risk, fastest-moving actions and controls where delay directly harms certification evidence.

**C-01 Information security policy**

This control is placed first because it is low effort and high visibility. The policy exists and has leadership approval, but the annual review has not happened. Completing it early establishes a current governance baseline and gives leadership a single document that can reference the rest of the program.

**C-03 Access management**

The discovery of 4 active accounts belonging to people who left more than a month ago is a direct access-hygiene failure. Immediate cleanup is required. A formal joiner, mover, and leaver process should be established now because access control is closely tied to client data exposure. The company should begin a full access review now and build the evidence trail for recurring reviews.

**C-04 Multi-factor authentication**

The four administrator accounts lacking MFA are a clear and quickly closable gap. MFA on administrative accounts is also an auditor-visible control. It should be completed immediately because it is low effort and reduces a known exposure.

**C-07 Patch management**

Server critical patches are being applied outside the required 14-day window, with the last critical patch taking 51 days. This is a direct technical risk. The company should identify outstanding critical server patches and start a 14-day compliance process now. An interim server and system list is required to make the process auditable.

**C-09 Logging and monitoring**

This control is placed early because time is a constraint. Logs are currently kept only 30 days and reviewed ad hoc. To be credible by the 12-month certification point, the company needs to start 12-month retention and weekly review immediately. If log retention is delayed, the company may struggle to show a full 12 months of log evidence at audit time, depending on how the auditor interprets the requirement.

**C-10 Incident response**

There is currently no documented incident response plan. Payroll data breaches and access anomalies would likely require coordinated action. The plan should be created early because it also supports other controls, such as access management, logging, backups, supplier incidents, and client data exposure response. A tabletop test can establish the annual testing cycle.

## 3–6 months: Foundational inventory and dependent technical controls

This phase builds the inventory and data protection evidence needed to prove that controls cover the whole environment. Some interim lists may be produced during the first phase, but the full inventory control is assigned here for completion.

**C-02 Asset inventory**

The asset inventory is foundational. It must cover hardware, software, and data stores with named owners. It cannot credibly be completed without interviews, technical reconciliation, and business ownership decisions. It is placed in this phase because the immediate technical fixes have started, but Bramblewood needs a complete inventory to verify that patching, logging, encryption, backups, continuity, and risk assessment cover everything relevant. The interim lists used in the 0–3 month phase should feed into the full inventory.

**C-05 Encryption**

Encryption cannot be fully proved without knowing all client data stores. After the inventory is substantially complete, the company should verify encryption across payroll data stores, file shares, client portal data, backup copies, endpoints, and any other data locations identified. Encryption work is placed here because it depends on knowing where client data exists.

**C-06 Backups**

Daily backups exist, but the company must document backup scope, confirm restore capability, and perform a quarterly restore test. Restore testing depends on knowing which client data stores are in scope. Once the inventory provides a clearer data-store list, Bramblewood should perform the first full restore test and establish quarterly evidence.

**C-11 Supplier security**

The company has 9 suppliers handling client data and has never assessed them. Supplier due diligence requires outreach, responses, follow-up, and decision-making, so it should begin after the company has a clearer view of its own client-data exposure and critical dependencies. This phase allows time to assess the 9 suppliers and begin the annual cycle.

**C-15 Risk assessment**

A risk assessment should not be done before basic facts about assets, systems, data flows, suppliers, access issues, and current control gaps are documented. By 3–6 months, Bramblewood will have enough input from inventory, access reviews, patching, logging, backups, supplier assessments, and incident response planning to produce a meaningful risk assessment. The risk assessment can then prioritize remaining actions and give leadership a clear treatment plan.

## 6–12 months: Resilience, assurance, and certification readiness

This phase completes the larger resilience program and gives the company time to test and mature controls before audit.

**C-14 Business continuity**

Business continuity is assigned to the final phase because it depends on knowing the key systems, backup arrangements, alternate access needs, office dependencies, suppliers, and risk priorities. Developing and testing a continuity plan takes time and cannot be credibly rushed immediately. Bramblewood should develop the plan, align it with the risk assessment, test it, and document results so the annual test requirement is satisfied before the auditor arrives. The plan must cover loss of office and loss of key systems.

The roadmap is ordered this way because a payroll provider cannot simply purchase or document its way to certification. The company must first stop the most obvious technical exposures, then build an inventory that supports evidence, then test resilience capabilities that require time and coordination. The 12-month window is achievable, but only if the 0–3 month work starts immediately.

# 6. Resourcing and Budget Considerations

This section helps leadership approve a realistic budget. The facts do not provide current costs, salaries, tooling licenses, supplier contracts, auditor fees, or existing capital budgets, so this report cannot produce a precise monetary budget. It can, however, convert the remediation effort categories into a planning view and identify the budget drivers.

The effort estimates are based on the control gaps described above and the definitions provided:

- **S**: up to 5 person-days.
- **M**: 6 to 20 person-days.
- **L**: more than 20 person-days.

For controls already Met, the effort shown as S represents maintenance of evidence, not remediation.

## Planning effort profile

Controls requiring remediation that are assessed as **S**:

- C-01 Information security policy
- C-04 Multi-factor authentication

Controls requiring remediation that are assessed as **M**:

- C-03 Access management
- C-05 Encryption
- C-06 Backups
- C-07 Patch management
- C-10 Incident response
- C-11 Supplier security
- C-15 Risk assessment

Controls requiring remediation that are assessed as **L**:

- C-02 Asset inventory
- C-09 Logging and monitoring
- C-14 Business continuity

Using the minimum boundaries of the categories, the remediation program represents at least approximately:

- 2 S controls at up to 5 person-days each: up to 10 person-days.
- 7 M controls at 6 person-days each: at least 42 person-days.
- 3 L controls at more than 20 person-days each: at least 60 person-days.

This produces a minimum planning figure of about 112 person-days for the gap controls, before considering evidence collection, meeting time, rework, supplier delays, tooling implementation, and auditor follow-up. If the M controls require the upper end of their range and the L controls require significantly more than 20 person-days each, the effort could rise substantially above 200 person-days. Leadership should treat the effort estimate as a planning baseline that requires validation once asset inventory and technical discovery begin.

## Workstream model

The work should be organized into workstreams rather than treated as a single IT project. A practical model would be:

1. **Program governance and evidence management**
   - Owner: Operations Director or assigned certification program lead.
   - Responsibilities: control mapping, evidence tracker, timeline, leadership reporting, auditor readiness, budget approval, and cross-team coordination.

2. **Identity, access, and admin security**
   - Owner: IT manager with HR cooperation.
   - Controls: C-03, C-04.
   - Work: leaver cleanup, access review, MFA on admin accounts, access request and review records.

3. **Asset, data, and infrastructure hygiene**
   - Owner: IT manager with application and payroll operations input.
   - Controls: C-02, C-05, C-06, C-07, C-08, C-09.
   - Work: inventory, encryption verification, backup restoration, patch process, log retention, endpoint monitoring evidence.

4. **Supplier, risk, incident, and continuity program**
   - Owner: Operations Director with finance, payroll, HR, and external support where needed.
   - Controls: C-10, C-11, C-14, C-15.
   - Work: supplier assessments, risk register, incident response plan and test, continuity plan and test.

5. **Training and development assurance**
   - Owner: HR for training; developers for portal assurance.
   - Controls: C-12, C-13.
   - Work: maintain evidence, ensure new hires are enrolled, keep review and security-requirement records.

## Roles likely required internally

Based on the facts and business size, the following internal roles will need meaningful time:

- Operations Director: program ownership, prioritization, leadership reporting, client risk decisions.
- IT manager: access, MFA, servers, patching, logging, endpoint, backup, inventory, incident response, technical evidence.
- HR: leaver data, training evidence, joiner/mover/leaver process, staff records.
- Payroll operations staff: identify client-data processes, data flows, file exchange workflows, continuity impacts.
- Developers: client portal data store inventory, encryption verification, release evidence, continuity for portal.
- Finance or senior leadership: budget approval, supplier contract follow-up, risk treatment decisions.
- A named evidence owner: not necessarily IT; could be operations or compliance, responsible for organizing auditor-ready records.

## External resources to consider

The facts do not show external resources currently engaged. To meet the 12-month timeline and reduce internal capacity pressure, Bramblewood should consider:

- A security consultant or interim compliance lead for program design, evidence structure, and auditor preparation.
- Log management or SIEM implementation support, especially for C-09, because 12-month retention and weekly review are substantial and evidence-heavy.
- Backup restore testing support if internal staff have never performed a restore.
- Business continuity and incident response workshop facilitation, particularly for tabletop and continuity tests.
- Penetration testing or technical validation of the client portal if the company chooses to add assurance beyond C-13, although the facts do not currently indicate such a test is required by KDSS.
- Independent supplier assessment review if supplier responses are complex or if 9 supplier assessments reveal material gaps.

## Major budget drivers

Leadership should expect costs in these areas:

1. **Staff time**
   - The largest internal cost will be time across IT, payroll operations, HR, developers, and leadership. This must be protected, not assumed away.

2. **Inventory tooling or management effort**
   - If inventory is built manually, the cost is time. If automated discovery is used, cost may include tools, licenses, and integration effort.

3. **Log storage and log management**
   - Moving from 30-day logs to 12-month logs is one of the clearer technical and budget risks. Storage, cloud logging services, collection agents, and review tooling may all cost money.

4. **MFA and administrative account changes**
   - MFA may require identity provider configuration, licensing, device enrollment, support time, and testing. The current facts show admin accounts lack MFA, so this should be treated as a priority configuration and support cost.

5. **Backup restore testing**
   - Restore testing may require isolated test environments, storage, staff time, and possibly vendor support. The cost may be higher than expected because no one has ever tested a restore.

6. **Patch process implementation**
   - If servers are patched manually, bringing them into a 14-day critical patch process may require maintenance windows, change management, automation tools, or additional IT capacity.

7. **Supplier assessment costs**
   - Costs may include staff time, questionnaire tooling, follow-up meetings, and potentially contractual or replacement decisions if supplier risk is high.

8. **Continuity plan testing**
   - Continuity testing may require alternate workspace arrangements, downtime simulations, staff coordination, and possibly technical failover support.

9. **Auditor and external review costs**
   - The company intends to hire an auditor. Auditor fees should be planned, but the auditor should not be expected to perform remediation. The audit fee should be separate from remediation effort.

## Evidence management budget

A significant but often underestimated cost is evidence management. Certification requires records, not only controls. Bramblewood should budget for:

- A control evidence matrix.
- Screenshots or reports of MFA, anti-malware, backups, logs, patch status, access reviews, training completion, supplier assessments, and tests.
- Meeting minutes showing board or leadership approval.
- Review sign-offs.
- Incident response and continuity test reports.
- Risk treatment actions and owners.
- Change records for policy, portal, access, and technical controls.

Without a disciplined evidence owner, the company may do the work but still face certification delay because proof is scattered or incomplete.

# 7. Risks to the Certification Timeline

Bramblewood has 12 months before the largest client’s certification condition becomes a renewal issue. That is enough time to close the identified gaps, but only if the program starts now and leadership treats the work as a company-wide initiative rather than an IT checklist.

## 1. The 12-month log retention requirement is time-sensitive

The most timeline-dependent control is C-09. Current logs are kept for 30 days. The standard requires security logs from key systems to be kept for 12 months. If the company waits months to implement 12-month retention, it may not have a full 12-month evidence trail at audit time. Even if the auditor focuses on current retention capability rather than historical retention, the company will be stronger if retention starts immediately.

Timeline risk level: High.

## 2. The asset inventory may reveal more gaps than currently visible

The current facts show no asset inventory. When inventory work begins, Bramblewood may discover unknown servers, laptops, cloud applications, data stores, legacy interfaces, local copies of client data, test environments, shared drives, developer environments, or third-party connections. Each new asset may require ownership, patching, logging, backup, encryption, access, and monitoring decisions.

Timeline risk level: High.

## 3. Access review and leaver cleanup may be larger than the four known accounts

The internal check found 4 active accounts belonging to people who left more than a month ago. Because the company has no asset inventory and access has never been reviewed, that number may understate the issue. The company may also find orphaned application access, stale service accounts, privileged local admin accounts, excessive file-share permissions, or client portal administrator access.

Timeline risk level: High.

## 4. Administrator MFA may affect operational access patterns

MFA is currently absent from four administrator accounts. Enforcing MFA on those accounts is necessary, but administrator access often involves scripts, automation, jump hosts, maintenance windows, or break-glass scenarios. The facts do not show how administrator accounts are used, so implementation may require careful testing. Delay or failure to test could either create unnecessary risk or allow continued MFA gaps.

Timeline risk level: Medium.

## 5. Server patching requires a reliable system list and maintenance discipline

The company knows that the last critical server patch took 51 days, but it does not have a full asset inventory. To meet the 14-day requirement across all systems, Bramblewood needs a complete list of servers, network devices, operating systems, application platforms, and supporting components. It also needs a patch compliance record. Without that, the company may improve patching but still lack proof that all systems are covered.

Timeline risk level: Medium.

## 6. Backup restore testing may uncover failures that take time to fix

The company backs up client data every night but has never tested a restore. The first restore test may reveal that backups are incomplete, encrypted, corrupted, missing application configuration, missing database transaction logs, or unable to restore in a usable payroll timeframe. If the first test fails, remediation may take additional time.

Timeline risk level: High.

## 7. Supplier assessments may reveal dependency problems

There are 9 suppliers handling client data, and none have been security-assessed. Supplier assessments can take weeks because suppliers may respond slowly, refuse to provide evidence, or reveal significant issues. If a supplier cannot meet the company’s expectations, replacement or compensation controls may take longer than the certification timeline allows.

Timeline risk level: Medium to High, depending on supplier responses.

## 8. Business continuity cannot be credibly completed without dependencies being known

A continuity plan for loss of office and loss of key systems depends on knowing which systems are key, what data they process, who uses them, what suppliers are involved, what backups exist, and what alternate access is acceptable. Because Bramblewood lacks an asset inventory, incident response plan, and risk assessment today, continuity work cannot start from a complete foundation. Starting it too late would compress the timeline for developing, approving, testing, and remediating the plan.

Timeline risk level: High.

## 9. Incident response testing may expose gaps in client communication

The current facts show no documented incident response plan and no tested process. Payroll incidents may affect client businesses, employees, and payroll data. The company will need to decide how to handle internal containment, external communication, evidence retention, and client notifications. These decisions may require leadership, legal, and client relationship input. If those inputs are slow, the plan and test may be delayed.

Timeline risk level: Medium.

## 10. Risk assessment may conflict with current priorities if done too early or too late

A risk assessment that is too early may miss important inventory, supplier, logging, and backup facts. A risk assessment that is too late may leave little time to implement treatment actions. Bramblewood needs to update the risk assessment after key remediation starts, then again after test results. Failing to do so may leave leadership without a clear view of residual risk before the audit.

Timeline risk level: Medium.

## 11. Evidence quality may become the bottleneck

Several controls appear operationally achievable within 12 months, but certification depends on showing evidence. The company will need records for: policy review, asset inventory, access approvals, access reviews, leaver removal, MFA enforcement, encryption coverage, backup restore tests, patch deployment, endpoint monitoring, log retention and weekly review, incident response tests, supplier assessments, training completion, portal security reviews, continuity plan tests, and risk assessments.

Evidence collection should start alongside remediation, not after it.

Timeline risk level: High.

## 12. Auditor expectations may exceed the current-state facts

The current-state facts support this gap analysis, but an auditor may ask for additional records, interviews, or technical validation. For example, an auditor may ask to see access review reports, backup test logs, weekly log review sign-offs, incident response test minutes, supplier questionnaires, or continuity test evidence. If controls are implemented but not documented in the auditor’s expected form, the company may fail an otherwise substantive control.

Timeline risk level: Medium to High.

## 13. Single-person dependencies create schedule vulnerability

The facts indicate that IT often operates around the IT manager: past incidents were handled by the IT manager, servers are patched by hand, and admin accounts are managed internally. A certification program cannot depend on one person being available for every task. Backup, logging, access review, inventory, patching, incident response, continuity testing, and evidence preparation all need named owners and deputies.

Timeline risk level: High.

## 14. The client deadline may force risk decisions before all gaps are closed

Because the largest client’s renewal is conditioned on certification in 12 months, leadership may need to decide what level of risk remains acceptable while remediation continues. This is normal, but it should be deliberate. The company should document residual risk decisions, especially if any control remains partially met at audit time.

Timeline risk level: Medium.

# Module 1: Welcome to Quillstone Support

## Objectives

1. Explain Quillstone’s mission and the customers Quillstone support serves, including small business owners and bookkeepers.
2. Apply the Quillstone support basics, including the priority matrix, first-response targets, CLEAR tone guidelines, and escalation path.
3. Begin answering a customer support ticket using Quillstone’s tone and first-response expectations.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 1, and it introduces new support agents to the work of helping small businesses and their bookkeepers use cloud accounting software. Quillstone exists to make accounting simpler, more reliable, and less stressful for businesses that do not have large internal finance teams. A small business owner may need to send an invoice, understand whether a transaction is correctly recorded, or check that payroll can be run before payday. A bookkeeper may manage several client companies and need quick, accurate help with subscription access, bank feeds, payroll features, and account security. In both cases, a support reply can directly affect whether the customer feels confident and whether their business runs smoothly.

At Quillstone support, your role is to be calm, clear, accurate, and kind. Customers often contact us when something is confusing, urgent, or causing a delay. A good reply does more than solve the immediate technical issue. It helps the customer understand what happened, what they need to do, and what Quillstone support will do next. New agents are expected to use the CLEAR tone guideline in every reply. CLEAR means Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next. For example, if a bookkeeper writes, “I can’t access my client’s company file,” a CLEAR first line could be: “I understand you cannot access your client’s company file, and I will help you restore access.”

Quillstone uses a priority matrix so agents can work on the right items first. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are based on priority. P1 must receive a first response within 30 minutes. P2 must receive a first response within 2 hours. P3 must receive a first response within 8 business hours. P4 must receive a first response within 2 business days. These targets are not marketing promises. They are the support team’s commitment to customers who rely on Quillstone for real business operations.

The escalation path is Tier 1, which new agents use, then Tier 2, which senior agents use, then the on-call engineer, but only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve. New agents should not feel pressure to escalate every difficult issue to engineering. Tier 1 agents can resolve many issues with guidance, knowledge articles, and careful customer communication. If a P3 ticket has a clear workaround, it should remain with Tier 1. If a P1 or P2 issue is stuck after senior review, then it can move beyond Tier 2. The on-call engineer is not the first stop for every technical problem, because engineering time must be reserved for critical incidents that cannot be resolved through the support tier.

Concrete examples help set expectations. If a customer says, “How do I add a new invoice template?” that is usually P3, because it is a how-to question with a workaround through the product interface. If a customer says, “I cannot open Quillstone at all from any device and I need to pay staff today,” that is P1, because the customer cannot use Quillstone and payroll may be blocked. If a customer writes, “Please add a button to export invoices to CSV,” that is P4, because it is feature feedback. If a customer writes, “The import button returns an error and the alternative upload method is also unavailable,” that is P2, because a key feature is broken with no workaround.

# Module 2: Our Product in One Day

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 2 and gives new agents a one-day understanding of the Quillstone product so they can answer common questions without guessing. Quillstone is cloud accounting software for small businesses and their bookkeepers. The product helps customers manage books, invoices, subscriptions, client companies, bank feeds, payroll, and related accounting workflows. A support agent does not need to know everything on the first day, but new agents do need a reliable foundation. Knowing the plans prevents incorrect statements, which protects customer trust and prevents unnecessary escalations.

Quillstone has three main plans. Starter costs €12 per month and includes one user with no payroll. Team costs €29 per month and includes up to five users and payroll for up to ten employees. Practice costs €79 per month and is designed for bookkeepers, with unlimited client companies. When a customer asks whether a plan is suitable, agents should use plain language. A reply should be helpful without becoming a substitute for professional tax advice.

The same support basics apply while learning the product. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. A growing team with five users and eight employees might fit Team. Agents should not pressure customers into upgrades, but they should give accurate, non-confusing information. If a customer asks whether Quillstone can replace their accountant, the answer is no. Quillstone can help manage records and tax features, but customers must consult their accountant for tax decisions.

# Module 3: The Ticketing System and Priorities

## Objectives

1. Classify support tickets accurately using Quillstone’s priority matrix.
2. Apply first-response targets and the escalation path while working a ticket queue.
3. Use a ticketing-system mindset to capture the facts needed to resolve or escalate an issue.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 3 and focuses on how Quillstone support prioritises work in a ticketing system. Every customer message becomes a ticket. The ticket is not just a place to answer; it is the record of what the customer said, what the agent understood, what actions were taken, what priority was assigned, and who else was involved. Good ticket handling prevents handover errors. A senior agent reviewing a ticket should understand the issue without needing to ask the customer to repeat basic facts.

The priority matrix is the backbone of queue work. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. The CLEAR tone guideline applies to every reply: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next. The escalation path is Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve.

Triage is the skill of deciding priority and next steps quickly. A customer may use strong language, but priority is not set by anger alone. A customer may write, “This is ridiculous, I cannot open Quillstone and payroll is today,” which is P1 because a payroll run is blocked on payday. A customer may write angrily about wanting a new feature, which may still be P4 because it is feedback. A customer may be calm but describe a P2 issue, such as an export function failing with no alternative. Agents should separate emotion from priority and then choose the right tone based on the situation.

In the ticketing system, the first response should not be empty. Even if the issue is not solved, the first response should confirm the problem and state what is happening. For example: “I understand you cannot export bank transactions and there is no workaround available, and I am treating this as P2 while we investigate.” That response confirms the problem, leads with the classification, explains the current status, avoids jargon, and gives the customer a sense of next steps. If a P1 ticket arrives, the first response must be urgent and focused. If a P4 ticket arrives, the first response may acknowledge feedback and explain that product teams review requests during planning cycles.

Concrete examples help avoid mistakes. A ticket saying “I forgot how to add a user” is usually P3. A ticket saying “I cannot log in because the system is down for everyone” may be P1 or P2 depending on scope, but if the customer cannot use Quillstone at all, it is P1. A ticket saying “Please improve the mobile view” is P4. A ticket saying “The payroll button is missing and cannot be found by any user” is P2 unless it blocks payroll on payday, in which case it is P1. Agents should not guess. If a reply would require a product decision, a security decision, or an engineering judgement, they should gather facts and use the escalation path appropriately.

# Module 4: Writing Great Replies

## Objectives

1. Apply the CLEAR tone guideline in written customer replies.
2. Rewrite unclear support responses into clear, customer-friendly replies.
3. Use priority and first-response targets to shape the urgency and next steps in a reply.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 4 and focuses on writing support replies that customers can trust and act on. In Quillstone support, good writing is not decoration. It is part of the service. A confused customer may make worse business decisions, contact multiple agents, or lose trust in the product. A clear reply reduces effort for the customer and reduces repeated contacts for support. The main writing standard is the CLEAR tone guideline: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next.

Confirm the problem means the customer should immediately know you understood them. If the customer writes, “I cannot reconcile a bank transaction because the categories disappear,” do not start with unrelated system details. Start with: “I understand you cannot reconcile a bank transaction because the categories disappear.” Lead with the answer means state the main next step, workaround, or status quickly. For a P3 how-to issue, the answer may be the actual steps. For a P2 issue, the answer may be that the issue is confirmed and investigation is underway. For a P1 issue, the answer may be a workaround and immediate escalation if needed.

Explain the steps means give simple, numbered or sequential instructions when the customer must do something. Avoid jargon means translate internal language into customer language. Instead of “The OAuth token expired,” say “Your bank connection needs to be approved again.” Instead of “The tenant is inaccessible,” say “You cannot access your company file right now.” Recap what happens next means end with what the customer should do and what Quillstone will do. For example: “Please try the steps above and reply with a screenshot if they fail. If the error continues, we will review the logs and update you within the target response time for this priority.”

The priority matrix must remain visible even in writing. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday, with a first-response target of 30 minutes. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround, with a first-response target of 2 hours. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question, with a first-response target of 8 business hours. P4 means feedback and feature requests, with a first-response target of 2 business days. The escalation path is Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve. A reply should never claim a solution that has not been confirmed, and should never blame the customer.

A strong reply has a predictable structure. First, acknowledge the issue. Second, state the most important answer or next step. Third, give instructions if the customer has a task. Fourth, include what information is needed if the customer must reply. Fifth, recap what happens next. For example, for a P2 export failure: “I understand the invoice export button shows an error and there is no workaround. We are treating this as a P2 issue and investigating now. If a temporary workaround becomes available, we will send it to you as soon as it is confirmed. Please reply with your user email and the approximate time of the last failed export so we can check the logs.”

A weak reply says, “We received your request and are looking into it.” It may technically be true, but it gives no confirmation, answer, steps, or clear recap. A better reply is specific, even if the issue is not solved. Quillstone customers need to know that the agent understands the impact. A bookkeeper managing client companies has a different workload than a sole trader, and a reply that recognises that impact is more effective.

A good answer should confirm the problem, lead with the next action, explain that support is investigating urgently, avoid jargon, and recap the next update. The first-response mindset should be 30 minutes.

# Module 5: Handling Billing and Subscriptions

## Objectives

1. Explain Quillstone’s plans, pricing, and refund policy accurately to customers.
2. Use identity checks and the escalation path when billing or subscription changes are requested.
3. Respond to billing issues using CLEAR tone and the correct priority target.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 5 and gives agents the knowledge needed to handle billing, subscriptions, refunds, plan changes, and related account questions. Billing issues can feel urgent because customers often link them to business survival. A failed payment may block invoices, a plan change may affect payroll access, and a refund question may determine whether a customer stays with Quillstone. Agents must be precise and calm. The priority matrix still governs urgency. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. Tone follows CLEAR: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next.

Quillstone plans are Starter €12 per month, Team €29 per month, and Practice €79 per month. Starter includes one user and no payroll. Team includes up to five users and payroll for up to ten employees. Practice is designed for bookkeepers and includes unlimited client companies. If a customer asks why they were charged a different amount, agents should not assume fraud, error, or entitlement before checking facts. Common causes include plan changes, number of users, tax adjustments, or customer-requested upgrades. The agent’s first job is to confirm the issue, lead with a clear next step, and explain what verification is needed.

Before any account change, identity must be verified. The agent confirms the account email plus two of the following: the last invoice amount, the company registration number, and the date the account was opened. Agents never ask for a customer’s password, and they never share data from one customer’s account with another person, even within the same company, without the account owner’s permission. This rule is especially important when a bookkeeper contacts support about a client company. A bookkeeper may manage many companies, but the person requesting a change must have permission from the account owner. A reply should explain this respectfully, because customers may see the request as annoying, but it protects their financial data.

The refund policy is simple: full refund within 30 days of the first payment on any plan; after that, no refunds for partial months. Agents should state this clearly, without sounding harsh. For example: “I understand you would like a refund for the unused portion of this month. Because the refund period of 30 days from the first payment has passed, we cannot refund the partial month, but I can confirm your current subscription end date and the options available to you.” If the customer disputes the charge and claims no authorisation, the ticket may become P2 or P3 depending on impact. If a failed payment locks the customer out of Quillstone, it is P1. If a customer wants to downgrade and can use the product normally, it is usually P3.

Concrete examples help. A customer says, “I paid for Practice but the Team price appears on my invoice.” The agent should confirm the issue, check the account, verify identity, and explain whether it is a tax display issue, plan mismatch, or billing error. If it is a billing system failure preventing access, it may be P1 or P2. If it is only a question about the invoice, it is usually P3. The escalation path remains Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve. Billing questions that are factual and answerable remain with Tier 1. Billing incidents that block payroll on payday are treated as P1 and may require senior and engineering attention if Tier 2 cannot resolve them.
