# Module 6: Bank Feeds and Reconciliation Problems

## Objectives

1. Explain how Quillstone bank feeds work and what customers can do when a feed breaks.
2. Triage bank feed and reconciliation problems using the priority matrix and first-response targets.
3. Write CLEAR guidance that avoids promising actions Quillstone support cannot perform.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 6 and covers one of the most common support areas: bank feeds and reconciliation problems. Quillstone uses a third-party connection service to connect customer bank accounts to the product. Because the connection depends on both Quillstone and the bank connection service, agents must be careful not to imply that Quillstone can always fix it immediately. In most cases, a broken bank feed requires the customer to re-authorise the connection with their bank, and agents cannot do that for them. This fact is central to writing honest, helpful replies. Customers may feel that the bank should do it for them, but the re-authorisation must be completed by the customer through the normal bank connection flow.

The priority matrix helps prevent overreacting or underreacting. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. The escalation path is Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve. Tone is CLEAR: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next.

Most bank feed tickets begin as P3 because the customer can re-authorise. For example, if a feed says “Connection disconnected” and the customer has not tried re-authorising, the answer is: “Please re-authorise the bank connection in the Connections page.” That is a workaround or standard action, so the issue is not automatically P2. If the customer tries re-authorising and receives an error, then the next step is to gather details such as bank name, error message, time of attempt, and screenshot. If many customers report the same issue, the incident may become P2 or P1 depending on impact. If a payroll run is blocked on payday because bank balance data is missing, that may become P1 if it truly blocks payroll; if payroll can continue without the feed, it may remain P2 or P3.

Reconciliation problems can be P3 or P2 depending on workaround. If a customer cannot categorise a transaction but can use manual reconciliation, it is likely P3. If reconciliation is impossible and there is no workaround, it is P2. If reconciliation failure also prevents payroll on payday, it may become P1 only if the payroll run is blocked on payday. Agents should not claim that Quillstone can edit bank data without permission. Agents should also avoid sharing one customer’s data with another. The rule is that agents never ask for a customer’s password, and never share data from one customer’s account with another person, even within the same company, without the account owner’s permission.

A good reply for a bank feed problem might be: “I understand your bank feed stopped syncing and the error says the connection is disconnected. The first step is to re-authorise the bank connection, which your bank requires you to do yourself. Please open the Connections page, select your bank, choose Reconnect, and follow the prompts. If the error returns, reply with the bank name, the exact error message, and a screenshot. If it still fails, we will review the logs and tell you the next step.” This reply confirms, leads, explains, avoids jargon, and recaps.

Please fix it.” Classify the issue and write a reply. A good answer should recognise that because there is a workaround, it is likely P3 unless another critical process is blocked. The reply should confirm the issue, lead with the re-authorisation step, explain that the customer must re-authorise with their bank, avoid saying Quillstone can fix it on their behalf, and recap what happens if re-authorisation fails.

# Module 7: Payroll and Tax Questions

## Objectives

1. Recognise when a payroll issue is P1, P2, P3, or P4 using the priority matrix.
2. Support payroll workflows without giving tax advice.
3. Use CLEAR replies and the escalation path for payroll and tax-related support requests.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 7 and focuses on payroll and tax questions. These topics carry high business risk because payroll deadlines are time-sensitive and tax compliance is sensitive. Quillstone’s priority matrix is especially important here. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. The escalation path is Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve. Tone is CLEAR: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next.

Payroll issues can change priority depending on timing. If a payroll run fails on payday, it is P1 because the customer cannot pay staff on time. If a payroll button is broken outside of payday but there is no workaround, it is P2. If a customer asks how to create an employee record, that is usually P3. If a customer requests a new payslip format, that is P4 unless the current payslip is unusable and blocks a required process with no workaround. Agents must ask the customer whether the payroll run is blocked on payday before deciding. A customer may say “payroll is broken” and mean a minor display problem, or they may mean they cannot pay employees today. The difference is critical.

Tax questions require a firm boundary. Agents never give tax advice. They can explain how to use Quillstone’s tax features, such as where to enter a tax code, how to view a tax report, or how to export records for an accountant. Agents must refer tax questions to the customer’s accountant. A good reply is: “I understand you are unsure whether your tax code is correct. Quillstone can show you where the tax code is entered and how to view payroll tax reports, but I cannot confirm whether this code is correct for your business. Please check with your accountant, then return if you need help locating the setting in Quillstone.” This is helpful, safe, and clear.

When handling payroll or tax tickets, agents must also follow identity and data rules. Before any account change, confirm the account email plus two of the following: the last invoice amount, the company registration number, and the date the account was opened. Agents never ask for a customer’s password, and never share data from one customer’s account with another person, even within the same company, without the account owner’s permission. This is important for bookkeepers, because one bookkeeper may manage many client companies. A support agent should not treat a bookkeeper’s access as automatic permission to change every client account without verification.

A strong P1 payroll reply may be: “I understand the payroll run is failing on payday and staff cannot be paid. I am treating this as P1 and will investigate urgently. If there is an immediate workaround, I will tell you as soon as it is confirmed. Please reply with the error message, employee name affected if applicable, and the time of the failed run. If the issue is unresolved after Tier 2 review and is still blocking payroll, we will escalate according to the support path.” This confirms, leads with urgency, explains steps, avoids jargon, and recaps next steps.

## Exercise

A customer writes: “Payroll will not process and I cannot pay employees until Friday because the run says ‘Tax configuration incomplete.’ What do I do?” Classify and reply. A good answer should first determine whether payroll is blocked on payday. If the customer cannot pay employees on the scheduled payday, classify as P1. If they can complete the run later using a confirmed workaround or can contact their accountant, adjust accordingly. The reply should confirm the issue, lead with the next step, explain that Quillstone cannot advise on the tax configuration itself but can explain where to update it or where to find the relevant report, and recap what happens next.

## Quiz

1. What makes a payroll issue P1?
A) The customer is angry
B) A payroll run is blocked on payday
C) The customer wants a new payslip design
D) The customer has a how-to question

2. What is the first-response target for P1?
A) 30 minutes
B) 2 hours
C) 8 business hours
D) 2 business days

3. Can a Quillstone support agent tell a customer which tax code to use?
A) Yes, if the customer is on Team
B) Yes, if the agent has used Quillstone for one month
C) No, agents explain tax features and refer tax questions to the customer’s accountant
D) No, but they can create tax filings

4. If payroll will not process on payday and there is no workaround, what priority is likely?
A) P4
B) P3
C) P2 or P1 depending on whether it blocks payroll on payday
D) Only P4 if it is called a bug

5. What must happen before changing payroll settings on the customer’s account?
A) The agent may change settings if the email looks familiar
B) The agent must verify identity using account email plus two approved details
C) The agent can ask for the password
D) The agent can share data with another client of the bookkeeper without permission

## Answer Key

1. B) A payroll issue is P1 when a payroll run is blocked on payday.
2. A) P1 has a first-response target of 30 minutes because payroll may be needed urgently.
3. C) Agents never give tax advice, but they can explain tax features and refer tax questions to the customer’s accountant.
4. C) If payroll will not process, it may be P1 when it blocks payroll on payday and P2 when a key feature is broken without workaround but not on payday.
5. B) Before changing payroll settings, the agent must verify identity using account email plus two approved details.

# Module 8: Difficult Conversations

## Objectives

1. De-escalate angry or frustrated customers using the CLEAR tone guideline.
2. Maintain accurate priorities when customers are emotional or pressuring for action.
3. Handle account-change requests in difficult conversations using identity checks and safe data boundaries.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 8 and prepares agents for difficult conversations. Customers may contact support during a bad week. A bookkeeper may have four clients behind schedule. A business owner may be trying to pay staff before a holiday. A customer may feel ignored, confused, or embarrassed by a mistake. The agent’s goal is not to argue, match the customer’s emotion, or promise things that are not true. The goal is to create clarity, trust, and forward motion. The CLEAR tone guideline is the main tool: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next.

The priority matrix must still guide the reply. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. The escalation path is Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve. Difficult conversations do not automatically change priority. A customer may be very angry about a feature request, but if the issue is feedback, it remains P4. A customer may be calm but report a payroll run blocked on payday, which is P1.

De-escalation requires specificity. Do not say “Calm down.” Do not say “That is not our fault.” Do not say “I am sorry if you feel that way.” Better: “I understand this delay is affecting your payroll deadline, and I am sorry for the impact. Here is what I can confirm: the payroll run is failing, and I am checking this now.” If Quillstone made a mistake, admit it plainly: “You are right, our response was slower than promised, and I am sorry.” Accountability builds trust. If the customer asks for a manager, explain the escalation path without making it sound like a punishment: “I am Tier 1 support. I am handling this, and if it needs senior review, I can bring Tier 2 in without asking you to repeat everything.”

Identity and data protection remain strict even under pressure. Before any account change, confirm the account email plus two of the following: the last invoice amount, the company registration number, and the date the account was opened. Agents never ask for a customer’s password, and never share data from one customer’s account with another person, even within the same company, without the account owner’s permission. An angry caller may say, “I know the owner, just fix it now.” A good agent says, “I understand the urgency, and I can move quickly once we complete the required verification. Please provide the account email plus two of the approved details. I cannot access or change the account without this.”

Concrete examples help. If a customer writes, “This is unacceptable, your bank feed is broken and I have been waiting all day,” the priority may be P3 if there is a manual workaround, not automatically P1. The reply should acknowledge frustration, confirm the issue, lead with the workaround or next step, explain the steps, avoid jargon, and recap next steps. If the customer says, “Payroll is today and it will not run,” the priority may be P1, and the reply should be short, direct, urgent, and transparent.

## Exercise

A customer writes: “Your support has taken three days and my invoice export is still broken. I am not leaving another ticket. Fix it now or I am cancelling.” First, classify if the export is broken with no workaround and whether payroll is affected. Then write a reply. A good answer should not argue about the delay. It should confirm the customer’s frustration, lead with the current status, explain whether it is P2 or P3 based on impact, avoid jargon, and recap what the agent will do next. If the issue is P2, the reply should reflect the 2-hour first-response target and a clear escalation to Tier 2 if needed.

## Quiz

1. What is the best first step in a difficult support reply?
A) Tell the customer to be patient
B) Confirm the problem in your own words
C) Explain all internal systems
D) Promise a refund without checking policy

2. Does anger automatically make a ticket P1?
A) Yes
B) No, priority depends on impact and the priority matrix
C) Only for Team customers
D) Only for Practice customers

3. If Quillstone responded slowly, what should the agent do?
A) Deny the delay
B) Admit it, apologise, and focus on next steps
C) Blame the customer
D) Escalate to the on-call engineer immediately for any P3

4. Can an agent change an account while being pressured to skip identity verification?
A) Yes, if the customer is upset
B) Yes, if the customer claims to know the owner
C) No, identity verification is required before account changes
D) Only if the ticket is P4

5. What is the escalation path?
A) Tier 2 to Tier 1 to engineering
B) Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve
C) Directly to engineering for all angry tickets
D) No escalation path exists

## Answer Key

1. B) Confirming the problem in your own words is the best first step because it shows understanding and reduces conflict.
2. B) Anger does not automatically make a ticket P1; priority is determined by impact using the priority matrix.
3. B) If Quillstone responded slowly, the agent should admit it, apologise, and focus on next steps.
4. C) Identity verification is required before account changes, even when a customer is angry or pressuring the agent.
5. B) The escalation path is Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve.

# Module 9: Escalation and Working with Engineering

## Objectives

1. Know when a ticket should remain Tier 1, move to Tier 2, or require engineering.
2. Write escalation notes that save time and preserve customer context.
3. Use the priority matrix, response targets, CLEAR tone, and escalation rules to handle critical issues.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 9 and explains escalation without making escalation mysterious. Escalation is not a personal failure. It is a way to move a ticket to the right people at the right time. New agents are Tier 1. They handle first responses, standard troubleshooting, how-to questions, and known workarounds. Tier 2 consists of senior agents. They help with complex issues, coaching, and tickets that Tier 1 cannot resolve. The on-call engineer is involved only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve. This path is important because engineering time must be protected from routine support questions while still supporting true incidents.

The priority matrix is required to decide escalation. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. Tone is CLEAR: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next. Escalation should not be confused with first-response. Even if a ticket needs escalation, the customer must still receive the first response target for its priority.

A good escalation note should be structured enough to let Tier 2 or engineering understand quickly. It should include the customer’s exact problem, whether it blocks payroll on payday or prevents Quillstone use, the customer impact, the priority assigned, what Tier 1 checked, what the customer tried, screenshots or error text, account details where permitted, and the desired next action. For example: “P2 customer cannot run payroll; error ‘Tax API timeout’; payroll run not on payday today, so not P1 yet; customer retried on two browsers; logs show repeated failure; Tier 2 asked to confirm whether this is account-specific or broader.” This note is better than “Payroll broken, please fix.” It saves time and avoids asking the customer to repeat themselves.

Agents should avoid two common errors. First, they should not escalate P3 or P4 issues to engineering. A how-to question, a feature request, or a workaround issue belongs with Tier 1 or Tier 2. Second, they should not delay escalation when Tier 2 is stuck on a true P1 or P2. If a payroll run is blocked on payday, Tier 1 should not spend 30 minutes silently searching when a short customer update and Tier 2 handoff are faster. If a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, the first response should come quickly, and escalation should follow the path.

Working with engineering requires discipline. Engineering needs facts, not adjectives. Instead of “This is terrible for the customer,” write “This customer cannot access Quillstone from any device and has three users affected.” Instead of “Probably a bank bug,” write “The bank connection service returned HTTP 401 during re-authorisation at 14:06 UTC; customer has completed re-authorisation twice.” Data protection still applies. Agents never ask for a customer’s password, and never share data from one customer’s account with another person, even within the same company, without the account owner’s permission. Identity checks are required before account changes. A P1 ticket does not suspend security rules.

A good customer-facing update during escalation should be transparent but not too technical. “We are still investigating and will update you by [time].” If the first-response target is 30 minutes for P1, the customer should receive something within that time, even if it is only an acknowledgement and a plan. If the first-response target is 2 hours for P2, the update should be equally clear. The recap should say who owns the next action: the customer, Tier 2, or engineering. If the customer must provide more information, ask for only what is needed and explain why.

## Exercise

A customer writes: “The Quillstone login page shows a maintenance message for all our users, and we have payroll scheduled in 40 minutes.” Classify, write the first customer response, and write a short internal escalation note. A good answer should classify this as P1 because Quillstone appears unusable and payroll is blocked or may be blocked on payday. The customer response should confirm the problem, lead with the urgent action, explain what is happening, avoid jargon, and recap the next update. The internal note should include priority, impact, login symptom, payroll deadline, checks performed, and the request to Tier 2.

## Quiz

1. Who are Tier 2 support personnel?
A) Engineers
B) Senior agents
C) Customers
D) Accountants

2. When may the on-call engineer be involved?
A) For any P4 feature request
B) Only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve
C) For all P3 how-to questions
D) Whenever a customer uses caps lock

3. What is the first-response target for P2?
A) 30 minutes
B) 2 hours
C) 8 business hours
D) 2 business days

4. Which escalation note is most useful?
A) “Urgent, customer angry”
B) “Please help”
C) “P1: payroll blocked on payday, login error 500 at 10:14 UTC, user retried twice, Tier 2 review requested”
D) “They think it is a bug”

5. Should a P1 ticket wait until the problem is solved before the customer receives a first response?
A) Yes
B) No, the customer must still receive a first response within 30 minutes
C) Only if engineering is already involved
D) Only for P3 tickets

## Answer Key

1. B) Tier 2 consists of senior agents who help resolve complex tickets and support Tier 1 agents.
2. B) The on-call engineer is involved only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve.
3. B) P2 has a first-response target of 2 hours because a key feature is broken with no workaround.
4. C) A useful escalation note includes priority, impact, technical facts, checks performed, and the specific request.
5. B) A P1 ticket requires a first response within 30 minutes, even if the issue is not yet resolved.

# Module 10: Data Protection and Account Security

## Objectives

1. Apply identity verification and data-sharing rules before account changes or sensitive requests.
2. Recognise P1, P2, P3, and P4 scenarios in security incidents while protecting customer trust.
3. Write secure, CLEAR replies that never ask for passwords or expose another customer’s data.

## Content

This module is usually taught on Day 10 and focuses on data protection and account security. Quillstone handles financial data, invoice records, bank transaction summaries, payroll data, and tax-related information. A single security mistake can harm a business, so security is not a minor policy topic. It is part of the product promise. Every support agent must understand the priority matrix because security issues can be urgent. P1 means a customer cannot use Quillstone at all, or a payroll run is blocked on payday. P2 means a key feature is broken with no workaround. P3 means a problem with a workaround, or a how-to question. P4 means feedback and feature requests. First-response targets are P1 30 minutes, P2 2 hours, P3 8 business hours, and P4 2 business days. Tone is CLEAR: Confirm the problem in your own words; Lead with the answer; Explain the steps; Avoid jargon; Recap what happens next. The escalation path is Tier 1 to Tier 2 to the on-call engineer, only for P1 and P2 issues that Tier 2 cannot resolve.

The core identity rule is simple. Before any account change, the agent confirms the account email plus two of the following: the last invoice amount, the company registration number, and the date the account was opened. Account changes include email changes, password reset guidance that requires backend action, adding or removing users, plan changes, billing changes, payroll settings, and access changes. A request does not need to sound dangerous to require verification. A simple request such as “Please remove a former employee” still needs verification.

Two absolute rules apply: agents never ask for a customer’s password, and never share data from one customer’s account with another person, even within the same company, without the account owner’s permission. This second rule is critical for bookkeepers. A bookkeeper may manage several client companies, but each client company belongs to the account owner. If a bookkeeper asks for transaction totals from one client to send to another, the agent must not do it without owner permission. If a person says they are the owner’s assistant, verification must be handled according to account access rules, not assumptions.

Security incidents can become P1 if they prevent Quillstone access or block payroll on payday. For example, “I cannot log in at all, and the system is down for everyone” is P1 because the customer cannot use Quillstone. “I can log in but cannot run payroll on payday because the account was unexpectedly locked” is P1. A suspicious login alert may be P2 if a key security feature is broken with no workaround. A general question such as “How do I change my password?” is usually P3. Feature feedback about the login screen is P4. Priority depends on impact, not only on whether the word “security” appears in the message.

A secure reply protects the customer while remaining helpful. Example: “I understand you believe someone else accessed your account. For your safety, I cannot share account details with anyone until we verify the account owner. Please provide the account email plus two of last invoice amount, company registration number, or date the account was opened. I cannot ask for your password. If you need to reset it, I can point you to the secure reset flow.” This reply confirms, leads with the next step, explains steps, avoids jargon, and recaps. It also demonstrates that security is for the customer’s benefit.

Data protection also means careful internal behaviour. Agents should not paste one customer’s invoice amount into a reply to another customer as an example. They should not ask for bank passwords, payroll passwords, or accountant portal passwords. They should not confirm whether a specific person owns an account to an unverified caller. They should not treat “I know this is true” as verification. When a customer resists verification, agents can explain the reason without lecturing: “These checks protect your financial records from unauthorised access.”

## Exercise

A caller says: “I am the bookkeeper for Maple Ltd. The owner is travelling, so please change their account email immediately and send their last invoice amount to my new email address.” How should the agent respond? A good answer should identify that the request involves an account change and data sharing. The agent should confirm the request, explain that verification is required, ask for the account email plus two approved details, explain that they cannot ask for a password, and state that data cannot be shared without owner permission unless the person has verified account access. If the customer cannot complete verification, the ticket may be P3 or P2 depending on whether they can still use Quillstone, but the security rule remains non-negotiable.

## Quiz

1. What is required before any account change?
A) Customer email only
B) Account email plus two of last invoice amount, company registration number, or date the account was opened
C) The customer’s bank login
D) A verbal promise

2. When must an agent never ask for a password?
A) Only during billing calls
B) Only for P1 tickets
C) Never
D) Only for Starter customers

3. When can an agent share data from one customer’s account with another person?
A) When the person says they are the owner’s assistant
B) When the person is a bookkeeper managing many clients
C) Only with the account owner’s permission, and within verified account access rules
D) When the ticket is P2

4. If a security problem prevents Quillstone use entirely, what priority may it be?
A) P4
B) P3
C) P2 only
D) P1 if the customer cannot use Quillstone or payroll is blocked on payday

5. What should a secure reply do when verification is needed?
A) Ask for the password to make verification easier
B) Confirm the request, explain verification, ask for allowed details, and recap next steps
C) Skip verification if the customer is upset
D) Share some account details to prove the agent knows the account

## Answer Key

1. B) Before any account change, the agent confirms the account email plus two of last invoice amount, company registration number, or date the account was opened.
2. C) Agents never ask for a customer’s password, regardless of ticket type or priority.
3. C) Data cannot be shared from one customer’s account with another person without the account owner’s permission and proper verified access.
4. D) A security problem may be P1 when it prevents Quillstone use or blocks payroll on payday.
5. B) A secure reply confirms the request, explains verification, asks only for allowed details, and recaps next steps without asking for a password.

output.text:
# 1. Overview

Inkwell is a note-taking app intended for people who need to capture, organise, and retrieve written material quickly, while keeping control of their notes. The product is for web, iOS, and Android. Notes are stored locally on the device first, encrypted locally, and synced to a private server when a network is available. The product is rich text, but uses Markdown shortcuts because the target users want speed and predictability, not a heavy publishing interface.

The first public release is assumed to be a public beta in 20 weeks, followed by general availability in week 24. The company is a 14-person startup, so the first release must prove the core promise—fast, private, offline-first notes that sync reliably—without taking on every feature in the research wish list. The MVP therefore prioritises creation, editing, organisation, search, offline work, sync, and trash/restore. Attachments, web clipping, PDF annotation, version history, pin/favourite, and note locking are scheduled after the MVP. This trade-off is explained in the MVP Cut section.

Inkwell’s free plan supports up to three active devices for one account. Inkwell Plus costs €4 per month and removes the device limit. The full Plus promise also includes 10 GB of attachment storage and 30 days of version history, but those two entitlements are not available in the first public beta because their storage, sync, retention, and privacy costs are too large for a 20-week release window. At launch, the device-limit enforcement is the primary visible difference between free and Plus. This is a deliberate MVP trade-off, not a change to the business model.

The core object is a **note**. A note has a title, body, notebook assignment, tags when available in later releases, timestamps, and a sync status. Notes can be created, edited, deleted, restored from trash, and synced across devices. A **notebook** is a single-assignment container for notes; a note can appear in only one notebook at a time. **Tags** are multi-assignment labels. In the MVP, both notebooks and tags are in scope because the personas show two different organisation behaviours: Maya thinks in courses or projects, while Daniel thinks in client, meeting, and time-based filters.

The product supports a local-first architecture. “Local-first” means the app reads and writes from a local encrypted database, and the user can complete core workflows without a network connection. The server is used for cross-device sync and, later, subscription entitlement checks and attachments. The local database must survive device reboot and remain available if the server is unavailable.

The MVP is not a complete replacement for all note-taking workflows. It does not include attachments, PDFs, clips, annotation, version history, pinned notes, or locked notes. Those are after-MVP stories in this PRD. That means the first release must be judged against its narrow goal: become a fast, reliable, trustworthy text note app that people use daily.

The PRD is written for engineers, designers, and the CEO. It should be read as a set of testable requirements. If a statement cannot be checked by a tester, it is not a requirement. The first release should be measured by whether users can create and find notes without the app feeling slow, whether offline edits sync predictably, and whether the product avoids surprising data loss.

# 2. Goals and Non-Goals

**Goals**

- **G-1: Make text capture fast.** A signed-in tester can create a note and enter at least 50 visible characters before the app prompts for anything else. The note appears in the current notebook list within 1 second.
- **G-2: Make Markdown editing predictable.** The editor recognises at least heading 1, bullet list, ordered list, bold, italic, inline code, and checkbox shortcuts from the MVP scope. Each shortcut converts visible content in the same step and supports undo.
- **G-3: Make notes findable.** Full-text search works offline across local notes and returns matching title and body content. With the reference 10,000-note dataset, search results appear with p95 latency under 500 ms.
- **G-4: Protect data from accidental deletion.** Deleted notes enter Trash for 30 days and can be restored. A tester can confirm that a note deleted 1 day ago can be restored to its original notebook and appears in normal search.
- **G-5: Sync across devices reliably for small notes.** When a device is online, a note change becomes visible on another device for the same account within 10 seconds. When a device reconnects after offline editing, the sync queue completes within 10 seconds for text edits.
- **G-6: Support the free plan device limit.** A free account can activate at most three active device tokens at once. A tester can attempt a fourth sign-in and observe a blocked state plus an upgrade path.
- **G-7: Preserve privacy expectations.** Note content and attachment bytes are encrypted at rest with AES-256 on device and server when those data paths exist. Network transport uses TLS 1.2 or higher.
- **G-8: Meet accessibility expectations.** The MVP UI passes WCAG 2.1 AA checks on the supported platforms, including keyboard navigation, visible focus, accessible names for controls, contrast, and target size.
- **G-9: Stay within first-release scope.** The MVP includes exactly eight user stories: US-01, US-02, US-03, US-04, US-05, US-06, US-07, and US-12. Any feature outside those eight is either not shipped or explicitly labelled as beta/not supported.

**Non-Goals**

- **NG-1: Real-time collaboration.** The MVP does not support two users editing one note simultaneously, shared notebooks, permissions, comments, or presence indicators.
- **NG-2: Attachments in the MVP.** The MVP does not upload or sync images, PDFs, or other files. Attachments are after-MVP and tied to Inkwell Plus.
- **NG-3: PDF annotation in the MVP.** Highlighting, commenting, drawing, and page-level annotations on PDFs are after-MVP.
- **NG-4: Web clipping in the MVP.** Browser extensions, reader-mode extraction, and saved article metadata are after-MVP.
- **NG-5: Version history in the MVP.** 30-day version history is a Plus feature and is after-MVP. The MVP uses Trash plus sync conflict copies, not full revision history.
- **NG-6: PIN or biometric note locking in the MVP.** Note-level locking is after-MVP.
- **NG-7: Pin and favourite in the MVP.** Pinned and favourited note sorting are after-MVP.
- **NG-8: Export in the MVP.** Markdown and PDF export are after-MVP, even though data ownership is important. Export is deferred to keep the first release testable within 20 weeks.
- **NG-9: Desktop native apps.** The first release supports web, iOS, and Android. Desktop-specific packaging is not in scope.
- **NG-10: Offline attachments.** The first release does not support offline storage or syncing of attachments.
- **NG-11: End-to-end encrypted search on the server.** The first release may rely on local search indexes. Any server-side search or indexing model must be decided in Open Questions.
- **NG-12: Full conflict resolution beyond conflict copies.** The MVP does not merge overlapping text edits automatically. It prevents silent loss by keeping conflict copies.

# 3. Personas

**Maya, university student**

Maya is a third-year undergraduate who lives on a laptop during the day and a phone in the evening. She takes lecture notes on the laptop, then reviews them on the bus, in bed, or before an exam. She is not a power user of file formats, but she is sensitive to friction. If a note app requires a stable connection before she can write, she loses trust. If the sync is slow, she stops trusting the phone version. If search does not work, she rewrites notes by hand.

In the MVP, Maya needs to create and edit notes quickly, keep course notes in notebooks, search by keywords, and work offline. She benefits from trash/restore because students often delete or edit accidentally while reorganising. She does not strongly need PDF annotation or web clips in the first release; she needs a note app that never feels fragile. The MVP choice of notebooks, tags, offline, sync, and trash supports her primary journey. The absence of pin/favourite and export is an acceptable MVP trade-off, although pin/favourite can increase review speed later.

**Daniel, consultant**

Daniel is an independent consultant who holds client knowledge in his notes. He stores meeting notes, decisions, follow-ups, and long-running project context. He has years of notes and needs to find the exact phrase, client name, or decision from an old meeting. His biggest pain is not writing speed; it is retrieval and trust. He avoids cloud tools if he does not understand where client data lives, but he also cannot tolerate losing a note because of a sync bug.

Daniel pushes the product toward notebooks, tags, strong full-text search, offline work, and safe deletion. He also benefits from version history and export, but those are high-effort and after-MVP. The MVP needs to make his core trust loop strong: create a note, search it later, and restore deleted notes. The sync conflict behaviour must be conservative: if two devices edit the same note offline, the app should keep both versions rather than silently choosing one and losing data.

**Aiko, researcher**

Aiko is a research assistant who collects sources from the web, saves PDFs, and writes summaries in her own words. She clips articles, attaches papers, highlights PDFs, and annotates them. In the full product, she is the persona that pushes Inkwell beyond plain notes. She wants stable attachment storage, clean clipping, and annotations that survive sync.

For the MVP, Aiko is not fully served. Inkwell can be useful to her as a place to write text summaries, but it cannot yet be her primary research workflow because web clipping, attachments, PDF annotation, and export are after-MVP. This is a deliberate risk: the first release validates text notes and sync reliability before taking on large binary storage and complex rendering. Aiko should be invited to test only the text-note portions in beta, with clear expectations about what is missing.

# 4. User Stories

### US-01: Create a note

As Maya, I want to create a new note quickly, so that I can capture lecture content without thinking about folders, login, or network state.

- Given the tester is signed in on web, iOS, or Android, when the tester taps “New note”, then an empty editable note appears within 500 ms and is added to the current notebook list within 1 second.
- Given the device is offline, when the tester types at least one visible character into a new note and navigates away, then the note is persisted in the encrypted local database and displays an “Unsynced” status.
- Given the tester creates a note with visible content and then restarts the app or device, when the tester opens the app, then the note appears in the local note list without network access and without requiring sign-in.

### US-02: Edit with Markdown shortcuts

As Maya, I want Markdown shortcuts to work while typing, so that I can format notes without moving my hands away from the keyboard.

- Given the cursor is at the start of an empty paragraph, when the tester types “# ” followed by text, then the paragraph becomes Heading 1 and the literal “# ” is not visible as plain text.
- Given the tester is on a new line, when the tester types “- ” followed by text, then the line becomes a bullet list item, and when the tester types “1. ” followed by text, then the line becomes an ordered list item.
- Given the tester selects existing text, when the tester presses the bold toolbar action or the keyboard shortcut Ctrl/Cmd+B, then the text is wrapped in Markdown bold syntax and rendered as bold, and one undo step restores the previous state.

### US-03: Organise notes in notebooks

As Daniel, I want to move notes into notebooks, so that client or project material is grouped in a predictable place.

- Given the tester is signed in, when the tester creates a notebook named “Clients” with a 7-character name, then the notebook appears in the notebook pane and a note can be assigned to it.
- Given a note exists in notebook “Lectures”, when the tester moves the note to notebook “Meetings”, then the note’s notebook label updates on the current device within 500 ms and the server accepts the change within 10 seconds when the device is online.
- Given notebook “Projects” contains notes, when the tester deletes notebook “Projects” and confirms, then the notebook is removed from the notebook pane and all notes previously in that notebook appear in the default “Unfiled” notebook within 1 second.

### US-04: Tag notes

As Daniel, I want to tag notes, so that I can filter notes by client, topic, or status without relying only on one notebook.

- Given the tester opens a note, when the tester types “meeting” in the tag field and presses Enter, then the tag appears on the note and in the tag navigation area.
- Given the tester saves a tag with leading or trailing spaces, when the tag is persisted, then spaces are trimmed and the tag is matched case-insensitively, so “Client” and “ client ” behave as the same tag.
- Given two notes exist and only one has the tag “client-a”, when the tester selects the tag filter “client-a”, then only the tagged note appears in the result list, including when the device is offline.

### US-05: Full-text search

As Daniel, I want to search across notes quickly, so that I can find an old meeting note by a phrase I remember.

- Given the reference phone contains 10,000 local notes with average visible length of 500 characters and the device is offline, when the tester searches for “budget”, then results render with p95 latency under 500 ms.
- Given a note title contains “Q3 report” and the body contains “Q3-report”, when the tester searches “Q3”, then the note appears in results and the matching substring is visually highlighted in the note preview.
- Given the tester searches while the device is offline, when results are shown, then no server request spinner appears and no server error is displayed for local results.

### US-06: Work offline

As Maya, I want to keep using Inkwell without network, so that airplane mode, campus Wi-Fi failures, or server outages do not stop note-taking.

- Given the tester is signed in, when the tester disables network on the device and launches the app, then the local note list opens without a forced login screen and a recent note can be opened.
- Given the device is offline, when the tester creates a note, edits an existing note, deletes another note, and restarts the app, then all local changes persist and each affected item shows an “Unsynced” or “Offline” state.
- Given the device remains offline for 7 days, when the tester continues to create, edit, delete, and search notes during that period, then all MVP note features remain available from local data.

### US-07: Sync across devices

As Maya, I want notes to sync between my laptop and phone, so that I can write in one place and review in another.

- Given the same account is signed in on two online devices, when the tester creates a note on device A, then the note appears on device B in the correct notebook within 10 seconds.
- Given a free account already has three active devices, when the tester signs in on a fourth device, then the fourth device cannot sync and the UI shows a clear message that the free plan supports up to three devices and offers an upgrade path.
- Given the same note has been edited on two devices while both were offline since their last successful sync, when both devices reconnect, then one current version becomes active and the non-winning edit is preserved as a note titled “Conflict: [original title]” rather than being discarded.

### US-08: Attach images and PDFs

As Aiko, I want to attach images and PDFs to a note, so that the source material lives beside the note.

- Given a Plus account with available attachment storage, when the tester attaches a 5 MB JPEG image to a note, then an image thumbnail appears in the editor and the attachment becomes available on another online Plus device within 10 seconds of the note syncing.
- Given a Plus account has already used 10 GB of attachment storage, when the tester attempts to upload an additional 1 MB PDF, then the upload is rejected with a storage-limit error and no additional attachment appears on either the current device or server.
- Given the device is offline, when the tester attaches an image or PDF smaller than the per-file limit of 20 MB, then the attachment is queued locally and is transferred to the server within 30 seconds after the device reconnects.

### US-09: Clip a web page

As Aiko, I want to clip web pages into Inkwell, so that I can save readable article text for later annotation or summarising.

- Given a signed-in tester uses the supported browser extension on a standard article page, when the tester clicks “Clip”, then a note is created with the page title, source URL, and readable main text containing the first 200 visible words of the article body.
- Given the tester clips a page from an account that has reached the free three-device limit, when the server receives the clip request, then the clip is rejected and the extension shows a message saying the device limit has been reached and that upgrade is required.
- Given the tester clips the same URL twice from the same signed-in account, when both clips complete, then two separate notes are created with distinct creation timestamps, unless the tester confirms an explicit “replace existing clip” action.

### US-10: Annotate a PDF

As Aiko, I want to annotate a PDF inside a note, so that highlights and comments stay with the source document.

- Given a note contains an attached PDF, when the tester selects text on page 2 and adds a highlight with a comment, then the annotation is stored with the page number, normalized text location, comment text, and creation timestamp, and it is visible when the note is reopened.
- Given a synced account with a PDF annotation, when the tester opens the note on a second online device within 10 seconds after sync, then the same highlight and comment appear at the same page and text location.
- Given the tester deletes the PDF attachment and the deletion syncs, when the tester searches for the annotation text in normal notes, then the deleted attachment and its annotations do not appear in search results or previews.

### US-11: Pin and favourite notes

As Maya, I want to pin and favourite important notes, so that I can review key material without hunting through notebooks.

- Given a note list contains three unpinned notes, when the tester pins one note, then the pinned note appears before all unpinned notes in the current notebook view and in the global “All notes” view.
- Given two notes are pinned, when the tester pins a third note, then the pinned notes appear in order of most recent pin action, with the newest pin first.
- Given a note is marked as favourite, when the tester selects the “Favourites” filter, then only favourited notes appear, and favourite status is visible on another online device within 10 seconds.

### US-12: Trash and restore

As Daniel, I want deleted notes to stay recoverable for 30 days, so that I can undo an accidental deletion without contacting support.

- Given a note is visible in a notebook, when the tester chooses “Delete note” and confirms, then the note disappears from normal notebooks and normal search and appears in Trash with a deleted timestamp.
- Given a note has been in Trash for 1 day, when the tester selects “Restore”, then the note returns to its original notebook and appears in normal search on that device within 1 second.
- Given a note has been in Trash for 31 days and is not restored, when the tester checks local and server data, then the note is permanently removed from the local database and server storage for that account.

### US-13: Export notes

As Daniel, I want to export notes as Markdown and PDF, so that my material remains usable outside Inkwell.

- Given a note contains a title, headings, tags, and body content, when the tester chooses “Export Markdown”, then a `.md` file is created containing YAML front matter with `id`, `title`, `notebook`, `tags`, `created_at`, and `updated_at`, followed by the note body in Markdown.
- Given a notebook contains five notes with titles “Alpha”, “Beta”, “Alpha”, “Gamma”, and “Delta”, when the tester exports the notebook, then the ZIP contains five Markdown files, duplicate title collisions are resolved by appending a short unique suffix, and no file is omitted.
- Given a note is open and the tester chooses “Export PDF”, then the system print or PDF flow completes and the generated PDF contains the note title and visible body text without adding tracking pixels or external image requests.

### US-14: Version history

As Daniel, I want 30 days of version history, so that I can recover a useful earlier version of a note after an accidental edit.

- Given a Plus account, when the tester saves edits to the same note during three separate 15-minute windows, then the version history list contains at least one version entry for each distinct editing window and each entry shows its timestamp and first 60 characters of content.
- Given a free account, when the tester opens a note, then no version history control is displayed for normal use, or the control is disabled and shows an upgrade message before creating or restoring a version.
- Given a Plus account, when the tester restores a version from 20 days ago, then the current note is replaced with the selected version and a new version is created containing the immediately prior current content before the restore.

### US-15: Lock a note

As Aiko, I want to lock sensitive notes with a PIN or biometrics, so that a borrowed or lost device does not expose note contents.

- Given the tester enables “Lock this note” and chooses a PIN, when the tester reopens the note, then a PIN screen covers the note content and the note body is not rendered until the correct PIN is entered.
- Given the device supports biometrics and the tester enables biometric unlock, when the tester opens the locked note, then the platform biometric prompt appears and a successful unlock opens the note within 1 second on the reference phone.
- Given the tester enters an incorrect PIN five times, when the fifth failed attempt occurs, then the note remains locked and the app prevents further PIN attempts for 60 seconds.

# 5. Non-Functional Requirements

1. **NFR-1: Note-open performance.** Opening a local note under 1 MB must complete in p95 under 300 ms on a mid-range phone. Reference phones: Pixel 6a running the latest supported Android version, and iPhone 12 running the latest supported iOS version. The test set contains 100 notes each under 1 MB with headings, lists, and plain text. Timing starts when the note row is tapped and ends when the first editable frame is shown.

2. **NFR-2: Search performance.** Search across 10,000 notes must complete in p95 under 500 ms while offline on the reference phones and in the latest two desktop browsers. The test dataset contains 10,000 notes with average visible length of 500 characters, distributed across 20 notebooks and 100 tags. The tester measures 200 searches using common words and client-like strings.

3. **NFR-3: Offline reconnect sync speed.** Offline text edits must sync within 10 seconds of the device reconnecting. The test script creates a text edit while offline, waits 2 minutes offline, re-enables network, and measures the time from the OS reporting connectivity to server acknowledgement and visibility on a second online device. p95 must be under 10 seconds for 100 trials.

4. **NFR-4: Sync service availability.** The sync service must provide 99.9% availability per calendar month. Availability is measured by the percentage of minutes in which the sync API health endpoint and core sync endpoints return healthy responses, excluding pre-announced maintenance windows of no more than 4 hours per month.

5. **NFR-5: Encryption at rest.** Note content and attachment bytes must be encrypted at rest on device and on the server using AES-256. On device, the local database and file cache must be protected by an encrypted-at-rest storage mechanism that can be demonstrated by inspecting the raw files. On server, object storage and databases must use AES-256 encryption for note-content fields and attachment blobs.

6. **NFR-6: Encryption in transit.** All client-server and server-server connections handling notes, auth, sync, attachments, and payments must use TLS 1.2 or higher. A tester can confirm this by scanning the public endpoints and verifying that older protocol versions and weak cipher suites are rejected.

7. **NFR-7: Accessibility.** All MVP UI on web, iOS, and Android must conform to WCAG 2.1 AA. The tester must pass automated axe checks on web, VoiceOver on iOS, and TalkBack on Android for note list, editor, notebook management, tag management, search, trash, and settings flows.

8. **NFR-8: Supported platforms.** The MVP supports the two latest major versions of iOS and Android, and the latest two versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari on desktop. A tester can verify the test matrix exists, is executed, and has no P0 or P1 bugs on the supported versions.

9. **NFR-9: Free device limit.** Free accounts must be limited to three active authenticated device tokens. A tester can sign in on three devices and confirm sync works on all three, then sign in on a fourth and confirm the fourth cannot sync, sees the device-limit message, and sees an upgrade path.

10. **NFR-10: Offline persistence duration.** The local database must retain MVP note content, notebook assignment, tags, and trash state for at least 30 days without network access. The tester creates notes, goes offline for 30 simulated or accelerated test-clock days, reopens the app, and verifies data remains accessible.

11. **NFR-11: Local save latency.** Local saving after a user pause must complete in p95 under 200 ms on the reference phones. The tester types a 200-character note, waits 500 ms, and measures time from the save trigger to local write acknowledgement.

12. **NFR-12: App cold start.** App cold start to the note list must complete in p95 under 2 seconds on the reference phones after a normal sign-in state exists. Cold start means the app process is killed and relaunched without network.

13. **NFR-13: Sync conflict safety.** When the same note is changed on multiple devices offline, the sync system must preserve all non-duplicate content by creating conflict copies rather than silently discarding edits. A tester can prove this by editing the same note on two offline devices, reconnecting both, and verifying that two notes are present and the original non-winning text remains recoverable.

14. **NFR-14: Trash retention enforcement.** Trashed notes must be retained for 30 days and purged after 31 days unless restored. The tester uses a controlled test clock or staging system to verify retention and purge behaviour on device and server.

15. **NFR-15: Local storage size.** A user dataset of 10,000 text notes averaging 500 characters must occupy under 100 MB of local storage, excluding attachments because attachments are out of MVP scope. The tester installs a seeded dataset and inspects the app storage report.

16. **NFR-16: Telemetry privacy.** Product analytics and crash reporting must not collect note text, attachment bytes, clip URLs, search queries, or tag values. The tester runs a scripted MVP journey and captures analytics and crash payloads for review; all forbidden content must be absent or truncated with no recoverable note content.

17. **NFR-17: Error handling for failed sync.** If the server is unavailable, the app must keep changes locally and queue them. After three consecutive sync failures, the UI shows a non-blocking warning but still allows local editing. The tester blocks the sync endpoint and verifies that note content remains editable.

18. **NFR-18: Time zones.** Timestamps must be stored in UTC and displayed in the device’s local time zone. A tester changes the phone time zone after creating notes and verifies that note timestamps display correctly without shifting stored content.

# 6. Success Metrics

| Metric | Definition | Target at 6 months after launch |
|---|---:|---:|
| Activation within 7 days | Percentage of new accounts that create at least one note with 50 or more visible characters and complete one successful sync event on at least two devices within 7 days of signup. | 35% |
| Day-30 retention | Percentage of accounts that launch the app and complete a successful sync event between day 20 and day 30 after account creation. | 25% |
| Search usage | Percentage of active accounts that run at least one full-text search per week for 4 consecutive weeks within the first 6 months. | 35% |
| Offline sync reliability | Percentage of offline edit events that reach server sync acknowledgement within 10 seconds of the device reconnecting. | 95% |
| Plus conversion | Percentage of active accounts that complete at least 30 consecutive days of paid Inkwell Plus subscription during the first 6 months. | 3% |

# 7. MVP Cut

### In the MVP

- US-01: Create a note
- US-02: Edit with Markdown shortcuts
- US-03: Organise notes in notebooks
- US-04: Tag notes
- US-05: Full-text search
- US-06: Work offline
- US-07: Sync across devices
- US-12: Trash and restore

### After the MVP

- US-08: Attach images and PDFs
- US-09: Clip a web page
- US-10: Annotate a PDF
- US-11: Pin and favourite notes
- US-13: Export notes
- US-14: Version history
- US-15: Lock a note

### Risks of the Cut

The MVP includes the five stories required for any trustworthy text-note app: creation, editing, search, offline, and sync. It also adds exactly three more stories because the personas and the 20-week release window point to three different non-negotiable gaps. US-03 and US-04 are chosen because organisation is not optional for Daniel and Maya. Daniel cannot live only in one flat list when he has years of client material; Maya needs course or project grouping, but tags give her a fast secondary filter. A flat note list would make the first release feel incomplete to the personas even if creation and sync worked perfectly. US-12 is chosen because data loss is the fastest way to destroy trust in a privacy product. Accidental deletion is common, and the free plan cannot afford support tickets saying “your note is gone.” Trash for 30 days is a clear, testable promise.

US-11, pin and favourite, was cut because it is useful but not blocking for the core loop. Maya may review pinned notes, but she can still create notebooks and search. The cost of pin/favourite is not only sorting logic; it introduces persistent state sync, notebook-view sorting, global view sorting, and accessibility testing. At week 20, it is acceptable to validate whether people use notebooks and search first.

US-13, export notes, was cut despite the product’s privacy positioning. Export is a privacy and data-ownership feature, and its absence is the most serious strategic trade-off. Markdown export looks simple, but PDF export creates real work: rendering fidelity, print styles, attachment handling, mobile share behaviour, and test coverage across iOS, Android, and browsers. For the first public beta, the company is choosing reliability over portability. The mitigation is to make export the first high-priority item after MVP and to state clearly in beta materials that export is not available yet. If beta users reject this, the next release may need to prioritise Markdown-only export before attachments or clipping.

US-08, US-09, and US-10 were cut because Aiko’s full research workflow depends on large binary files, extraction logic, rendering, and annotations. Attachments require storage quota, upload retry, file encryption, server-side storage costs, and offline queueing. Clipping requires browser extensions, reader-mode quality, and repeated tests on messy pages. PDF annotation requires page coordinates, text locations, rendering, and export behaviour. These are not 20-week MVP features; they are entire product surfaces. Cutting them means Aiko is only partially represented in beta, and her feedback will focus on what is missing rather than whether the core is good. That is acceptable only if the company communicates that the beta is a text-notes preview.

US-14, version history, was cut because it directly conflicts with the first-release scope. Version history is one of the main Plus differentiators, but it requires server-side snapshots, retention, restore, UI, and cost controls. If the MVP ships without version history, the company can still enforce the free three-device limit, but the perceived value of Plus is weak. This is the main monetisation risk. The mitigation is to prepare attachments and version history for the first release after MVP and to avoid overselling Plus benefits in launch copy until they are available.

US-15, note locking, was cut because it interacts with search, previews, local database permissions, and platform secure storage. Locking a note sounds simple, but “locked” can mean different things: hide preview, exclude from global search, require unlock after app background, require unlock after device unlock, or encrypt a separate note key. Those decisions change the architecture. The first release should use device-level and app-level privacy, then add note locking only after the local storage model is stable.

The biggest architectural risk introduced by the cut is sync conflict behaviour. To avoid silent data loss, the MVP uses whole-note conflict copies when the same note is edited offline on multiple devices. This is safer than last-write-wins, but it can create clutter and confuse users. If the startup later moves to paragraph merging or a CRDT, it should preserve this guarantee: no offline edit disappears without an obvious conflict artifact. If conflict copy behaviour is not accepted, the first release should not ship sync.

# 8. Open Questions

- Do we store search indexes on the server for cross-device search, or only on each device? If search is local-only, how do we explain that a new device cannot search old notes until they have been synced and indexed?
- Should server-side sync store note content as encrypted opaque blobs, or should it store structured Markdown for version history, conflict copies, and search? This affects encryption boundaries and cost.
- Which sync transport do we use: WebSockets, long polling, push notifications, or server-sent events? The choice affects iOS background sync, Android battery, and reconnect timing.
- What exactly counts as an “active device” for the free plan? Do we use device tokens, install UUIDs, authenticated sessions, or seats? How do we allow users to deactivate a lost phone?
- What is the sync model for rich-text notes? Is the note a single document string, a block list, or a tree of blocks? This determines conflict copies, rendering, and performance.
- Do locked notes in US-15 disappear from full-text search, notebook lists, and previews, or can their titles be shown? Should the title itself be encrypted until unlock?
- What are the attachment per-file, total, and thumbnail rules? Is the 20 MB per-file limit final, and what happens when users attach many small files versus one large PDF?
- Which storage provider and regions do we use for attachments, and what EU data residency requirements apply?
- How frequent should version-history snapshots be? Every save, every 15 minutes, every edit session, or only daily? This affects storage cost and user expectations.
- Is the free plan allowed to include any attachments at all? If attachments are Plus-only, should free users see upload options that prompt to upgrade, or should upload controls be hidden?
- Which browsers must be supported for web clipping? Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Brave, or a smaller subset?
- What analytics events are necessary to measure the success metrics without collecting private note content? Do we need an event schema review with design, privacy, and engineering?
- Do we offer a Plus trial at launch? If so, how is it communicated while attachments and version history are not yet available?
- Should the app include a Markdown-only export as a hidden feature, a debug feature, or a public fast-follow feature? This determines whether data ownership is a launch message or a week-20 roadmap item.
- Do we support desktop browsers as the full web experience without keyboard shortcuts that conflict with browser shortcuts, or do we provide a custom keyboard layout?
- What is the deletion retention policy for account deletion? How quickly must device and server copies be purged after a user deletes their account?
